[[8:17|and bore our diseases|Et ægrotationes portavit]], that is, He bore our sicknesses lovingly in others, and healed them by suffering with them; as the Apostle says: [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another’s burdens|Alter alterius onera portate]]. Yet there was not in Christ bodily infirmity arising from an ill-disposed constitution, according to Damascene. He did not, then, take on all our defects, but only those which are not contrary to the integrity and perfection of nature.

paras.t: Videns autem Jesus turbas multas circa se : quia ut dicit Marcus, tota civitas erat congregata ad januam; jussit ire secum discipulos suos trans fretum, id est ultra mare Galilææ, quod juxta Capharnaum decurrebat. Abiit ergo navigio a Capharnaum in locum desertum, ut Lucas et Marcus commemorant, ut doceret nos humanam laudem et gloriam fugere, tunc præsertim quando magnum aliquid egimus, et magis ab universis cum admiratione inspicimur. Quum enim prædicta miracula faceret, omnes in ejus præconium proruperunt. Dæmones quoque copiose clamabant, dicentes, Tu es Christus et Filius Dei, sicut alii referunt Evangelistæ. Alia ratio fuit, ut daret prædicatoribus ac prælatis exemplum sæpius recedendi a strepitu populi ad locum secretum, ad vacandum contemplationi ac orationi, ut sic repleantur gratia illustrationis divinæ, et quæ divinitus perceperunt, aliis affectuose eructent.
paras.en: [[8:18|And Jesus seeing great multitudes about him|Videns autem Jesus turbas multas circa se]], because, as Mark says, [[Mark 1:33|all the city was gathered together at the door|tota civitas erat congregata ad januam]], [[8:18|gave orders to pass over the water|jussit ire trans fretum]], His disciples with Him, that is, beyond the sea of Galilee, which flowed by Capharnaum. He went away by boat, then, from Capharnaum to a desert place, as Luke and Mark record[[Luke 4:42||]][[Mark 1:35||]], to teach us to flee human praise and glory, especially when we have done something great and are looked on by all with admiration. For when He worked the miracles described, all broke out in His praise. The demons too cried out abundantly, saying, Thou art Christ and the Son of God, as the other Evangelists relate[[Mark 1:24||]][[Luke 4:41||]]. Another reason was to give preachers and prelates an example of withdrawing often from the noise of the people to a secret place, to be free for contemplation and prayer, so that they may thus be filled with the grace of divine enlightenment, and pour out lovingly to others what they have received from God.

paras.t: Et accedens ad Jesum unus Scriba, id est eruditus in lege, ait illi : Magister, sequar te quocumque ieris, id est, tibi inseparabiliter adhærebo. Qua intentione hoc dixerit, ex subsequenti Christi responsione elicitur. Et dicit ei Jesus : Vulpes foveas habent, id est latibula sua sub terra, et volucres cœli ærii, in quo volant, habent nidos, in quibus quiescunt et pullos enutriunt; Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet, id est propriam domum. Sed nonne Maria, quæ erat unica suis parentibus, ex parte patris habuit domum parentum suorum? et Joseph (qui adhuc vixit, secundum quosdam) propriam habuit domum? Et respondendum, probabile esse quod Virgo beata omnia sua vendidit, egenisque contulit, similiter Joseph : aliter non implessent quod Christus edocuit alios, et Apostoli perfecerunt, qui relictis omnibus secuti sunt Christum. Christus ergo in summa vixit inopia, proprio carens hospitio. Propter quod Jeremias vehementer admirans, ait ad eum : Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum ! Quare venturus es quasi vir vagus? Quæritur, cur Christus pauperem vitam elegit. Dicendum : Primo, ut Scripturas Prophetarum impleret. Sic enim primus Christi adventus in paupertate describitur : Exsulta satis, filia Sion ; ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus et salvator, ipse pauper. Et in Psalmo : Pauper sum ego, et in laboribus a juventute mea. Unde patet cæcitas Judæorum exspectantium regem Messiam in primo suo adventu temporaliter regnaturum, et omnia regna sæculi possessurum. Secundo, ut faceret quod docere volebat. Venit enim ut mundi ac divitiarum prædicaret contemptum : non ergo debuit eas habere. Tertio, ut non solum verbis, sed etiam rebus futuri sæculi vitam doceret. Per hoc enim quod omnia temporalia contemnuntur, maxime declaratur esse vita alia post præsentem. Quarto, ne putaretur collatione divitiarum attraxisse sibi discipulos. Quinto, ut merito suæ paupertatis, veras divitias consequamur, quemadmodum dicit Apostolus : Propter nos egenus factus est, quum dives esset, ut illius inopia divites efficeremur.
paras.en: [[8:19|And a certain scribe came|Et accedens ad Jesum unus Scriba]], that is, one learned in the law, [[8:19|and said to him: Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou shalt go|ait illi : Magister, sequar te quocumque ieris]], that is, I will cleave to Thee inseparably. With what intention he said this is drawn from Christ’s answer that follows. [[8:20|And Jesus saith to him: The foxes have holes|Et dicit ei Jesus : Vulpes foveas habent]], that is, their lurking places under the earth, [[8:20|and the birds of the air nests|et volucres cœli ærii, in quo volant, habent nidos]], of the air, in which they fly, have nests in which they rest and rear their young; [[8:20|but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head|Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet]], that is, a house of His own. But did not Mary, who was the only child of her parents, have on her father’s side the house of her parents? And did not Joseph (who, according to some, was still alive) have a house of his own? It must be answered that it is probable that the Blessed Virgin sold all she had and gave it to the needy, and likewise Joseph; otherwise they would not have fulfilled what Christ taught others and the Apostles carried out, who left all things and followed Christ[[Matt 19:27||]]. Christ, then, lived in the greatest want, lacking a lodging of His own. For this reason Jeremias, greatly wondering, says to Him: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?|Quare quasi colonus futurus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum?]] Why wilt Thou be as a wandering man? It is asked why Christ chose a poor life. It must be said: first, to fulfil the Scriptures of the Prophets. For so the first coming of Christ is described in poverty: [[Zach 9:9|Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Sion|Exsulta satis, filia Sion]]; [[Zach 9:9|BEHOLD THY KING will come to thee, the just and saviour: he is poor|ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus et salvator, ipse pauper]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:16|I am poor, and in labours from my youth|Pauper sum ego, et in laboribus a juventute mea]]. Hence the blindness of the Jews is plain, who expect the King Messias in His first coming to reign temporally and to possess all the kingdoms of the world. Secondly, to do what He wished to teach. For He came to preach contempt of the world and of riches; He ought not, then, to have them. Thirdly, to teach the life of the world to come not only by words but also by deeds. For by the very fact that all temporal things are despised it is most clearly declared that there is another life after the present. Fourthly, lest He be thought to have drawn disciples to Himself by giving them riches. Fifthly, that by the merit of His poverty we may obtain true riches, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 8:9|that being rich he became poor for your sakes: that through his poverty you might be rich|Propter nos egenus factus est, quum dives esset, ut illius inopia divites efficeremur]].

paras.t: Ex prædicta Christi responsione elicitur, quod Scriba perversa intentione dixit, Sequar te, utpote quatenus conversando cum Christo congregaret sibi divitias. Quoniam enim litteratus fuit, cogitavit multis infirmis sanitatem a Christo acquirere, inducendo Christum ad sanationem illorum : sicque volebat pecuniam multam a sanatis colligere. Simili intentione Simon magus dixit Petro et Joanni : Date mihi hanc potestatem, ut cuicumque manus imposuero, recipiat Spiritum Sanctum. Jesus itaque videns mentem illius, repulit eum, dicendo : Vulpes foveas habent, etc., id est, quum ego tantam paupertatem elegerim, quid quæris mecum conversando congregare divitias ?
paras.en: From Christ’s answer it is drawn that the Scribe said, I will follow thee, with a perverse intention, namely so that by living with Christ he might gather riches for himself. For since he was a learned man, he thought to obtain health from Christ for many sick people by leading Christ to heal them; and so he wished to collect much money from those healed. With a like intention Simon Magus said to Peter and John: [[Acts 8:19|Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I shall lay my hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost|Date mihi hanc potestatem, ut cuicumque manus imposuero, recipiat Spiritum Sanctum]]. Jesus, therefore, seeing his mind, repulsed him, saying: [[8:20|The foxes have holes|Vulpes foveas habent]], etc.; that is, since I have chosen such poverty, why seekest thou to gather riches by living with Me?

paras.t: Alius autem de discipulis ejus, scilicet Jesu Christi, ait illi : Domine, permitte me primum, id est, antequam te inseparabiliter sequar, ire et sepelire patrem meum. Quidam dicunt istud non esse intelligendum, quasi pater hujus discipuli jam defunctus fuisset, et ipse ad sepeliendum patrem ire rogasset, quia hoc ei negatum non esset, quum sit opus pietatis; sed quod discipulus iste tenebatur carnali amore parentum, cum quibus usque ad mortem eorum voluit permanere, eisque sepultis Christo adhærere. Verumtamen Ambrosius, Isidorus, et Glossa super Lucam dicunt, quod pater discipuli hujus mortuus fuit, et ipse ad patris sepulturam ire optavit : quod magis consonat litteræ. Nec ratio illa concludit, videlicet, quod sepelitio patris non fuisset negata discipulo, quum sit opus pietatis. Nam apud divum Lucam. ubi factum istud narratur, alius legitur Christo dixisse : Sequar te, Domine, sed primum permitte mihi renuntiare his quæ domi sunt. Quod quamvis bonum sit, tamen Christus ei id negavit, propter periculum moræ. Similiter negavit huic patris sepelitionem, non quia mala, sed quia majoris boni impeditiva. Dicit itaque Ambrosius : Docet Christus minora bona pro utilitate esse prætermittenda. Majus est enim animas mortuas prædicando suscitare, quam corpus mortui in terra abscondere. Unde elicitur, quod quando parentes aliunde habere possunt sustentaculum vitæ, vel sepulturam, filii non impediuntur a religionis ingressu.
paras.en: [[8:21|And another of his disciples|Alius autem de discipulis ejus]], namely of Jesus Christ, [[8:21|said to him: Lord, suffer me first|ait illi : Domine, permitte me primum]], that is, before I follow Thee inseparably, [[8:21|to go and bury my father|ire et sepelire patrem meum]]. Some say that this is not to be understood as though the father of this disciple were already dead and he had asked to go and bury his father, because this would not have been refused him, since it is a work of piety; but that this disciple was held by carnal love of his parents, with whom he wished to remain until their death, and when they were buried to cleave to Christ. But Ambrose, Isidore and the Gloss on Luke say that this disciple’s father was dead and that he wished to go to his father’s burial; which agrees better with the letter. Nor is that reason conclusive, namely that the burial of his father would not have been refused the disciple because it is a work of piety. For in blessed Luke, where this deed is related, another is read to have said to Christ: [[Luke 9:61|I will follow thee, Lord; but let me first take my leave of them that are at my house|Sequar te, Domine, sed primum permitte mihi renuntiare his quæ domi sunt]]. Though this was good, yet Christ refused it him because of the danger of delay[[Luke 9:62||]]. In like manner He refused this one the burial of his father, not because it was evil but because it hindered a greater good. So Ambrose says: “Christ teaches that lesser goods are to be passed over for the sake of usefulness. For it is greater to raise dead souls by preaching than to hide the body of a dead man in the earth.” From this it is drawn that when parents can have the sustenance of life or burial from elsewhere, children are not hindered from entering religion.

paras.t: Jesus autem ait illi : Sequere me mentis affectu, operis imitatione, et corporis gressu. Nec obviat quod secundum Lucam Christus dixit, Vade et annuntia regnum Dei : quia hoc erat Christum sequi operis imitatione, corporaliter vero sequebatur eum sæpe seu congruis horis. Et dimitte mortuos, scilicet morte culpæ (sicut de vidua deliciosa dicit Apostolus, Vivens mortua est; et Joannes in Apocalypsi, Nomen, inquit, habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es), sepelire mortuos suos morte naturæ.
paras.en: [[8:22|But Jesus said to him: Follow me|Jesus autem ait illi : Sequere me]], with the affection of the mind, the imitation of works, and the steps of the body. Nor does it stand in the way that according to Luke Christ said, [[Luke 9:60|go thou and preach the kingdom of God|Vade et annuntia regnum Dei]]: for this was to follow Christ by the imitation of works; and he followed Him bodily often, or at fitting times. [[8:22|and let the dead|Et dimitte mortuos]], namely by the death of guilt (as the Apostle says of the pleasure-loving widow, [[1 Tim 5:6|is dead while she is living|Vivens mortua est]]; and John in the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 3:1|thou hast the name of being alive. And thou art dead|Nomen, inquit, habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es]]), [[8:22|bury their dead|sepelire mortuos suos]], by the death of nature.

paras.t: Et ascendente eo, videlicet Christo, in naviculam. Nunquam legitur Christus intrasse navim cortinatam negotiatorum aut piratorum, sed naviculam aut navim piscatorum : in quo ejus humilitas commendatur. Secuti sunt eum discipuli ejus, quia cum eo ingressi sunt navim, ut legitur in Luca. Secundum Origenem, Christus quum multa et magna fecisset in terra, perrexit ad mare, ut ibidem excellentiora opera demonstraret, quatenus terræ marisque Dominum se ostenderet. Ascendit autem in naviculam, ut pergeret ad locum secretiorem, et populum fugeret, propter causas paulo ante prætactas. Secundum Hieronymum, iste ascensus Christi in naviculam fuit quando exivit Capharnaum. Sed hoc intelligendum non est de exitu facto statim post sanationem socrus Petri. De navigatione namque seu transfretatione post illum exitum immediate prædictum est. Post quam rursus introivit Capharnaum post dies octo, ut habet Marcus. Et postea egressus Capharnaum, quum fecisset sermonem de parabola seminis eodem die, videlicet tempore vespertino, ingrediebatur naviculam istam, ut patet in Marco.
paras.en: [[8:23|And when he entered into the boat|Et ascendente eo, videlicet Christo, in naviculam]], namely Christ. Christ is never read to have entered a curtained ship of merchants or pirates, but a little boat or a fishermen’s ship; in which His humility is commended. [[8:23|his disciples followed him|Secuti sunt eum discipuli ejus]], because they went into the boat with Him, as we read in Luke[[Luke 8:22||]]. According to Origen, Christ, having done many great things on land, went on to the sea, to show still more excellent works there, so as to show Himself Lord of land and sea. And He went up into the boat to go to a more secret place and to flee the people, for the reasons touched on a little before. According to Jerome, this going up of Christ into the boat was when He went out of Capharnaum. But this is not to be understood of the going out made immediately after the healing of Peter’s mother-in-law. For the voyage or crossing immediately after that going out has been spoken of already[[8:18||]]. After it He entered Capharnaum again after eight days, as Mark has it[[Mark 2:1||]]. And afterwards, going out of Capharnaum, when He had given the sermon on the parable of the seed on the same day, namely in the evening, He went into this boat, as is plain in Mark[[Mark 4:35||]][[Mark 4:36||]].

paras.t: Et ecce motus magnus factus est in mari, id est in stagno Genesareth, ultra quod transfretavit : quod dicitur mare, juxta proprietatem idiomatis Hebræorum, qui quamlibet magnam collectionem aquarum, nominant mare, eo quod in Genesi legitur : Congregationes aquarum appellavit Deus maria. Motus hic maris creditur suscitatus magis virtute divina seu miraculose, quam naturaliter, ut Christi potentia atque divinitas panderentur per motionis hujusmodi sedationem. Naturaliter autem motus maris generatur ex vaporibus inferioribus aquarum ascendentibus, et vento flante ac occurrente in ære. Ita ut navicula operiretur fluctibus maris; nam aqua eam abundanter ingrediebatur. Ipse vero Jesus dormiebat in puppi super cervical, ut Marcus habet. Dormiebat autem secundum assumptam humanitatem, ut ejus veritatem ostenderet, et futurum miraculum gloriosius exhiberet; non secundum divinitatem, juxta illud in Psalmo : Ecce non dormitabit neque dormiet, qui custodit Isræl. Denique, secundum partem sensitivam, non secundum portionem intellectivam dormivit, juxta illud : Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat.
paras.en: [[8:24|And behold a great tempest arose in the sea|Et ecce motus magnus factus est in mari]], that is, in the lake of Genesareth, across which He crossed; which is called a sea according to the idiom of the Hebrews, who call any great gathering of waters a sea, because we read in Genesis: [[Gen 1:10|the gathering together of the waters, he called Seas|Congregationes aquarum appellavit Deus maria]]. This movement of the sea is believed to have been stirred up by divine power, or miraculously, rather than naturally, so that Christ’s power and Godhead might be made known by the calming of such a movement. Naturally, the movement of the sea is produced by vapours rising from the lower waters, and by wind blowing and meeting them in the air. [[8:24|so that the boat was covered with waves|Ita ut navicula operiretur fluctibus]] of the sea; for the water came into it abundantly. [[8:24|but he was asleep|Ipse vero Jesus dormiebat]], Jesus, in the stern, on a pillow, as Mark has it[[Mark 4:38||]]. He slept according to the humanity He had taken, to show its reality and to display the coming miracle more gloriously; not according to the Godhead, according to the words of the Psalm: [[Ps 120:4|Behold he shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel|Ecce non dormitabit neque dormiet, qui custodit Israel]]. Moreover, He slept according to the sensitive part, not according to the intellectual portion, according to the words: [[Cant 5:2|I sleep, and my heart watcheth|Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat]].

paras.t: Et accesserunt discipuli, et suscitaverunt eum, dicentes : Domine, salva nos, id est, a tempestate hac libera ; perimus hoc est, mergi incipimus. Et dicit eis Jesus : Quid timidi estis, inordinato timore qui ex defectu fidei oritur, non solum timore naturali qui ex imminentia periculi nascitur, modicæ fidei, id est, vos qui adhuc parvam, sed tamen aliquantulam fidem habetis? Quod enim dixerunt, Domine, salva nos, ex fide manavit, qua crediderunt eum esse Dei Filium, et ad salvandum potentem ; quod vero dixerunt, Perimus ex timore et pusillanimitate processit : quod autem suscitaverunt eum, ex ignorantia et fidei imperfectione descendit. Putabant enim quod Christo dormienti, minus innotescerent omnia, quam vigilanti quasi somnus actum rationis impediret in ipso. Unde increpari et audire meruerunt: Quid timidi estis, modicæ fidei? Nempe si magnæ fidei exstitissent, imperassent et ipsi tempestati, moxque cessasset, prout alibi ait Salvator : Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti, Tollere, et mitte te in mare, et obediet vobis.
paras.en: [[8:25|And they came to him, and awaked him, saying: Lord, save us|Et accesserunt discipuli, et suscitaverunt eum, dicentes : Domine, salva nos]], that is, deliver us from this tempest; [[8:25|we perish|perimus]], that is, we are beginning to sink. [[8:26|And Jesus saith to them: Why are you fearful|Et dicit eis Jesus : Quid timidi estis]] with a disordered fear that arises from a lack of faith, not only with the natural fear that springs from the nearness of danger, [[8:26|O ye of little faith?|modicæ fidei]], that is, you who still have little faith, yet some? For their saying, Lord, save us, flowed from faith, by which they believed Him to be the Son of God and mighty to save; but their saying, We perish, proceeded from fear and faintheartedness; and their waking Him came from ignorance and imperfection of faith. For they thought that all things were less known to Christ asleep than awake, as if sleep hindered the act of reason in Him. Hence they deserved to be rebuked and to hear: Why are you fearful, O ye of little faith? For if they had been of great faith, they too would have commanded the tempest and it would have ceased at once; as the Saviour says elsewhere: [[Matt 17:19|if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain|Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti]][[Matt 21:21||]][[Mark 11:23||]][[Luke 17:6||]]: Remove, and cast thyself into the sea, and it will obey you.

paras.t: Tunc surgens Jesus a somno, et puppi, seu loco dormitionis, imperavit, id est per modum imperantis potenter injunxit, mari, id est commotioni tempestatique maris, et ventis, ut cessarent ; et facta est tranquillitas magna, id est plena quies a procella præfata, in instanti, quoniam virtus divinitatis Christi quum sit infinita, agit in instanti. In quo opere Christus suæ divinitatis omnipotentiam demonstravit. Nam vento et mari imperare, et imperialiter subjecta habere ad nutum, non convenit nisi vero Deo. Propter quod Marcus, ut istud miraculum gloriosius commendaret, sic ait : Surgens, comminatus est vento, et dixit mari : Tace et obmutesce. In isto fundatur positio theologorum, ponentium in omni natura creata potentiam obedientialem, qua suo Creatori ad nutum obedit in omnibus.
paras.en: [[8:26|Then rising up|Tunc surgens]], Jesus, from sleep and from the stern, or the place of sleeping, [[8:26|he commanded|imperavit]], that is, enjoined powerfully in the manner of one commanding, [[8:26|the winds, and the sea|mari, id est commotioni tempestatique maris, et ventis]], that is, the commotion and tempest of the sea, that they should cease; [[8:26|and there came a great calm|et facta est tranquillitas magna]], that is, full quiet from the storm described, in an instant, since the power of Christ’s Godhead, being infinite, acts in an instant. In this work Christ showed the omnipotence of His Godhead. For to command the wind and the sea, and to have them subject to one’s nod as a ruler, befits none but the true God. For this reason Mark, to commend this miracle more gloriously, says thus: [[Mark 4:39|And rising up, he rebuked the wind, and said to the sea: Peace, be still|Surgens, comminatus est vento, et dixit mari : Tace et obmutesce]]. On this is founded the position of the theologians who place in every created nature an obediential potency [potentia obedientialis, the capacity of a creature to be raised by God beyond its natural powers], by which it obeys its Creator at His nod in all things.

paras.t: Porro homines exsistentes in navi, mirati sunt, viso tanto prodigio, dicentes : Qualis est hic? quasi dicant : Aliquid supra hominem apparet in eo, videlicet, quod sit Deus, vel Deo carissimus, ac summe familiaris. Quia venti et mare obediunt ei : de quo scriptum est, Tu dominaris potestati maris, motum autem fluctuum ejus tu mitigas. Inanimata autem proprie non obediunt nisi Deo, per auctoritatem. Si ceteris obedire dicantur in his quæ sunt supra naturam, intelligendum est, per ministerium, secundum Hieronymum et Bedam. Quod dicitur, Porro homines mimirati sunt, non de discipulis Christi, sed de nautis et aliis qui aderant intelligendum est. Aliis vero satis probabiliter videtur, quod de discipulis quoque hoc ipsum dicatur : quod ex verbis Marci et Lucæ sequi putatur. Miratio enim consurgit ex inspectione effectus et ignorantia causæ : quemadmodum homines videntes lunam eclipsari, et causam eclipsis ignorantes, mirari cœperunt. Quum ergo causa perfecte cognoscitur, cessat miratio : idcirco astrologus eclipsim non admiratur ut rusticus. Discipuli autem nondum cognoverant Christi divinitatem, cujus virtute facta sunt hæc. Ipsi ergo mimirati sunt, quamvis minus quam alii, quoniam magis soliti erant videre miracula Christi.
paras.en: [[8:27|But the men|Porro homines]] who were in the boat [[8:27|wondered|mirati sunt]], at the sight of so great a wonder, [[8:27|saying: What manner of man is this|dicentes : Qualis est hic]]? as if they said: Something above man appears in Him, namely that He is God, or most dear to God and supremely familiar with Him. [[8:27|for the winds and the sea obey him?|Quia venti et mare obediunt ei]]; of whom it is written: [[Ps 88:10|Thou rulest the power of the sea: and appeasest the motion of the waves thereof|Tu dominaris potestati maris, motum autem fluctuum ejus tu mitigas]]. Inanimate things properly obey no one but God, by authority. If they are said to obey others in things above nature, it is to be understood by way of ministry, according to Jerome and Bede. That it is said, But the men wondered, is to be understood not of Christ’s disciples but of the sailors and others who were present. To others, however, it seems quite probable that this is said of the disciples too; which is thought to follow from the words of Mark and Luke[[Mark 4:40||]][[Luke 8:25||]]. For wonder arises from seeing an effect and not knowing its cause; as men seeing the moon eclipsed, and not knowing the cause of the eclipse, began to wonder. When, then, the cause is perfectly known, wonder ceases; hence the astronomer does not wonder at an eclipse as the countryman does. But the disciples had not yet known the Godhead of Christ, by whose power these things were done. They therefore wondered, though less than the others, because they were more used to seeing Christ’s miracles.

paras.t: Præterea, per naviculam quidam mystice intelligunt crucem, in qua Salvator moriendo dormivit : quam secum ascenderunt discipuli, postmodum tollentes crucem suam quotidie. Quo pendente in cruce, facta est magna in mundo tempestas, quia a sexta hora usque ad nonam tenebræ factæ sunt, terra mota est, Apostoli quoque turbati fuerunt, suscitaveruntque Christum, ejus resurrectionem optando. Quo resurgente, magna cordis tranquillitas data est Christi discipulis. Chrysostomus per navim intelligit Ecclesiam, id est congregationem fidelium, ad quam Christus descendit per incarnationem et conversationem cum ea. Ipsa quoque portavit Christum, prædicando eum per totum mundum, qui est mare magnum de quo ait Salvator in Psalmo : Veni in altitudinem maris. Christo autem hanc navim ingresso, tentationum et adversitatum commotio irruit suÀ per discipulos; sed clamando ad Christum evaserunt. Navis enim Petri concuti potest, non mergi. Sic et nos in omni gravi tribulatione clamemus ad Christum, dicentes : Domine, salva nos, perimus.
paras.en: Further, by the boat some understand mystically the cross, on which the Saviour slept in dying; which the disciples went up into with Him, afterwards taking up their cross daily[[Luke 9:23||]]. While He hung on the cross a great tempest arose in the world, since from the sixth hour to the ninth there was darkness[[Matt 27:45||]], the earth was moved[[Matt 27:51||]], and the Apostles too were troubled, and they woke Christ by longing for His resurrection. When He rose again, great tranquillity of heart was given to Christ’s disciples. Chrysostom understands by the ship the Church, that is, the congregation of the faithful, to which Christ came down by the incarnation and by living with it. It too has carried Christ, preaching Him through the whole world[[Mark 16:20||]], which is the great sea of which the Saviour says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:3|I am come into the depth of the sea|Veni in altitudinem maris]]. When Christ had entered this ship, the commotion of temptations and adversities fell upon the disciples; but by crying to Christ they escaped. For the ship of Peter can be shaken, not sunk. So let us too, in every grave tribulation, cry to Christ, saying: [[8:25|Lord, save us, we perish|Domine, salva nos, perimus]].

paras.t: Et quum venisset Jesus cum discipulis, ttrans fretum, id est ultra stagnum seu mare prædictum, 22 regionem Gerasenorum, quæ erat ex alio littore hujus maris. Et dicitur regio Gerasenorum a principali civitate terræ illius, quæ dicitur Gerasa, vel Geneser. Occurrerunt ei duo homines habentes dæmonia : quia quilibet eorum, vel saltem unus, a multis dæmonibus fuit obsessus. Lucas enim refert, quod legio dæmonum fuit in eo. Marcus vero et Lucas non loquuntur nisi de uno habente dæmonia ; sed non est contradictio inter eos et Matthæum, quoniam numerus minor non excludit majorem, neque econtra. De monumentis exeuntes : quia non habitabant in domibus, sed in fossis factis pro sepultura; sævi nimis, id est valde feroces in se et in alios, quoniam a dæmonibus obsessi erant, quibus data fuit a Deo licentia exercendi crudelitatem magnam per homines istos ab ipsis obsessos. Et tam sævi erant, ita ut nemo posset illæsus atque securus transire per viam illam.
paras.en: [[8:28|And when he was come on the other side of the water|Et cum venisset trans fretum]], Jesus with His disciples, that is, beyond the lake or sea spoken of, [[8:28|into the country of the Gerasens|in regionem Gerasenorum]], which was on the other shore of this sea. And it is called the country of the Gerasens from the chief city of that land, which is called Gerasa or Geneser. [[8:28|there met him two that were possessed with devils|Occurrerunt ei duo homines habentes dæmonia]]: for each of them, or at least one, was possessed by many demons. For Luke relates that a legion of demons was in him[[Luke 8:30||]]. Mark and Luke speak only of one having demons[[Mark 5:2||]][[Luke 8:27||]]; but there is no contradiction between them and Matthew, since the smaller number does not exclude the greater, nor the reverse. [[8:28|coming out of the sepulchres|De monumentis exeuntes]]: for they did not live in houses but in pits made for burial; [[8:28|exceeding fierce|sævi nimis]], that is, very savage towards themselves and others, since they were possessed by demons, to whom leave had been given by God to exercise great cruelty through these men whom they possessed. And they were so savage [[8:28|so that none could pass by that way|ita ut nemo posset illæsus atque securus transire per viam illam]] unharmed and safely.

paras.t: Et ecce clamaverunt. Viso enim Jesu, dæmones loquebantur per vascula a se impleta, dicentes : Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu, Fili Dei? id est, quæ conventio vel similitudo inter nos insanos atque obsessos, et te sapientem ac sanctum? quasi dicant : Non debuisti venire ad nos. Hæc verba homines isti loquebantur, sed dæmonibus eos ad loquendum moventibus adscribuntur. Quod autem nominant Jesum Filium Dei, non ex certa cognitione, sed conjectura et suspicione procedit, secundum Hieronymum. Hæc quoque confessio ex necessitate potius quam ex voluntate processit, velut si servi fugitivi verbera metuentes, verba blanda suo domino loquantur, ut eis parcatur. Venisti huc ante tempus, id est valde cito et ante tempus a nobis præfixum, vel ante diem judicii, in quo erit plena et finalis reproborum damnatio, torquere nos, quoniam tua præsentia nobis pœnalis est, et timemus ejici a te : quod nobis grave est valde. Dæmones enim quum maxime odiant homines, delectantur eos torquendo, et dolent dum expelluntur. Ideo autem potissimum dixerunt, ut reor, Venisti ante tempus torquere nos, quoniam verebantur in infernum retrudi, in quem noverant se in die judicii retrudendos. Verumtamen ubique ferunt ignem suum secum.
paras.en: [[8:29|And behold they cried out|Et ecce clamaverunt]]. For at the sight of Jesus the demons spoke through the vessels they had filled, [[8:29|saying: What have we to do with thee, Jesus Son of God?|dicentes : Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu, Fili Dei?]]; that is, what agreement or likeness is there between us, mad and possessed, and Thee, wise and holy? as if they said: Thou oughtest not to have come to us. These words those men spoke, but they are ascribed to the demons moving them to speak. That they name Jesus the Son of God proceeds not from certain knowledge but from conjecture and suspicion, according to Jerome. This confession too proceeded from necessity rather than from will, as if runaway slaves, fearing the lash, should speak soft words to their master that they might be spared. [[8:29|art thou come hither to torment us before the time?|Venisti huc ante tempus]], that is, very soon and before the time fixed by us, or before the day of judgment, on which there will be the full and final damnation of the reprobate, [[8:29|to torment us|torquere nos]]; since Thy presence is a punishment to us, and we fear to be cast out by Thee, which is very grievous to us. For the demons, since they hate men most of all, delight in tormenting them, and grieve when they are expelled. And they said this above all, I think, Thou art come before the time to torment us, because they feared to be thrust back into hell, into which they knew they would be thrust on the day of judgment. Yet everywhere they carry their fire with them.

paras.t: Erat autem non longe ab illis dæmoniacis grex porcorum multorum usque ad duo millia, secundum Marcum, pascens, id est, nutrimentum sumens, in monte, de herbis atque graminibus. Dæmones autem rogabant eum, videlicet Jesum, dicentes : Si ejicis nos ab istis duobus obsessis, mitte, id est, ire permitte, nos in gregem porcorum, id est in porcos. Talis fuit ista petitio, velut si reus timens patibulum, quærat gladium, quia inter duo mala minus malum eligitur. Et ait illis Jesus : Ite. Hoc Christus concessit, non ad instantiam dæmonum, sed propter alias causas. Primo, ut ostenderetur hominibus quantus sit rancor dæmonum contra eos, propter hoc quod quærunt nocere jumentis et pecoribus hominum. Secundo, ut miraculum istud ejectionis dæmonum hac occasione amplius divulgaretur ad hominum informationem : quod et factum est, ut statim subjungitur. Tertio, quoniam homines regionis Gerasenorum suis peccatis hoc damnum meruerunt. Erant quippe gentiles, ut fertur. At illi dæmones exeuntes ab obsessis, abierunt in porcos. Imo in unum porcum plures dæmones intraverunt, secundum quod numerus dæmonum numerum porcorum excessit. In uno siquidem obsesso fuerat legio dæmonum. Et ecce impetu, id est cum strepitu veloci ac vehementi, seu motu celerrimo et rabido cursu, abiit totus grex porcorum per præceps, id est præcipitanter, seu per locum præcipitem et tortuosum, in mare Genesareth, dæmonibus porcos impellentibus. Porci namque potius agebantur, quam agebant. Et mortui sunt porci in aquis, id est submersi et suffocati.
paras.en: [[8:30|And there was, not far from them, a herd of many swine|Erat autem non longe ab illis dæmoniacis grex porcorum multorum]], about two thousand, according to Mark[[Mark 5:13||]], [[8:30|feeding|pascens]], that is, taking food, on the mountain, of herbs and grass. [[8:31|And the devils besought him, saying: If thou cast us out hence, send us into the herd of swine|Dæmones autem rogabant eum, dicentes: Si ejicis nos hinc, mitte nos in gregem porcorum]]: namely Jesus; if Thou cast us out from these two possessed men, send, that is, let us go, into the herd of swine, that is, into the swine. Such was this petition, as if a criminal fearing the gallows should ask for the sword, because between two evils the lesser is chosen. [[8:32|And he said to them: Go|Et ait illis Jesus : Ite]]. This Christ granted not at the instance of the demons but for other reasons. First, to show men how great is the rancour of the demons against them, in that they seek to harm even the beasts and cattle of men. Secondly, that this miracle of the casting out of demons might by this occasion be spread abroad more widely for the instruction of men; which was done, as is added at once. Thirdly, because the men of the country of the Gerasens deserved this loss by their sins. For they were Gentiles, as is said. [[8:32|But they going out went into the swine|At illi exeuntes abierunt in porcos]], the demons, out of the possessed; indeed several demons entered into one swine, inasmuch as the number of demons exceeded the number of swine. For in one possessed man there had been a legion of demons[[Mark 5:9||]]. [[8:32|and behold the whole herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea|Et ecce impetu abiit totus grex porcorum per præceps in mare]], that is, with swift and violent noise, or most rapid motion and mad running, headlong, or down a steep and winding place, into the sea of Genesareth, the demons driving the swine. For the swine were driven rather than drove themselves. [[8:32|and they perished in the waters|Et mortui sunt porci in aquis]], that is, drowned and suffocated.

paras.t: Pastores autem porcorum fugerunt, territi tam insolito horrendoque facto, et ne damnum ipsis imputaretur, et ne ipsi quoque a dæmonibus invaderentur ; et venientes in civitatem Geneser, metropolim hujus provinciæ : quæ fuit ex opposita Galilææ, ut Lucas commemorat ; nuntiaverunt omnia, civibus, scilicet de submersione porcorum, et de his duobus qui dæmonia habuerant, quomodo curati essent a Christo, de cujus licentia dæmones ingressi sunt porcos. Et ecce tota civitas, id est populus civitatis pro magna vel principaliori parte, exiit obviam Jesu, ut eum honorarent, vel signa facta viderent, ut asserit Marcus. Et viso eo, rogabant eum, ut transiret a finibus eorum, id est, ab ipsis et terra eorum recederet : vel quia se indignos reputabant ejus presentia, sicut centurio; vel ne talia damna amplius paterentur, si Christus plures dæmoniacos in terra ipsorum curaret. Verumtamen, si sapientes fuissent, potius Christum rogassent secum manere, quam omnino terram eorum exire.
paras.en: [[8:33|And they that kept them fled|Pastores autem porcorum fugerunt]], terrified by so unusual and horrible a deed, and lest the loss be imputed to them, and lest they too be seized by the demons; [[8:33|and coming into the city|et venientes in civitatem]] of Geneser, the capital of this province, which was opposite Galilee, as Luke records[[Luke 8:26||]], [[8:33|told every thing|nuntiaverunt omnia]] to the citizens, namely about the drowning of the swine, [[8:33|and concerning them that had been possessed by the devils|et de his duobus qui dæmonia habuerant]], how they had been healed by Christ, by whose leave the demons entered the swine. [[8:34|And behold the whole city went out to meet Jesus|Et ecce tota civitas exiit obviam Jesu]], that is, the people of the city for the greater or chief part, to honour Him, or to see the signs that had been done, as Mark asserts[[Mark 5:14||]]. [[8:34|and when they saw him, they besought him that he would depart from their coast|Et viso eo, rogabant eum, ut transiret a finibus eorum]], that is, would withdraw from them and their land: either because they reckoned themselves unworthy of His presence, like the centurion[[8:8||]]; or lest they should suffer further such losses if Christ healed more demoniacs in their land. Yet if they had been wise, they would rather have asked Christ to stay with them than to leave their land altogether.

paras.t: Mystice, per hoc quod Christus post maris transfretationem, dormitionem, et suscitationem, ingressus est terram Gerasenorum gentilem, significatur, quod post conversationem suam in hoc sæculo, turbulentissimo mari, post dormitionem in cruce ac monumento, et resurrectionem, intravit terras gentilium, mittendo ad eos Apostolos, et introeundo corda eorum per fidem et gratiam. Per sanationem quoque sævissimorum dæmoniacorum, designatur conversio habituatorum et obstinatorum in vitiis : qui quum in profundum peccatorum venerint, contemnunt; qui sine ullo timore perpetrant mala; super quos clausit puteus os suum. De quibus ait Psalmista : Prodiit quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum ; et Salomon, Lætantur quum malefecerint. Tales sæpius sanantur et convertuntur a Christo, ita ut omnes qui viderint, obstupescant.
paras.en: Mystically, by Christ’s entering the Gentile land of the Gerasens after crossing the sea, sleeping and being woken, it is signified that after His life in this world, a most turbulent sea, after His sleep on the cross and in the tomb, and His resurrection, He entered the lands of the Gentiles, sending the Apostles to them and entering their hearts by faith and grace. By the healing of the most savage demoniacs, too, is designated the conversion of those hardened and obstinate in vices, who, [[Prov 18:3|when he is come into the depths of sins, contemneth|quum in profundum peccatorum venerint, contemnunt]]; who commit evils without any fear[[Eccles 8:11||]]; over whom [[Ps 68:16|the pit|puteus]] has shut [[Ps 68:16|her mouth|os suum]]. Of them the Psalmist says: [[Ps 72:7|Their iniquity hath come forth, as it were from fatness|Prodiit quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum]]; and Solomon, [[Prov 2:14|Who are glad when they have done evil|Lætantur quum malefecerint]]. Such are often healed and converted by Christ, so that all who see it are astonished.

9.title: Explanatio capituli noni: Et ascendens in naviculam, transfretavit
9.title_en: Explanation of the ninth chapter: “And entering into a boat, he passed over the water”

paras.t: Et ascendens, id est ingrediens Jesus in naviculam, forte in eamdem in qua venit ad terram Gerasenorum, transfretavit, hoc est, navigando per mare prædictum reversus est cum sua comitiva; et venit in civitatem suam. Per hanc civitatem Hieronymus intelligit Nazareth, a qua Jesus dictus est Nazarenus. Augustinus vero intelligit per eam Capharnaum: et hoc communius tenetur, quoniam apud Marcum manifeste describitur sequens miraculum in urbe Capharnaum perpetratum. Quemadmodum ergo Nazareth dicitur civitas Christi, quia in ea conceptus, et Bethlehem, quia in ea natus; sic Capharnaum, quia in ea moratus, frequenter conversatus, et multa miracula operatus. Et ecce habitantes vel exsistentes in Capharnaum, offerebant, hoc est præsentabant, ei, videlicet Christo, paralyticum jacentem in lecto: qui secundum Marcum, a quatuor portabatur, quia per se ingredi non valebat. Denique, secundum Lucam, quum domum in qua Jesus fuerat, introire viri isti non possent, ascenderunt super tectum, et illo nudato, per tegulas submiserunt ægrotum in lecto ante Jesum, per funes, ut puto. Et videns Jesus oculo interiori, fidem illorum offerentium paralyticum, atque ipsius paralytici, qui etiam fidem habuit recipiendæ sanitatis et potentiæ Christi, quamvis forte minorem quam illi, dixit paralytico: Confide, fili, hoc est, spera te adepturum quod optas: imo majora recipies, nam remittuntur tibi peccata tua, propter quæ hanc sustines infirmitatem. Antequam Christus paralytico peccata sua indulsit, infudit ei quamdam displicentiam seu contritionem culparum.
paras.en: [[9:1|And entering into a boat|Et ascendens in naviculam]], that is, going into it, perhaps the same one in which He had come to the land of the Gerasens, [[9:1|he passed over the water|transfretavit]], that is, sailing over the aforesaid sea He returned with His company, [[9:1|and came into his own city|et venit in civitatem suam]]. By this city Jerome understands Nazareth, from which Jesus was called a Nazarene. Augustine, however, understands Capharnaum by it, and this is the more common opinion, since in Mark the following miracle is plainly described as done in the town of Capharnaum[[Mark 2:1||]]. So, just as Nazareth is called Christ's city because He was conceived there, and Bethlehem because He was born there, so is Capharnaum, because He stayed there, often lived there, and worked many miracles there. [[9:2|And behold they brought to him|Et ecce offerebant]], that is, the people living or staying in Capharnaum presented to Christ [[9:2|one sick of the palsy lying in a bed|paralyticum jacentem in lecto]], who, according to Mark, was carried by four[[Mark 2:3||]], because he could not come in by himself. Then, according to Luke, when these men could not get into the house where Jesus was, they went up onto the roof and, having uncovered it, let the sick man down through the tiles in his bed before Jesus[[Luke 5:19||]][[Mark 2:4||]], by ropes, I suppose. [[9:2|And Jesus, seeing their faith|Et videns Jesus oculo interiori, fidem illorum]] with His inward eye, the faith of those who brought the paralytic, and of the paralytic himself, who also had faith that he would receive health and in the power of Christ, though perhaps less than they had, [[9:2|said to the man sick of the palsy: Be of good heart, son|dixit paralytico: Confide, fili]], that is, hope that you will obtain what you desire; nay, you shall receive greater things, for [[9:2|thy sins are forgiven thee|remittuntur tibi peccata tua]], on account of which you bear this infirmity. Before Christ pardoned the paralytic his sins, He poured into him a certain displeasure at his faults, that is, contrition.

paras.t: Et ecce quidam de Scribis, quorum multi tunc aderant, ut Lucas evangelista refert: qui magis venerunt ex curiositate, vel animo calumniandi, quam desiderio proficiendi; dixerunt intra se: Hic blasphemat, usurpando sibi quod soli Deo possibile est, scilicet peccata remittere. Dixerant enim in cordibus suis: Quis potest peccata dimittere, nisi solus Deus! Quoniam ergo putabant Jesum esse hominem purum, imposuerunt sibi crimen blasphemiæ, eo quod præsumpsit alicui peccata dimittere.
paras.en: [[9:3|And behold some of the scribes|Et ecce quidam de Scribis]], many of whom were there at the time, as Luke the Evangelist relates[[Luke 5:17||]], and who had come more out of curiosity, or with a mind to find fault, than from a desire to profit, [[9:3|said within themselves: He blasphemeth|dixerunt intra se: Hic blasphemat]], claiming for Himself what is possible to God alone, namely to forgive sins. For they had said in their hearts: [[Mark 2:7|Who can forgive sins, but God only?|Quis potest peccata dimittere, nisi solus Deus]] So, since they thought Jesus a mere man, they charged Him with the crime of blasphemy because He presumed to forgive anyone's sins.

paras.t: Jesus vero probat se non blasphemasse, verumque Deum esse, aperiendo secreta cordis illorum, et paralyticum solo imperio propria virtute et auctoritate curando, quorum utrumque Deo est proprium. Quis enim novit quid agatur in homine, nisi spiritus hominis? Et quum vidisset oculo intellectuali, Jesus cogitationes illorum Scribarum: quas tunc videre non cœpit, sed a principio creationis animæ suæ eas cognovit, sicut et cetera futura; sed nunc ostendit se eas vidisse: ut sit sensus, Quum vidisset, id est, vidisse se ostendere vellet, Jesus cogitatus illorum perversos. Unde Joannes in suo evangelio protestatur: Necessarium Christo non erat, ut quis ei testimonium perhiberet de homine; ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine. Dixit eis: Ut quid cogitatis mala, id est falsa, in cordibus vestris, hoc est cum cordis consensu imputando mihi blasphemiam, qui non quæro gloriam meam, sed honorifico Patrem meum? Hoc idem ait Christus apud Jeremiam: Usquequo morabuntur in te cogitationes noxiæ?
paras.en: But Jesus proves that He has not blasphemed, and that He is true God, by laying open the secrets of their hearts and by curing the paralytic by His command alone, by His own power and authority, both of which belong to God alone. For who knows what goes on in a man, [[1 Cor 2:11|but the spirit of a man|nisi spiritus hominis]]? [[9:4|And Jesus seeing their thoughts|Et quum vidisset oculo intellectuali, Jesus cogitationes]], seeing them with the eye of the intellect, the thoughts of those scribes: which He did not begin to see then, but knew from the beginning of His soul's creation, as He knew all other things to come; but now He showed that He had seen them. So the sense is: 'when He had seen', that is, when He wished to show that He had seen, their perverse thoughts. Whence John bears witness in his Gospel that Christ [[John 2:25|needed not that any should give testimony of man: for he knew what was in man|ut quis ei testimonium perhiberet de homine; ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine]]. [[9:4|said: Why do you think evil|Dixit eis: Ut quid cogitatis mala]], that is, falsehoods, [[9:4|in your hearts|in cordibus vestris]], that is, with the consent of your hearts, charging Me with blasphemy, who [[John 8:50|seek not my own glory|non quæro gloriam meam]], [[John 8:49|but I honour my Father|sed honorifico Patrem meum]]? Christ says the same in Jeremias: [[Jer 4:14|how long shall hurtful thoughts abide in thee|Usquequo morabuntur in te cogitationes noxiæ]]?

paras.t: Deinde probat per experientiam se esse Deum, et posse relaxare peccata. Quid est facilius dicere, hoc est dicendo efficere, Remittuntur tibi peccata tua, an dicere, id est dicendo peragere, Surge, o paralytice, et ambula omnino sanatus? Ut autem sciatis quoniam Filius hominis (noverant turbæ quod per Filium hominis intellexit se ipsum) habet potestatem in terra, id est in hominibus qui demorantur in terra, dimittendi peccata, secundum quod Deus est, per auctoritatem, ita quod operari possit in anima, maculam culpæ per nitorem infusæ gratiæ auferendo. Loquitur autem Christus jam de potestate sua increata, divina ac infinita, non humana: aliter ratio sua non videretur concludere. Tunc ait paralytico. Hoc verbum interponit Evangelista. Christus nempe adjecit: Tibi dico, paralytice, surge sanus a lecto ægritudinis, tolle lectum tuum, in quo jaces, et vade in domum tuam: quæ forsan intra Capharnaum fuerat sita. Sed quæritur, quomodo ista argumentatio valeat, quum majus sit animam a languore peccati curare, quam corporalem infirmitatem sanare. Dicendum, quod Christus intendit probare utrumque soli divinæ posse convenire potentiæ. Nam licet paralysim curare possit naturaliter fieri, tamen tam imperialiter, subito et auctoritative eam curare, non competit nisi potentiæ infinitæ. Idcirco ostendendo se taliter posse sanare paralysim, demonstravit quoque se posse dimittere culpam.
paras.en: Next He proves by experience that He is God and can forgive sins. [[9:5|Whether is easier, to say|Quid est facilius dicere]], that is, to bring about by saying, [[9:5|Thy sins are forgiven thee|Remittuntur tibi peccata tua]], [[9:5|or to say|an dicere]], that is, to accomplish by saying, [[9:5|Arise, and walk|Surge, o paralytice, et ambula]], O paralytic, wholly healed? [[9:6|But that you may know that the Son of man|Ut autem sciatis quoniam Filius hominis]] (the crowds knew that by 'the Son of man' He meant Himself) [[9:6|hath power on earth|habet potestatem in terra]], that is, among men who dwell on earth, [[9:6|to forgive sins|dimittendi peccata]], inasmuch as He is God, by authority, so that He can work in the soul, taking away the stain of guilt by the brightness of infused grace. Christ here speaks of His uncreated, divine and infinite power, not of His human power; otherwise His argument would not seem to conclude. [[9:6|then said he to the man sick of the palsy|tunc ait paralytico]]: these words the Evangelist puts in. For Christ added: I say to thee, paralytic, [[9:6|Arise|surge]] healthy from the bed of sickness, [[9:6|take up thy bed|tolle lectum tuum]], in which you lie, [[9:6|and go into thy house|et vade in domum tuam]], which was perhaps in Capharnaum. But it is asked how this argument holds, since it is a greater thing to cure the soul of the sickness of sin than to heal a bodily infirmity. It must be said that Christ means to prove that both can belong only to the divine power. For although the curing of palsy can come about naturally, yet to cure it so commandingly, so suddenly and with such authority belongs only to an infinite power. Therefore, by showing that He could heal the palsy in this way, He showed also that He could forgive guilt.

paras.t: Et surrexit paralyticus jam sanatus, et abiit in domum suam, proprium portans lectum, ad declarandum quod nec vestigium pristinæ infirmitatis in eo permansit. Videntes autem turbæ tantum prodigium, timuerunt. Objectum timoris est malum. Nam timoris servilis objectum, est malum pœnæ: timoris vero filialis objectum, est malum culpæ, videlicet separatio a Deo, vel Dei offensa. Quid ergo vel cur timuerunt hæ turbæ, quum potius exsultare et amare debuerant? Et respondendum, quod ex tanto miraculo perpenderunt sanctitatem dignitatemque Christi, quem licet nondum putarent Deum, certissime tamen tenebant eum esse virum sanctissimum, divina potestate agentem: sicque considerata sanctitate ipsius, propriam pravitatem clarius attenderunt, quia opposita juxta se posita clarius innotescunt; sicque ultionem divinæ justitiæ metuebant, se ipsos abhorruerunt, et Christi præsentia se reputabant indignos, eumque offendere verebantur. Et glorificaverunt Deum, id est, gloriosum, pium et omnipotentem esse professi sunt, qui dedit potestatem talem hominibus, scilicet potestatem faciendi miracula. Cur non dixerunt, Qui dedit talem potestatem huic homini, singulariter, præsertim quum secundum Marcum, dixisse legantur, Quia nunquam sic vidimus? Dicendum, quod forte intendebant ponere plurale pro singulari; vel nondum putabant ampliorem potestatem collatam Christo, quam Moysi et Prophetis.
paras.en: [[9:7|And he arose|Et surrexit]], the paralytic, now healed, [[9:7|and went into his house|et abiit in domum suam]], carrying his own bed, to make plain that not a trace of his former infirmity remained in him. [[9:8|And the multitude seeing it, feared|Videntes autem turbæ tantum prodigium, timuerunt]], seeing so great a wonder. The object of fear is evil. For the object of servile fear is the evil of punishment; but the object of filial fear is the evil of guilt, namely separation from God, or offence against God. Why then, or what, did these crowds fear, when they ought rather to have rejoiced and loved? It must be answered that from so great a miracle they weighed the holiness and dignity of Christ, whom, though they did not yet think Him God, they held most surely to be a most holy man acting by divine power; and so, considering His holiness, they saw their own wickedness more clearly, because opposites set side by side are more clearly known. And so they feared the vengeance of the divine justice, they shrank from themselves, they thought themselves unworthy of Christ's presence, and they were afraid of offending Him. [[9:8|and glorified God|Et glorificaverunt Deum]], that is, they professed Him to be glorious, merciful and almighty, [[9:8|that gave such power to men|qui dedit potestatem talem hominibus]], namely the power of working miracles. Why did they not say in the singular, 'who gave such power to this man', especially since, according to Mark, they are said to have said: [[Mark 2:12|We never saw the like.|Quia nunquam sic vidimus]]? It must be said that perhaps they meant to put the plural for the singular; or they did not yet think that a fuller power had been given to Christ than to Moses and the Prophets.

paras.t: Consequenter gloriosus evangelista Matthæus, sui ipsius conversionem describit. Et quum transisset inde [Jesus], hoc est a Capharnaum, seu domo ubi sanavit hunc paralyticum, vidit hominem sedentem in telonio, id est occupatum in colligendo vectigalia seu tributa: et forte ad litteram tunc sedebat quantum ad situm corporis in telonio, id est in domo publica, ubi solvebantur prædicta. Vel telonium est mensa in qua computantur vectigalia. Matthæum nomine. Hic Matthæus alio nomine appellatus est Levi, sicque vocant eum Lucas et Marcus, dum ejus conversionem describunt: nam propter reverentiam nolunt eum usitato nomine designare, dum inhonestum ejus officium exprimunt. Et ait illi Jesus: Sequere me. Respexit Jesus Matthæum oculo corporali, sed multo profundius oculo pietatis interna seu compassionis affectu, quemadmodum respexit et Petrum, post trinam negationem. Similiter vocat Matthæum, verbo vocali ad extra corporales aures pulsando; sed multo virtuosius vocavit eum verbo inspirationis occulte, exhortationisque intima: de quo ait Propheta, Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus. Porro verba Christi operativa erant, et penetrativa cordis. Et surgens a pristina conversatione injusta, a loco telonii, et ab omni affectu terreno, secutus est eum, videlicet Christum mentis religiosa devotione, et corporis gressu promptissimo.
paras.en: Next the glorious Evangelist Matthew describes his own conversion. [[9:9|And when Jesus passed on from thence|Et quum transisset inde]], that is, from Capharnaum, or from the house where He healed this paralytic, [[9:9|he saw a man sitting in the custom house|vidit hominem sedentem in telonio]], that is, busy collecting tolls or taxes; and perhaps he was literally sitting, as to the posture of his body, in the custom house, that is, in the public building where these were paid. Or the telonium is the table on which the tolls are counted. [[9:9|named Matthew|Matthæum nomine]]. This Matthew was called by another name, Levi, and so Luke and Mark call him when they describe his conversion[[Luke 5:27||]][[Mark 2:14||]]: for out of reverence they will not name him by his usual name while they mention his dishonourable trade. [[9:9|and he saith to him: Follow me|Et ait illi Jesus: Sequere me]]. Jesus looked at Matthew with His bodily eye, but much more deeply with the inward eye of pity, that is, with a feeling of compassion, just as He looked also at Peter after his threefold denial[[Luke 22:61||]]. In the same way He calls Matthew with a spoken word, striking his bodily ears from without; but much more powerfully He called him with the word of hidden inspiration and of inward exhortation, of which the Prophet says: [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]]. Moreover, the words of Christ were effective, and pierced the heart. [[9:9|And he arose up|Et surgens]] from his former unjust way of life, from the place of the custom house, and from every earthly affection, [[9:9|and followed him|secutus est eum]], that is, Christ, with the religious devotion of his mind and with the most ready step of his body.

paras.t: Et factum est, discumbente eo, id est Christo manducante, in domo Matthæi, qui fecit Christo magnum convivium, secundum Lucam, non tamen immediate post conversionem suam, sed postea. Imo, quod hic dicitur de vocatione Matthæi, per recapitulationem dicitur, non secundum historiæ ordinem: ut habetur in Luca, quod Jesus ascendens in montem antequam illic sermocinaretur, vocavit ad se discipulos suos, elegitque ex eis duodecim Apostolos, quorum Matthæus exstitit unus; sermo autem in monte, diu factus fuit ante prædicti paralytici curationem, post quam hic describitur vocatio Matthæi. Sed forte convivium factum est statim post curationem paralytici hujus. Quamvis enim Matthæus primo mox secutus sit Christum, postea tamen de licentia Christi, una cum Christo et ejus discipulis rediit ad domum suam, forsitan dispositurus de negotiis suis, quia teloniarius fuit, et dominis suis rationem reddere debebat. Glossa tamen videtur aliter dicere. Ecce multi publicani, id est publici transgressores, et peccatores minus famosi in vitiis, venientes ad domum Matthæi, ab eo invitati, quoniam socii ejus fuerunt, et exemplo Matthæi Christum sequi ac pœnitere cœperunt: quemadmodum in libris Regum Eliseus ab Elia vocatus fecit convivium sociis suis, mactans boves duos; discumbebant cum Jesu et discipulis ejus in domo Matthæi. Porro, si Matthæus in sua vocatione omnia sua penitus reliquisset quasi non reversurus, nec dispositurus de eis, non redisset ad propriam domum, neque de suis facultatibus exhibuisset Christo et ceteris tam solenne convivium.
paras.en: [[9:10|And it came to pass as he was sitting at meat|Et factum est, discumbente eo]], that is, while Christ was eating, [[9:10|in the house|in domo]] of Matthew, who made a great feast for Christ, according to Luke[[Luke 5:29||]]; not, however, immediately after his conversion, but afterwards. Indeed, what is said here of Matthew's calling is said by way of recapitulation, not in the order of the history; for we have in Luke that Jesus, going up the mountain, before He preached there, called His disciples to Him and chose from them twelve Apostles[[Luke 6:13||]], of whom Matthew was one; and the sermon on the mount was given long before the curing of the aforesaid paralytic, after which the calling of Matthew is described here. But perhaps the feast took place immediately after the curing of this paralytic. For although Matthew first followed Christ at once, yet afterwards, with Christ's leave, he went back to his house together with Christ and His disciples, perhaps to settle his affairs, since he was a tax-gatherer and had to render an account to his masters. The Gloss, however, seems to say otherwise. [[9:10|behold many publicans|ecce multi publicani]], that is, public transgressors, [[9:10|and sinners|et peccatores]] less notorious in their vices, [[9:10|came|venientes]] to Matthew's house, invited by him, since they were his companions, and by Matthew's example they began to follow Christ and to repent; just as, in the books of Kings, Eliseus, when called by Elias, made a feast for his companions, killing two oxen[[3 Kings 19:21||]]. [[9:10|and sat down with Jesus and his disciples|discumbebant cum Jesu et discipulis ejus]] in Matthew's house. Moreover, if Matthew at his calling had left all his goods altogether, as though never to return or to dispose of them, he would not have gone back to his own house, nor have given Christ and the others so solemn a feast from his own means.

paras.t: Et videntes Pharisæi Christum et ejus discipulos cum publicanis comedere, dicebant discipulis ejus. Secundum Lucam et Marcum etiam Scribæ murmurabant, dicentes: Quare cum publicanis et peccatoribus manducat Magister vester? quasi dicant, Hoc indecens est: quum dicat Jeremias, Quid tritico cum paleis? et David, Superbo oculo et insatiabili corde, cum hoc non edebam. Et rursus Scriptura hortatur: Viri justi sint tibi commensales. Et Salomon in Proverbiis: Ne comedas, inquit, cum homine invido.
paras.en: [[9:11|And the Pharisees seeing it|Et videntes Pharisæi]], seeing Christ and His disciples eating with publicans, [[9:11|said to his disciples|dicebant discipulis ejus]]. According to Luke and Mark the scribes too murmured[[Luke 5:30||]][[Mark 2:16||]], saying: [[9:11|Why doth your master eat with publicans and sinners?|Quare cum publicanis et peccatoribus manducat Magister vester?]] As if to say: This is unbecoming, since Jeremias says, [[Jer 23:28|what hath the chaff to do with the wheat|Quid tritico cum paleis]]? and David: [[Ps 100:5|With him that had a proud eye, and an unsatiable heart, I would not eat.|Superbo oculo et insatiabili corde, cum hoc non edebam]] And again Scripture exhorts: [[Ecclus 9:22|Let just men be thy guests|Viri justi sint tibi commensales]]. And Solomon in the Proverbs: [[Prov 23:6|Eat not with an envious man|Ne comedas, inquit, cum homine invido]].

paras.t: At Jesus audiens ad minus aure cordis verba Pharisæorum, qui ista dixerunt ut quasi non audirentur a Christo, ait eis efficaciter respondendo, atque illorum præsumptionem ac elationem redarguendo: Non est opus, id est, necessarius non est, valentibus, id est sanis, medicus, loquendo de utrisque formaliter. Medicus enim ordinatur ad vulnerum atque morborum sanationem, qui in hominibus sanis non sunt, nec indigent medico quamdiu sunt tales: quod de spirituali et corporali sano, ac medico verum est. Sed male habentibus, id est infirmis opus est medicus. Nam spiritualiter vulneratis seu impiis necessarius est medicus spiritualis, qui possit animam peccatricem ad statum gratia revocare, et illud Apostoli implere: Corripite inquietos, consolamini pusillanimes, suscipite infirmos, patientes estote ad omnes. Talis fuerat Christus, qui in Isaia testatur: Dominus, inquiens, dedit mihi linguam eruditam, ut sciam sustentare eum qui lapsus est, verbo.
paras.en: [[9:12|But Jesus hearing it|At Jesus audiens]], hearing at least with the ear of His heart the words of the Pharisees, who said these things as though they would not be heard by Christ, [[9:12|said|ait]] to them, answering them effectively and rebuking their presumption and pride: [[9:12|They that are in health need not a physician|Non est opus … valentibus … medicus]], that is, a physician is not necessary for the healthy, speaking of both formally. For a physician is ordained to the healing of wounds and diseases, which are not in healthy men, nor do they need a physician as long as they are such: and this is true of the spiritually and the bodily healthy, and of the spiritual and the bodily physician. [[9:12|but they that are ill|Sed male habentibus]], that is, the sick, need a physician. For the spiritually wounded, that is, the wicked, need a spiritual physician, who can call the sinful soul back to the state of grace and fulfil that saying of the Apostle: [[1 Thess 5:14|rebuke the unquiet, comfort the feeble-minded, support the weak, be patient towards all men|Corripite inquietos, consolamini pusillanimes, suscipite infirmos, patientes estote ad omnes]]. Such was Christ, who testifies in Isaias, saying: [[Is 50:4|The Lord hath given me a learned tongue, that I should know how to uphold by word him that is weary|Dominus … dedit mihi linguam eruditam … qui lapsus est, verbo]].

paras.t: Itaque misericordia miseris necessaria est: quod Christus consequenter probat auctoritate Osee prophetæ, dicens: Euntes autem, id est, corporaliter a me recedentes, vel spiritualiter a præsumptione, crudelitate, et ignorantia abeuntes. Nam dupliciter peccatis: primo, quod vos ipsos justificatis; secundo, quod alios spernitis, judicatis, et condemnare audetis. Discite quid est, id est, quomodo intelligi debeat et observari: Misericordiam volo, hoc est compassionem et subventionem ad proximum indigentem, et non sacrificium legale, quasi illud sit per se acceptum ac meritorium sicut misericordia; vel, Non sacrificium legale pro tempore evangelicæ legis, in quo misericordia maxime prædicatur. Simili modo scriptum est apud Isaiam prophetam, dicentem: Holocausta arietum et adipem pinguium nolui. Quid autem velit Deus subjungitur illico, scilicet, Subvenite oppresso. Unde Michæas propheta hoc ipsum clarius introducit, dicens: Numquid offeram Domino holocautomata? numquid placari potest Deus in millibus arietum? quasi dicat, Nequaquam. In quo ergo placatur adjecit; Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam.
paras.en: So mercy is necessary for the wretched, which Christ goes on to prove by the authority of the prophet Osee[[Osee 6:6||]], saying: [[9:13|Go then|Euntes autem]], that is, going away from Me bodily, or going away in spirit from presumption, cruelty and ignorance. For you sin in two ways: first, in that you justify yourselves; second, in that you despise others, judge them, and dare to condemn them. [[9:13|and learn what this meaneth|Discite quid est]], that is, how it should be understood and kept: [[9:13|I will have mercy|Misericordiam volo]], that is, compassion and help for a neighbour in need, [[9:13|and not sacrifice|et non sacrificium]] of the law, as though that were acceptable and meritorious of itself, as mercy is; or, not the sacrifice of the law in the time of the Gospel law, in which mercy is above all preached. In like manner it is written in the prophet Isaias, saying: [[Is 1:11|I desire not holocausts of rams, and fat of fatlings|Holocausta arietum et adipem pinguium nolui]]. And what God does want is added at once, namely: [[Is 1:17|relieve the oppressed|Subvenite oppresso]]. Whence the prophet Micheas brings in the same thing more clearly, saying: [[Mich 6:6|shall I offer holocausts unto him|Numquid offeram Domino holocautomata]]? [[Mich 6:7|May the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams|numquid placari potest Deus in millibus arietum]]? As if to say: By no means. And he added what He is appeased by: [[Mich 6:8|I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily to do judgment, and to love mercy|Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam]].

paras.t: Consequenter subditur causa vel potius signum, quod Deus vult misericordiam potius quam sacrificium. Von enim ven? vocare justos, sed peccatores. Hoc est quod alibi ait Salvator: Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat; et Apostolus, Fidelis sermo, et omni acceptione dignus, quoniam Christus Jesus venit in hunc mundum peccatores salvos facere. Sed nonne Christus vocavit Jacobum justum, Petrum, qui nunquam comedit omne immundum, Andream, Joannem, et alios quosdam justissimos? Et nonne Apostolus veraciter asserit, Quos prædestinavit, hos et vocavit? Quomodo ergo non venit Christus vocare justos? Et respondendum dupliciter: Primo, quia secundum Ambrosium, per justos intelligit Scribas et Pharisæos, de sua justitia præsumentes, qui tamen veraciter justi non erant, sed vani atque elati. Per peccatores vero intelliguntur humiliter peenitentes, qui veraciter justi sunt. Illos ergo justos Christus non venit vocare per salutarem effectum, seu efficientiam, et consecutionem salutis (juxta quem modum Christus non est crucifixus pro reprobis, sed electis), quia de taliter justis dicit Apostolus: Ignorantes Dei justitiam et suam volentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti. Istos vero peccatores venit vocare efficienter atque finaliter: de quibus infra testatur, loquens ad Pharisæos, Quia videbitis publicanos et peccatores præcedere vos in regnum Dei. Secundo, dicendum quod Christus loquitur hic de vocatione ad pœnitentiam, qua peccatoribus competit, non justis, secundum quod tales sunt. Unde apud Lucam sic legitur respondisse: Non veni vocare justos, sed peccatores in penitentiam. Justos vero vocavit et vocat ad gratiæ incrementum et vitæ spiritualis perfectionem.
paras.en: Next is added the reason, or rather the sign, that God wills mercy rather than sacrifice: [[9:13|For I am not come to call the just, but sinners.|Non enim veni vocare justos, sed peccatores]] This is what the Saviour says elsewhere: [[Luke 19:10|the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost|Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]]; and the Apostle: [[1 Tim 1:15|A faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners|Fidelis sermo, et omni acceptione dignus, quoniam Christus Jesus venit in hunc mundum peccatores salvos facere]]. But did not Christ call James the Just, Peter, who never ate anything unclean[[Acts 10:14||]], Andrew, John, and certain others most just? And does not the Apostle truly assert: [[Rom 8:30|And whom he predestinated, them he also called|Quos prædestinavit, hos et vocavit]]? How then did Christ not come to call the just? It must be answered in two ways. First, according to Ambrose, by 'the just' He means the scribes and Pharisees, who presumed on their own justice, yet were not truly just, but vain and proud; while by 'sinners' are meant those who humbly repent, who are truly just. Those 'just', then, Christ did not come to call with a saving effect, that is, effectively and to the attaining of salvation (in the way in which Christ was not crucified for the reprobate but for the elect), because of the 'just' of this kind the Apostle says: [[Rom 10:3|not knowing the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God|Ignorantes Dei justitiam et suam volentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti]]. But these sinners He came to call effectively and to their end: of them He testifies below, speaking to the Pharisees, that you will see publicans and sinners go before you into the kingdom of God[[Matt 21:31||]]. Secondly, it must be said that Christ is speaking here of the call to penance, which belongs to sinners, not to the just as such. Whence in Luke He is read to have answered thus: [[Luke 5:32|I came not to call the just, but sinners to penance|Non veni vocare justos, sed peccatores in pœnitentiam]]. The just He called, and calls, to the increase of grace and the perfection of the spiritual life.

paras.t: Denique auctoritates inductæ ad hoc, quod eum peecatoribus vescendum non sit, intelligi possunt de peccatoribus penitus obstinatis, de quorum conversione non est spes, et de justis imperfectis, quibus obesse valet conversatio cum injustis, juxta quod scriptum est: Cum perverso perverteris. Unde Apostolus: Cum hujusmodi, ait, nec cibum sumere. Christo autem nocere non potuit conversatio cum perversis. Publicani quoque et peccatores cum eo vescentes, non erant inconvertibiles: ideo ut illuminarentur et converterentur, Christus se ad eos humane ac affabiliter habuit.
paras.en: Lastly, the authorities brought forward to show that one must not eat with sinners can be understood of sinners wholly obstinate, of whose conversion there is no hope, and of the just who are imperfect, whom keeping company with the unjust can harm, according to what is written: [[Ps 17:27|with the perverse thou wilt be perverted|Cum perverso perverteris]]. Whence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 5:11|with such a one, not so much as to eat|Cum hujusmodi, ait, nec cibum sumere]]. But company with the perverse could not harm Christ; and the publicans and sinners who ate with Him were not beyond conversion. So, that they might be enlightened and converted, Christ behaved towards them humanely and kindly.

paras.t: Interea, per corporale convivium quod Christo Matthæus exhibuit, mystice intelligitur spirituale convivium quod ei in anima sua paravit, præbendo Christo delicias cordis, per hoc quod eum in anima toto recepit affectu, aperiens ei ostium mentis. De quo convivio ait Salvator in Proverbiis Salomonis: Deliciæ meæ, esse cum filiis hominum; et in Apocalypsi: Ego sto ad ostium, et pulso; si quis aperuerit mihi, intrabo ad illum, et cœnabo cum eo, et ipse mecum. Preterea, per corporale illud convivium designatur spirituale convivium quod Christo facit Matthæus quotidie in tota Ecclesia, ubicumque ejus evangelium legitur et auditur: ex cujus auditione corda hominum proficiunt, Christo se offerunt, eum recipiunt, et cum eo spiritualiter epulantur. Sed et dum exemplo Matthæi graves transgressores convertuntur et corriguntur, facit Matthæus Christo solenne convivium. In vocatione quippe publicani et teloniarii ad discipulatum, apostolatum, et Evangelistæ officium, proponitur omnibus quantumcumque perversis, grandis fiducia pœnitendi ac venia.
paras.en: Meanwhile, by the bodily feast that Matthew gave Christ is understood mystically the spiritual feast which he prepared for Him in his soul, offering Christ the delights of his heart, in that he received Him into his soul with all his affection, opening to Him the door of his mind. Of this feast the Saviour says in the Proverbs of Solomon: [[Prov 8:31|my delights were to be with the children of men|Deliciæ meæ, esse cum filiis hominum]]; and in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:20|I stand at the gate, and knock|Ego sto ad ostium, et pulso]]; if any man open to me, [[Apoc 3:20|I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me|intrabo ad illum, et cœnabo cum eo, et ipse mecum]]. Further, that bodily feast signifies the spiritual feast which Matthew makes for Christ daily in the whole Church, wherever his Gospel is read and heard: from the hearing of which men's hearts make progress, offer themselves to Christ, receive Him, and feast with Him spiritually. And also when, by Matthew's example, grave transgressors are converted and amended, Matthew makes a solemn feast for Christ. For in the calling of a publican and tax-gatherer to discipleship, to the apostolate and to the office of Evangelist, great confidence of repentance and of pardon is set before all, however perverse.

paras.t: Tunc, id est, postquam Salvator sua responsione confudit et obturavit ora Pharisæorum, ut dictum est, accesserunt ad eum discipuli Joannis Baptistæ, dicentes: Quare nos et Pharisæi jejunamus frequenter, videlicet sæpius quam in lege præcipitur, ex speciali devotione, discipuli autem tui non jejunant tam sæpe (quamvis jejunia præcepta servaverint)? In hac interrogatione multipliciter peccant Joannis discipuli: Primo, quod se de suo jactant jejunio, quod potius fuerat occultandum, maxime quoad illud quod supererogationis exstiterat. Secundo, quod se Pharisæis conjunxerant, quos a Joanne noverant reprobatos. Tertio, quod Christi discipulos, imo et Christum redarguere presumpserunt, quem a Joanne laudatum sciebant.
paras.en: [[9:14|Then|Tunc]], that is, after the Saviour by His answer had confounded and stopped the mouths of the Pharisees, as has been said, [[9:14|came to him the disciples of John|accesserunt ad eum discipuli Joannis]] the Baptist, [[9:14|saying: Why do we and the Pharisees, fast often|dicentes: Quare nos et Pharisæi jejunamus frequenter]], that is, more often than the law commands, out of special devotion, [[9:14|but thy disciples do not fast|discipuli autem tui non jejunant]] so often (though they kept the fasts that were commanded)? In this question John's disciples sin in many ways. First, in that they boast of their fasting, which ought rather to have been hidden, above all where it went beyond what was required. Second, in that they had joined themselves to the Pharisees, whom they knew John had condemned. Third, in that they presumed to rebuke Christ's disciples, and indeed Christ Himself, whom they knew John had praised.

paras.t: Et ait illis Jesus: Numquid possunt filii sponsi, id est spirituales filii et discipuli mei, qui sum sponsus Ecclesiæ (de quo legitur, Tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo; de quo dicit Apostolus, Despondi vos uni viro virginem castam exhibere Christo), lugere quamdiu cum illis est sponsus, id est affligi et contristari, jejunando frequenter, et alia rigorosa exercitia prosequendo? tanquam dicat: Hoc non decet; amicus autem et filius sponsi, qui stat et audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Veniet autem tempus quum auferetur ab eis sponsus, videlicet dies passionis et ascensionis, quando Christus ablatus est, quantum ad corporalem præsentiam, quemadmodum ait: Pauperes semper habebitis vobiscum, me autem non semper habebitis; et iterum: Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum; iterum relinquo mundum, et vado ad Patrem. Quantum vero ad divinæ majestatis naturam, et gratiosam ac spiritualem inhabitationem, semper erat et est cum suis fidelibus, juxta illud: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Et tunc jejunabunt, corporaliter abstinendo: sicut et Jacobus, qui vovit se non comesturum, donec vidisset Filium hominis resurrexisse a mortuis, et Petrus, qui egressus flevit amare, quousque Christum resurrexisse audivit. Certum est autem Apostolos, et totam primitivam Ecclesiam, post Christi passionem in magna sobrietate vixisse.
