paras.t: Et qui susceperit in visceribus caritatis, seu domo ad hospitandum ac reficiendum, unum parvulum talem, videlicet innocentem ac humilem, de quo in Proverbiis æterna Sapientia inquit: Si quis est parvulus, veniat ad me; in nomine meo, id est ideo quia fidelis est, vel propter me atque ad gloriam nominis mei; me suscipit in membro meo mystico, quamvis non in memetipso. Itaque, Suscipit me, id est, mihi fieri judico quod fit illi, et tam gratum est mihi, ac si mihi in propria persona exhiberetur. Ecclesia nempe est mysticum corpus Christi, et ipse est caput ipsius: quod ergo fit membris, fit capiti. In tantum quoque diligit Christus parvulos et egenos, ut sibi fieri arbitretur quod impenditur illis. Unde Paulo ait: Quid me persequeris? Et per Zachariam: Qui tetigerit (inquit) vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei.
paras.en: [[18:5|And he that shall receive one such little child|Et qui susceperit unum parvulum talem]] in the bowels of charity, or into his house to lodge and refresh him, namely one innocent and humble, of whom eternal Wisdom says in Proverbs, [[Prov 9:4|Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me|Si quis est parvulus, veniat ad me]]; [[18:5|in my name|in nomine meo]], that is, because he is one of the faithful, or for My sake and for the glory of My name; [[18:5|receiveth me|me suscipit]] in My mystical member, though not in Myself. So, receiveth Me, that is, I judge to be done to Me what is done to him, and it is as pleasing to Me as if it were shown to Me in person. For the Church is the mystical body of Christ, and He is its head: so what is done to the members is done to the head. Christ so loves the little and the needy that He reckons done to Himself what is spent on them. Hence He says to Paul: [[Acts 9:4|why persecutest thou me|Quid me persequeris]]? And through Zacharias: [[Zach 2:8|he that toucheth you, toucheth the apple of my eye|Qui tetigerit (inquit) vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei]].

paras.t: Qui autem scandalizaverit, id est, verbo vel facto suo inordinato ad peccandum induxerit, unum, id est aliquem, de pusillis istis qui in me credunt, id est de fidelibus adhuc imperfectis incipientibus, vel etiam proficientibus nondum perfectis; expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus. Per molam asinariam, quam equi vel asini trahunt cum rota in molendinis, intelligitur quodcumque grande saxum seu lapis gravissimus. Et demergatur in profundum maris. Utilius enim sibi est juste occidi, quam impie vivere: utilius est enim corporalem perpeti mortem, quam alium ad animæ mortem inducere. Utilius ei est in vita hac puniri, quam æternaliter condemnari. Istud potissimum verum est de scandalizatione activa et passiva prout sunt peccata mortalia. Tunc enim scandalum activum mortale est, quando verbum vel factum scandalizantis est in se mortale, videlicet caritati vel justitiæ contrarium; vel quando est in se veniale, et tamen homo per illud intendit aut nititur alium ad peccatum mortale inducere, parvi pendens ejus salutem, per hoc quod non vult sibi placentia omittere propter fratris salutem. Quod quam sit iniquum, patet ex verbis Pauli dicentis: Sic autem in fratres peccantes et percutientes conscientiam eorum infirmam, in Christum peccatis; et rursus, Hoc (inquit) judicate, ne ponatis fratribus offendiculum vel scandalum. Denique melius esset occidi quam scandalizare alium, quamvis scandalizantis et scandalizati peccatum esset veniale. Peccatum namque est infinitæ fugibilitatis, magisque debet homo eligere mortem pati, quam venialiter peccare.
paras.en: [[18:6|But he that shall scandalize|Qui autem scandalizaverit]], that is, lead into sin by his disordered word or deed, [[18:6|one of these little ones that believe in me|unum, id est aliquem, de pusillis istis qui in me credunt]], one, that is, anyone, of the faithful who are still imperfect beginners, or even making progress but not yet perfect; [[18:6|it were better for him that a millstone should be hanged about his neck|expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus]]. By the millstone [literally "ass's mill"], which horses or asses turn with a wheel in mills, is understood any great rock or very heavy stone. [[18:6|and that he should be drowned in the depth of the sea|Et demergatur in profundum maris]]. For it is better for him to be justly put to death than to live wickedly; it is better to suffer bodily death than to lead another to the death of the soul; it is better for him to be punished in this life than to be condemned eternally. This is true above all of active and passive scandal insofar as they are mortal sins. For active scandal is mortal when the word or deed of the one who gives scandal is mortal in itself, that is, contrary to charity or justice; or when it is venial in itself, yet a man intends or tries by it to lead another into mortal sin, holding his salvation cheap by not being willing to give up what pleases him for the sake of his brother's salvation. How wicked this is appears from the words of Paul: [[1 Cor 8:12|when you sin thus against the brethren and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ|Sic autem in fratres peccantes et percutientes conscientiam eorum infirmam, in Christum peccatis]]; and again: [[Rom 14:13|judge this rather, that you put not a stumblingblock or a scandal in your brother's way|Hoc (inquit) judicate, ne ponatis fratribus offendiculum vel scandalum]]. Indeed, it would be better to be killed than to scandalize another, even if the sin of the one giving scandal and of the one scandalized were venial. For sin is infinitely to be fled, and a man ought rather to choose to suffer death than to sin venially.

paras.t: Et bene ait Salvator, Qui scandalizaverit unum ex pusillis istis: quia ut ait Hieronymus, qui scandalizatur parvulus est; majores enim scandala non recipiunt. Unde perfectorum non est scandalizare aut scandalizari, quia tam fortiter cum Deo uniti sunt, ut tam magnum malum non operentur, unde merito aliquis debeat scandalizari, quamvis sæpe venialiter peccent. Hoc enim humanæ indulgendum est fragilitati. Similiter ex verbis et factis aliorum inordinatis non scandalizantur, sed compatiuntur, et cautiores redduntur, imo et feliciores, juxta illud: Felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum. Hinc ait Psalmista: Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam, et non est illis scandalum; et Apostolus, Quis nos separabit a caritate Dei?
paras.en: And the Saviour rightly says, he that shall scandalize one of these little ones: for, as Jerome says, he who is scandalized is a little one; the greater do not take scandal. So it is not for the perfect to scandalize or be scandalized, since they are so strongly united with God that they do not commit so great an evil that anyone should rightly be scandalized by it, although they often sin venially; for this must be pardoned to human frailty. Likewise they are not scandalized by the disordered words and deeds of others, but feel compassion and become more careful, indeed happier, according to that saying: "Happy the man whom others' dangers make careful." Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law, and to them there is no stumbling block|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam, et non est illis scandalum]]; and the Apostle: [[Rom 8:35|Who then shall separate us from the love|Quis nos separabit a caritate]] of God?

paras.t: Væ mundo, id est mundanis et intimoratis hominibus, a scandalis, id est propter scandala quæ invicem inferunt et patiuntur, in quibus æternam pœnam merentur. Et merito, Væ mundo a scandalis, quum non possit evadere, necesse est enim ut veniant, id est oriantur, scandala activa et passiva, videlicet offendicula culpæ ex quibus procedunt nocumenta animæ. Hoc necesse est, non absolute, sed ex suppositione, quia videlicet homines nolunt peccata sua relinquere: ideo necessario concomitatur scandalum aliorum, maxime pusillorum et impiorum. Sic ergo necesse est ut veniant scandala, quomodo ait Apostolus: Necesse est ut veniant hæreses, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant. Unde quod dictum est, Necesse est ut veniant scandala, quidam exponunt sic: Expediens est ad exercitationem et probationem aliorum. Verumtamen væ, id est, æterna damnatio imminet ac debetur, homini illi per quem, id est a quo, scandalum venit, id est, qui alium scandalizat mortaliter. Ex hoc concluditur quod scandala evenire, non sit absolute necessarium, quia tunc quilibet excusaretur a vitio scandali. Radix namque peccati in libertate fundatur.
paras.en: [[18:7|Woe to the world|Væ mundo]], that is, to worldly men without the fear of God, [[18:7|because of scandals|a scandalis]], that is, because of the scandals they give and suffer from one another, by which they deserve eternal punishment. And rightly, woe to the world because of scandals, since it cannot escape them: [[18:7|For it must needs be that scandals come|Necesse est enim ut veniant scandala]], that is, arise, active and passive, namely stumbling-blocks of sin, from which harm to the soul comes. This is necessary not absolutely, but on a supposition, namely because men will not give up their sins; so scandal to others, above all to the little and the wicked, necessarily goes with them. So it must needs be that scandals come in the way the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:19|For there must be also heresies: that they also, who are approved may be made manifest|Necesse est ut veniant hæreses, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant]]. Hence some explain the saying "it must needs be that scandals come" thus: it is expedient for the exercise and testing of others. [[18:7|but nevertheless woe|Verumtamen væ]], that is, eternal damnation threatens and is owed, [[18:7|to that man by whom the scandal cometh|homini illi, per quem scandalum venit]], that is, who scandalizes another mortally. From this it follows that it is not absolutely necessary for scandals to come, for then everyone would be excused from the vice of scandal; for the root of sin is grounded in freedom.

paras.t: Si autem manus tua vel pes tuus scandalizat, id est, ad culpam inducit te, per actum seu operationem quamcumque, vel per gressum ac cursum illicitum, abscinde eum, videlicet pedem ac manum, non membra abscindendo, sed inordinatum usum membrorum vitando: juxta quem sensum dicit Apostolus, Mortificate membra vestra quæ sunt super terram; et projice abs te, id est, spiritualiter separa te a vitiosis actibus membrorum istorum. Sic enim ait Apostolus: Vos autem in carne non estis, sed in spiritu; et, Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt. Bonum est tibi ad vitam ingredi, id est, melius est tibi salvari, debilem vel claudum, id est inordinatis, delectabilibus et solitis actibus manuum et pedum carentem, quam duas manus vel duos pedes habentem, id est, vitiosis ac placitis actibus membrorum istorum utentem, mitti in ignem æternum. Quemadmodum ergo castratus propter regnum cœlorum vocatur, qui amore felicitatis futuræ ab omni concubitu abstinet, non qui membra generationis abscindit; sic Christus docet manum ac pedem abscindere, et sic claudus ac debilis nuncupatur, qui membra ista ab actibus malis restringit.
paras.en: [[18:8|And if thy hand, or thy foot, scandalize thee|Si autem manus tua vel pes tuus scandalizat, id est, ad culpam inducit te]], that is, leads you into sin by any act or work, or by unlawful walking and running, [[18:8|cut it off|abscinde eum]], the foot or the hand, that is, not by cutting off the limbs, but by avoiding the disordered use of the limbs; in which sense the Apostle says: [[Col 3:5|Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth|Mortificate membra vestra quæ sunt super terram]]; [[18:8|and cast it from thee|et projice abs te]], that is, separate yourself spiritually from the sinful acts of these limbs. For so the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:9|But you are not in the flesh, but the spirit|Vos autem in carne non estis, sed in spiritu]]; and, [[Rom 8:8|they who are in the flesh cannot please God|Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt]]. [[18:8|It is better for thee to go into life maimed or lame|Bonum est tibi ad vitam ingredi, id est, melius est tibi salvari, debilem vel claudum]], that is, it is better for you to be saved lacking the disordered, pleasant and habitual acts of hands and feet, [[18:8|than having two hands or two feet, to be cast into everlasting fire|quam duas manus vel duos pedes habentem mitti in ignem æternum]], that is, using the sinful and pleasing acts of these limbs. So as he is called a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven[[Matt 19:12||]] who for love of future happiness abstains from all intercourse, not one who cuts off the members of generation, so Christ teaches us to cut off hand and foot, and he is called lame and maimed who restrains these limbs from evil acts.

paras.t: Et si oculus tuus scandalizat te, per immoderatum, incautum, impudicum aut vanum adspectum, erue eum, quantum ad usum hujusmodi, et projice abs te, sicut de manibus dictum est. Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur: Averte oculos tuos a muliere compta. Et Propheta: Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem. Maxime necessaria est ista projectio sive erutio oculorum. Oculo enim quid nequius creatum est? Et in libro Numerorum Dominus jussit filiis Israel, ne sequerentur oculos suos per res varias fornicantes. Custodiendus ergo et diligentissime refrenandus est oculus, maxime tempore orationis, contemplationis, divinique cultus, et in ecclesia, ac coram aliis. A visu enim suo cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei, sensatus, prudens. Bonum, id est melius, est tibi cum uno oculo, id est cum moderato usu oculorum et refrenatione eorum, ad vitam ingredi, quam duos oculos habentem, id est, oculis ad libitum tuum utentem et undique circumspicientem, mitti in gehennam ignis.
paras.en: [[18:9|And if thy eye scandalize thee|Et si oculus tuus scandalizat te]], by immoderate, careless, shameless or vain looking, [[18:9|pluck it out|erue eum]], as to such use, [[18:9|and cast it from thee|et projice abs te]], as was said of the hands. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 9:8|Turn away thy face from a woman dressed up|Averte oculos tuos a muliere compta]]. And the Prophet: [[Ps 118:37|Turn away my eyes that they may not behold vanity|Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem]]. This casting away or plucking out of the eyes is most necessary. For [[Ecclus 31:15|What is created more wicked than an eye|Oculo enim quid nequius creatum est?]]? And in the book of Numbers the Lord commanded the children of Israel not to follow [[Num 15:39|their own thoughts and eyes going astray after divers things|oculos suos per res varias fornicantes]]. The eye, then, is to be guarded and most carefully curbed, above all at the time of prayer, contemplation and divine worship, and in church, and in the presence of others. For [[Ecclus 19:26|A man is known by his look, and a wise man, when thou meetest him, is known by his countenance|A visu enim suo cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei, sensatus]]. [[18:9|It is better for thee having one eye to enter into life|Bonum … est tibi cum uno oculo … ad vitam ingredi]], that is, with a moderate use of the eyes and a curbing of them, [[18:9|than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire|quam duos oculos habentem mitti in gehennam ignis]], that is, using your eyes as you please and looking about everywhere.

paras.t: Porro præhabita alio modo exponi possunt; eritque sensus: Si manus tua vel pes tuus, id est aliquis tibi tam carus, propinquus, aut auxiliativus, ut propria manus vel pes, scandalizat te, pertrahendo te in peccata, vel quia carnales affectiones habes exsistendo cum ipso, abscinde eum, id est, segrega te ab ipso mente et corpore, sed non caritate, si fieri potest. Bonum est tibi ad vitam ingredi debilem vel claudum, id est talium amicitia atque subsidio destitutum, quam duas manus vel duos pedes habentem, id est talium auxilio et amore vallatum, damnari. Simili modo intelligendum de oculo est. Quidam obtusi ista superficialiter intelligentes, putabant licitam esse mutilationem membrorum propter vitanda peccata, quum simili ratione liceret se ipsum occidere. Talis quoque mutilatio concupiscentiam non auferret, et multa virtuosa opera impediret.
paras.en: Further, these words can be explained in another way, and the sense will be: if thy hand or thy foot, that is, someone as dear to you, as close or as helpful as your own hand or foot, scandalize thee by drawing you into sins, or because you have carnal affections when you are with him, cut him off, that is, separate yourself from him in mind and body, but not in charity, if it can be done. It is better for you to go into life maimed or lame, that is, without the friendship and help of such people, than having two hands or two feet, that is, surrounded by their help and love, to be damned. The eye is to be understood in the same way. Some dull people, understanding these things superficially, thought that mutilation of the limbs was lawful in order to avoid sins, whereas by the same reasoning it would be lawful to kill oneself. Such mutilation, besides, would not take away concupiscence, and would hinder many virtuous works.

paras.t: Videte ne contemnatis unum, id est aliquem, quantumcumque vilem ac modicum, ex his pusillis, id est imperfectis fidelibus ministrantibus mihi. Per hoc Salvator excludit causam ac fomitem scandalizationis. Multi namque idcirco non curant nec metuunt alios scandalizare, quoniam parvi pendunt eorum personam, nec attendunt dignitatem naturæ ad Dei imaginem factæ, nec pretium sanguinis Christi pro illis effusi. Consideremus ergo nobilitatem animæ rationalis, et beatitudinem ad quam condita est, et quanta pro ejus salute tota Trinitas fecit, quanta Christus sustinuit, quanta beneficia contulit, inter quæ est superdignissimum corporis et sanguinis sui Sacramentum; et sic fiet ut neminem aspernemur, sed cum Apostolo dicemus: Quis scandalizatur, et ego non uror? Itemque: Si esca scandalizat fratrem meum, non manducabo carnem in æternum. Præterea, quam vitiosum sit contemnere quempiam, patet ex eo quod in Isaia scriptum est: Væ qui spernis, nonne et ipse sperneris? Quum fatigatus desieris contemnere, contemneris. Et Malachias inquit: Numquid non pater unus omnium nostrum? numquid non Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo unusquisque nostrum despicit fratrem suum? Cur autem non sint pusilli spernendi, subjungitur. Dico enim vobis, quia angeli eorum, id est custodes animarum ipsorum exsistentes, ut in pluribus, in cœlis, id est in cœlo empyreo, quod est locus et mansio Beatorum, semper, id est indesinenter atque in ævo omne tempus comprehendente, vident clare et immediate per speciem, oculo intellectuali, faciem Patris mei, id est essentiam Dei Patris præsentialiter et luculenter eis objectam, qui in cœlis est. Quum ergo sit tanta dignitas hominum, ut custodiantur a spiritibus angelicis Deum clare videntibus, non sunt spernendi. Porro, secundum Dionysium, ecclesiastica hierarchia ab angelica gubernatur: ideo angeli infimi ordinis immediate custodiunt homines, bona suggerendo, a malis plurimis retrahendo, a diversis periculis defendendo, pro ipsis orando, gratiam impetrando, dæmonum potestatem et impetum coercendo. Et secundum doctores, quilibet homo sortitus est angelum specialem: imo secundum Thomam et alios quosdam, etiam pueri nondum nati, in utero matrum habent custodientes se angelos, propter pericula quæ possunt ante partum et in partu occurrere.
paras.en: [[18:10|See that you despise not one of these little ones|Videte ne contemnatis unum ex his pusillis]], one, that is, anyone, however mean and small, of these little ones, that is, imperfect believers who serve Me. By this the Saviour removes the cause and tinder of giving scandal. For many do not care about or fear scandalizing others because they think little of their person, and do not consider the dignity of a nature made in the image of God, nor the price of Christ's blood shed for them. Let us consider, then, the nobility of the rational soul, the blessedness for which it was made, how much the whole Trinity has done for its salvation, how much Christ endured, how many benefits He bestowed, among which is the most surpassingly worthy Sacrament of His body and blood; and so it will come about that we despise no one, but shall say with the Apostle: [[2 Cor 11:29|Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire|Quis scandalizatur, et ego non uror]]? And again: [[1 Cor 8:13|if meat scandalize my brother, I will never eat flesh|Si esca scandalizat fratrem meum, non manducabo carnem in æternum]]. Moreover, how sinful it is to despise anyone appears from what is written in Isaias: Woe to thee [[Is 33:1|that despisest, shalt not thyself also be despised|qui spernis, nonne et ipse sperneris]]? [[Is 33:1|when being wearied thou shalt cease to despise|Quum fatigatus desieris contemnere]], thou shalt be despised. And Malachias says: [[Mal 2:10|Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why then doth every one of us despise his brother|Numquid non pater unus omnium nostrum? numquid non Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo unusquisque nostrum despicit fratrem suum]]? Why the little ones are not to be despised is added: [[18:10|for I say to you, that their angels|Dico enim vobis, quia angeli eorum]], that is, the guardians of their souls, as is so in most cases, [[18:10|in heaven|in cœlis]], that is, in the empyrean heaven, which is the place and dwelling of the Blessed, [[18:10|always|semper]], that is, unceasingly and in the aeviternity that includes all time [aevum, the measure of angelic existence], [[18:10|see|vident]] clearly and immediately, face to face, with the eye of the intellect, [[18:10|the face of my Father who is in heaven|faciem Patris mei, id est essentiam Dei Patris præsentialiter et luculenter eis objectam, qui in cœlis est]], that is, the essence of God the Father, presented to them directly and brightly. Since, then, the dignity of men is so great that they are guarded by angelic spirits who see God clearly, they are not to be despised. Further, according to Dionysius, the ecclesiastical hierarchy is governed by the angelic: so angels of the lowest order guard men directly, suggesting good things, drawing them back from very many evils, defending them from various dangers, praying for them, obtaining grace for them, and restraining the power and assault of the demons. And according to the doctors every man has been allotted a particular angel; indeed, according to Thomas and some others, even children not yet born have angels guarding them in their mothers' wombs, because of the dangers that can occur before and during birth.

paras.t: At vero alia ratio subditur, cur nemo quamvis pusillus spernendus sit. Venit enim, per incarnationem, Filius hominis salvare, id est sua passione redimere, quod perierat, id est perditum genus hominum. Quum ergo tantæ æstimationis coram Deo pusilli sint, ut Christus dignum duceret mori pro ipsis, non sunt parvi pendendi, nec salus eorum negligenda est. Quod autem Christus venit ad salvandum quod periit, probat per simile.
paras.en: Another reason is added why no one, however little, is to be despised. [[18:11|For the Son of man is come|Venit enim, per incarnationem, Filius hominis]] by the incarnation [[18:11|to save|salvare]], that is, to redeem by His Passion, [[18:11|that which was lost|quod perierat]], that is, the lost human race. Since, then, the little ones are of such worth before God that Christ thought it fitting to die for them, they are not to be held cheap, nor their salvation neglected. That Christ came to save what was lost He proves by a comparison.

paras.t: Quid vobis videtur? Si fuerint alicui centum oves, id est, centum oves habuerit, et si erraverit, id est, si perdita fuerit, una ex illis, nonne relinquit nonaginta novem oves in montibus in quibus pascuntur, et vadit quærere eam quæ erravit? Et si contigerit ut inveniat eam, amen dico vobis, quia gaudet super eam, id est de ea et ejus inventione, magis quam super nonaginta novem oves quæ non erraverunt. Non quod simpliciter plus amet illam unam quam ceteras omnes, sed quia speciali atque recenti quadam lætitia propter eam afficitur. Quod accidit propter duo: primo, quoniam eam magis considerat quam alias oves; secundo, quoniam propter præcedentem de perditione ovis tristitiam, magis sentit oppositum gaudium. Hoc totum ad litteram sic est. Mystice vero, homo iste est Christus, qui habuit centum oves, id est perfectum numerum electorum. Quumque una errasset, id est, humanum genus peccando perisset, reliquit nonaginta novem, id est novem ordines angelorum, in montibus, id est in cœlis, de quibus legitur, Levavi oculos meos in montes; et venit in mundum, quærens et salvans genus humanum. Magis autem lætatur Christus, et etiam angeli, de una ove perdita reperta, quam super nonaginta novem; vel, ut Lucas refert: Gaudium est angelis Dei super uno peccatore pœnitentiam agente, quam super nonaginta novem justis qui non indigent pœnitentia. Non quod absolute loquendo, peccator pœnitens melior aut magis dilectus sit, quam multi justi perseverantes in bono; imo comparando statum statui, meliores sunt innocentes quam pœnitentes. Sed hæc ideo dicta sunt, quia de peccatore pœnitente habet Christus quoddam speciale gaudium. Lætatur enim Dominus in operibus suis. Et in Nehemia habetur: Gaudium Domini est fortitudo vestra. Et quia in his frequenter abundant fervor et gratia, in quibus abundavit malitia, sicque amabiliores redduntur.
paras.en: [[18:12|What think you? If a man have an hundred sheep|Quid vobis videtur? Si fuerint alicui centum oves]], that is, if he has a hundred sheep, [[18:12|and one of them should go astray|et si erraverit, id est, si perdita fuerit, una ex illis]], that is, be lost, [[18:12|doth he not leave the ninety-nine in the mountains|nonne relinquit nonaginta novem oves in montibus]] where they graze, [[18:12|and goeth to seek that which is gone astray|et vadit quærere eam quæ erravit]]? [[18:13|And if it so be that he find it: Amen I say to you, he rejoiceth more for that|Et si contigerit ut inveniat eam: amen dico vobis, quia gaudet super eam magis]], that is, over it and over finding it, [[18:13|than for the ninety-nine that went not astray|quam super nonaginta novem oves quæ non erraverunt]]. Not that he simply loves that one more than all the rest, but that he is moved by a special and fresh joy because of it. This happens for two reasons: first, because he is paying more attention to it than to the other sheep; second, because, after his previous sadness at the loss of the sheep, he feels the opposite joy more. All this is so in the letter. Mystically, this man is Christ, who had a hundred sheep, that is, the perfect number of the elect. When one had gone astray, that is, when the human race had perished by sinning, He left the ninety-nine, that is, the nine orders of angels, in the mountains, that is, in the heavens, of which we read: [[Ps 120:1|I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains|Levavi oculos meos in montes]]; and He came into the world, seeking and saving the human race. And Christ, and the angels too, rejoice more over the one lost sheep found than over the ninety-nine; or, as Luke reports: [[Luke 15:7|there shall be joy|Gaudium est]] to the angels of God [[Luke 15:7|upon one sinner that doth penance, more than upon ninety-nine just who need not penance|super uno peccatore pœnitentiam agente, quam super nonaginta novem justis qui non indigent pœnitentia]][[Luke 15:10||]]. Not that, speaking absolutely, a penitent sinner is better or more loved than many just men persevering in good; indeed, comparing state with state, the innocent are better than the penitent. But this is said because Christ has a special joy over a penitent sinner. For [[Ps 103:31|the Lord shall rejoice in his works|Lætatur enim Dominus in operibus suis]]. And in Nehemias [2 Esdras] we have: [[2 Esd 8:10|the joy of the Lord is our strength|Gaudium Domini est fortitudo vestra]]. And because fervour and grace often abound in those in whom malice abounded, and so they are made more lovable.

paras.t: Sic non est voluntas ante Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est, id est in Patre cœlesti, ut pereat, id est damnetur, unus de pusillis istis. Quamvis enim divina voluntas sit causa salutis prædestinatorum, non tamen est causa damnationis reproborum; nec ipse vult eos damnari voluntate antecedente vel voluntate signi, sed voluntate consequente, considerata culpa eorum. Sed posset aliquis dicere: Si non est voluntas Dei ut pereat unus ex pusillis, ergo voluntas Dei est ut omnes pusilli salventur. Quod etiam sacra Scriptura testatur. Dicit enim Apostolus, loquens de Deo: Qui, inquiens, vult omnes homines salvos fieri, et ad veritatis agnitionem venire. Et Petrus: Patienter, inquiens, agit Dominus, nolens aliquem perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam converti. Unde per Ezechielem Dominus loquitur: Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii, dicit Dominus, et non ut convertatur et vivat? Et denuo: Nolo, inquit, mortem morientis. Sed si ita est, videtur sequi quod omnes salvabuntur. Nam teste Apostolo: Voluntati ejus quis resistit? In Isaia quoque perhibet Dominus: Consilium, inquiens, meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet. Denique omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus fecit in cœlo et in terra. Hæc atque similia concordando respondet Damascenus, quod Dominus vult omnes salvari voluntate antecedente, non consequente: quæ duplex voluntas in Deo sola ratione distinguitur. Dicitur namque voluntas antecedens, qua quis aliquid vult secundum communem et absolutam considerationem ipsius. Hac voluntate vult princeps omnes subditos suos permanere in vita, in quantum sunt subditi sui. Voluntas vero consequens dicitur, qua quis aliquid vult, pensatis particularibus circumstantiis ejus. Hac voluntate vult princeps multos subditorum suorum occidi, in quantum sunt latrones, aut fures, vel rei publicæ adversantes. Itaque voluntas dicitur antecedens, quia secundum ordinem rationis præcedit distinctam considerationem rei, seu conditionem ipsius; consequens vero, quia consequitur eam. Sic ergo et Deus vult omnes salvari voluntate antecedente, considerando eos in quantum sunt creaturæ ad Dei imaginem factæ, beatitudinis susceptivæ; non autem voluntate consequente, videlicet in quantum sunt impii. Et quia voluntas fertur in rem sicut in se est, ideo voluntas antecedens, non est voluntas simpliciter, sed secundum quid; voluntas vero consequens est voluntas simpliciter. Ideo quidquid hac voluntate vult Deus, impletur. Et de ea loquuntur auctoritates quibus ostenditur adimpleri quidquid voluerit Deus. Potest etiam dici, quod non est voluntas ante Deum ut pereat aliquis, quoniam Deus vult omnes salvari, quantum in se est, ita quod ex parte ipsius non est defectus, nullumque ad se venientem repellit, quoniam singulis gratiam suam infundere est paratus, si fecerint quod in ipsis est. De hac materia plenius dixi super epistolas Pauli.
paras.en: [[18:14|Even so it is not the will of your Father, who is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish|Sic non est voluntas ante Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est, … ut pereat … unus de pusillis istis]]: the will, that is, in the heavenly Father; perish, that is, be damned. For although the divine will is the cause of the salvation of the predestined, it is not the cause of the damnation of the reprobate; nor does He will them to be damned by His antecedent will, or by His will of sign [that is, His will as made known by signs such as precepts], but by His consequent will, their guilt being considered. But someone might say: if it is not God's will that one of the little ones should perish, then it is God's will that all the little ones be saved. And holy Scripture testifies to this too; for the Apostle says of God: [[1 Tim 2:4|Who will have all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth|Qui, inquiens, vult omnes homines salvos fieri, et ad veritatis agnitionem venire]]. And Peter: the Lord [[2 Pet 3:9|dealeth patiently for your sake, not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance|Patienter, inquiens, agit Dominus, nolens aliquem perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam converti]]. Hence the Lord says through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:23|Is it my will that a sinner should die, saith the Lord God, and not that he should be converted from his ways, and live|Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii, dicit Dominus, et non ut convertatur et vivat]]? And again: [[Ezech 18:32|I desire not the death of him that dieth|Nolo, inquit, mortem morientis]]. But if this is so, it seems to follow that all will be saved. For, as the Apostle testifies: [[Rom 9:19|who resisteth his will|Voluntati ejus quis resistit]]? And in Isaias the Lord declares: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done|Consilium, inquiens, meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet]]. And [[Ps 134:6|Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done, in heaven, in earth|omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus fecit in cœlo et in terra]]. Damascene, reconciling these and similar texts, answers that the Lord wills all to be saved by His antecedent will, not by His consequent will; and this twofold will in God is distinguished by reason alone. That will is called antecedent by which one wills something according to a general and absolute consideration of it: by this will a prince wills all his subjects to remain alive, inasmuch as they are his subjects. That will is called consequent by which one wills something after weighing its particular circumstances: by this will a prince wills many of his subjects to be put to death, inasmuch as they are robbers, thieves, or enemies of the commonwealth. So a will is called antecedent because in the order of reason it comes before the distinct consideration of the thing, or of its condition; and consequent because it follows it. So God too wills all to be saved by His antecedent will, considering them as creatures made in the image of God and capable of blessedness; but not by His consequent will, namely inasmuch as they are wicked. And because the will bears on a thing as it is in itself, the antecedent will is not will simply, but in a certain respect; whereas the consequent will is will simply. So whatever God wills by this will is fulfilled; and the authorities that show that whatever God wills is fulfilled speak of this will. It can also be said that it is not the will of God that anyone should perish, because God wills all to be saved as far as lies in Him, so that there is no failing on His side, and He repels no one who comes to Him, being ready to pour His grace into each, if they do what lies in them. I have spoken of this matter more fully on the Epistles of Paul.

paras.t: Superius docuit Christus ut neminem scandalizemus; nunc præcipit ut proximos ex caritate ædificemus, vitia eorum ordinate, pie et caritative increpando. Si autem peccaverit in te frater tuus, vade et corripe eum inter te et ipsum solum. Per fratrem intelligitur quilibet proximus. Quod autem dicitur, In te, intelligi potest tripliciter: Primo, secundum Augustinum, In te, id est te sciente: quia qui alio sciente peccat, quantum in se est illum scandalizat; sicque scientia culpæ læsiva est, sicut cognitio boni est ad melius provocativa. Secundo, juxta Hieronymum, In te, id est contra te directe, non contra Deum directe. Si enim fieret blasphemia vel impugnatio fidei, non oporteret servare ordinem subsequentem. Tertio, In te, id est te solum læserit. Si enim alios læderet, vel coram aliis peccaret, non servaretur modus subscriptus. Vade, mentis promptæ affectu, vel si opus est, etiam corporis gressu, et corripe eum inter te et ipsum solum, videlicet in secreto, ne confundatur, exasperetur, aut diffametur, et diffamatus de cetero non retrahatur a vitiis timore diffamiæ, sed fiat ei frons meretricis, et peccet sine rubore. Si te audierit aure mentali, id est, tuæ increpationi humiliter acquieverit, lucratus es fratrem tuum, id est, perditum recuperasti, et de jugo peccati ac damnatione diaboli eripuisti.
paras.en: Above, Christ taught that we should scandalize no one; now He commands that we build up our neighbours out of charity, rebuking their faults in an orderly, loving and charitable way. [[18:15|But if thy brother shall offend against thee, go, and rebuke him between thee and him alone|Si autem peccaverit in te frater tuus, vade et corripe eum inter te et ipsum solum]]. By brother is meant any neighbour. "Against thee" can be understood in three ways. First, according to Augustine: against thee, that is, with your knowledge; for one who sins with another's knowledge scandalizes him as far as lies in him; and so knowledge of a fault does harm, as knowledge of good spurs one to better. Second, according to Jerome: against thee, that is, directly against you, not directly against God; for if it were blasphemy or an attack on the faith, the order that follows would not need to be kept. Third: against thee, that is, he has injured you alone; for if he injured others, or sinned before others, the procedure described would not be kept. Go, with a ready mind, or if need be with bodily steps too, and rebuke him between thee and him alone, that is, in private, lest he be put to shame, angered or defamed, and, once defamed, no longer be held back from vice by the fear of infamy, but take on [[Jer 3:3|a harlot's forehead|frons meretricis]] and sin without blushing. [[18:15|If he shall hear thee|Si te audierit]] with the ear of the mind, that is, humbly accept your rebuke, [[18:15|thou shalt gain thy brother|lucratus es fratrem tuum]], that is, you have recovered him who was lost, and snatched him from the yoke of sin and the damnation of the devil.

paras.t: Si autem te non audierit, hoc est, verba tua contempserit, vel se excusaverit, vel id quod fecit, bonum esse affirmaverit, non peccatum, adhibe tecum unum testem vel duos, id est, in præsentia unius vel duorum testium corripe eum, ne cito coram omnibus diffametur, sed paulatim peccatum ejus deducatur in publicum, ut in ore, id est sermone, duorum testium vel trium, videlicet duorum quos adduxisti, et tui qui primo culpam novisti, stet, id est, probetur atque credatur, omne verbum quod delinquenti objicitur, scilicet accusatio. Quod si non audierit eos, qui simul tecum corripiunt eum, dic Ecclesiæ, id est prælato seu judici vel congregationi communiter, quid ille fecerit vel omiserit impie, et quomodo correptionem secretam ac testium adhibitionem abjecit, manens in sua duritia. Si autem Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus, id est gentilis, et publicanus, qui manifeste et quasi incorrigibiliter peccat, ut usurarii: id est, tunc omnino recedas, et retrahas te ab eo, quasi ab eo qui per excommunicationem ecclesiasticamque censuram separari meretur a communione fidelium.
paras.en: [[18:16|And if he will not hear thee|Si autem te non audierit]], that is, if he despises your words, or excuses himself, or affirms that what he did is good and not a sin, [[18:16|take with thee one or two more|adhibe tecum unum testem vel duos]], that is, rebuke him in the presence of one or two witnesses, lest he be quickly defamed before all, but so that his sin may be brought into the open little by little; [[18:16|that in the mouth of two or three witnesses|ut in ore, id est sermone, duorum testium vel trium]], in the mouth, that is, by the word, of the two whom you brought and yourself, who first knew of the fault, [[18:16|every word may stand|stet omne verbum]], that is, every charge brought against the offender, the accusation, may be proved and believed. [[18:17|And if he will not hear them|Quod si non audierit eos]], who rebuke him together with you, [[18:17|tell the church|dic Ecclesiæ]], that is, the prelate or judge, or the community in general, what wicked thing he has done or left undone, and how he rejected the private rebuke and the calling of witnesses, remaining in his hardness. [[18:17|And if he will not hear the church, let him be to thee as the heathen and publican|Si autem Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus, id est gentilis, et publicanus]]: the heathen, that is, the Gentile, and the publican, who sins openly and as if incorrigibly, like usurers; that is, then withdraw from him altogether and keep away from him, as from one who deserves to be separated from the communion of the faithful by excommunication and ecclesiastical censure.

paras.t: Porro, quod Apostolorum et successorum eorum, videlicet prælatorum, excommunicatio et sententia vim habeant, et divino judicio approbentur, atque a Deo efficientiam sortiantur, ostendit Salvator subdendo: Amen dico vobis Apostolis, et in persona vestra successoribus vestris, quæcumque facta vel genera hominum alligaveritis, per excommunicationem, reprobationem, vel condemnationem, super terram, erunt ligata et in cœlo, id est, a Deo ligata reputabuntur, si tamen ordinate procedatur; et quæcumque solveritis, id est, dimiseritis seu relaxaveritis, super terram, erunt soluta et in cœlo. Hoc superius dictum est Petro, illicque diligentius expositum est.
paras.en: That the excommunication and sentence of the Apostles and of their successors, namely the prelates, have force, are approved by the divine judgment, and receive their efficacy from God, the Saviour shows by adding: [[18:18|Amen I say to you|Amen dico vobis]] Apostles, and in your person to your successors, [[18:18|whatsoever you shall bind upon earth|quæcumque … alligaveritis … super terram]], whatever deeds or kinds of men, by excommunication, rejection or condemnation, [[18:18|shall be bound also in heaven|erunt ligata et in cœlo]], that is, will be reckoned bound by God, provided that the proceedings are orderly; [[18:18|and whatsoever you shall loose upon earth|et quæcumque solveritis super terram]], that is, forgive or release, [[18:18|shall be loosed also in heaven|erunt soluta et in cœlo]]. This was said above to Peter, and explained more carefully there[[Matt 16:19||]].

paras.t: Denique, quum præsens materia sit practica, utilis et quotidiana, oportet paulisper plenius loqui de correptione fraterna, de testium inductione, et publica denuntiatione. Primo ergo sciendum, quod vitium delinquentis consideratur dupliciter: Primo, in quantum nocet peccanti. Et sic peccantem arguere, actus est caritatis, ad quem omnes tenemur, quemadmodum et ad caritatem, quum ista correptio non sit nisi remedium contra peccatum. Unde in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Unicuique mandavit Deus de proximo suo. Secundo, consideratur peccatum prout est aliorum scandalizativum, vel boni communis læsivum ac turbativum, aut divinæ majestatis inhonorativum. Sicque peccantem arguere, est actus justitiæ, pertinens ad prælatos ac judices potius quam ad alios; quoniam talis correptio ordinatur præcipue ad debitam punitionem peccantis propter conservationem justitiæ, et non semper ad correctionem peccantis, quia interdum occiditur, ut vel sic alii terreantur, reprimanturque a similibus malis. Insuper, quum præceptum de correptione fraterna sit affirmativum, obligat semper, sed non ad semper. Propterea correptio ista exercenda est cum debitis circumstantiis actus virtuosi, videlicet pro loco, causa, et tempore, secundum quod utile est ad emendationem alterius. Unde fraterna correptio tribus modis omittitur: Primo, meritorie et ex caritate, quando videlicet congruum tempus exspectatur, vel de ampliori induratione peccantis probabiliter formidatur. Teste enim Scriptura, Qui derisorem instruit, ipse sibi injuriam facit; et, Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit. Secundo, omittitur vitiose, et cum mortali peccato, ut dum ex cupiditate, vel timore corporalis pœnæ seu damni temporalis, vel simili causa quæ non est caritati præferenda, omittitur. Tertio, cum veniali peccato, ut dum causæ prædictæ correptionem fraternam retardant, non tamen omnino impediunt.
paras.en: Further, since the present matter is practical, useful and of daily concern, we must speak a little more fully of fraternal correction, of the bringing in of witnesses, and of public denunciation. First, then, it should be known that the fault of the offender is considered in two ways. First, inasmuch as it harms the sinner; and so to reprove the sinner is an act of charity, to which we are all bound, as we are to charity, since this correction is nothing but a remedy against sin. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 17:12|he gave to every one of them commandment concerning his neighbour|Unicuique mandavit Deus de proximo suo]]. Second, sin is considered as it scandalizes others, or harms and disturbs the common good, or dishonours the divine majesty; and so to reprove the sinner is an act of justice, belonging to prelates and judges rather than to others; since such correction is ordered chiefly to the due punishment of the sinner for the preserving of justice, and not always to the amendment of the sinner, since sometimes he is put to death so that at least others may be terrified and held back from like evils. Moreover, since the precept of fraternal correction is affirmative, it binds always but not for always [that is, it is always in force but does not oblige at every moment]. Therefore this correction is to be exercised with the due circumstances of a virtuous act, namely of place, cause and time, as is useful for the amendment of the other. So fraternal correction is omitted in three ways. First, meritoriously and out of charity, namely when a fitting time is awaited, or when a greater hardening of the sinner is probably feared; for, as Scripture testifies, [[Prov 9:7|He that teacheth a scorner, doth an injury to himself|Qui derisorem instruit, ipse sibi injuriam facit]]; and, [[Prov 15:12|A corrupt man loveth not one that reproveth him|Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit]]. Second, it is omitted sinfully and with mortal sin, as when it is omitted out of greed, or fear of bodily punishment or temporal loss, or some like cause that is not to be preferred to charity. Third, with venial sin, as when these causes delay fraternal correction but do not prevent it altogether.

paras.t: Denique subditi prælatos suos corripere debent in vitiis manifestis vel correptione dignis, servatis tamen debitis circumstantiis, scilicet congruo loco, non in conventu, debito tempore, et debita forma, non proterve et dure, sed reverenter et mansuete. Unde Apostolus Colossenses hortatur, ut episcopum suum, scilicet Archippum, filium Philemonis, cui Paulus brevem ac specialem scripsit epistolam, admoneant, dicens: Archippo dicite: Vide ministerium tuum quod accepisti in Domino, ut illud impleas. Unde et Moyses qui quotidie angelico perfruebatur colloquio, documento ac magisterio, dedignatus non est viri gentilis Jethro increpationem et informationem recipere. Imo quo prælatus pluribus occupatur atque distrahitur, eo amplius indiget admonitione frequenti ac diligenti, nisi esset vehementer perfectus: quod non debet de se ipso sentire. Sed debet filiorum suorum humilem correptionem ac caritativam exhortationem dignanter et affectuose recipere. Ait enim Salomon in Proverbiis: Argue (inquiens) sapientem, et diliget te; da sapienti occasionem, et addetur ei sapientia; doce justum, et festinabit accipere. Præterea, fraterna correptio, ut est actus justitiæ pertinens ad prælatos, non est omittenda ob id ne correptus fiat deterior, quoniam talis correptio habet potestatem cogendi. Et ergo per pœnam compellendus est peccans, ut cesset a malo, si aliter nolit desistere. Ex tali quoque correptione utilitas oritur communitati, dum ordo justitiæ observatur, et alii exemplo puniti terrentur, ne agant similia. Propter quod scriptum est: Pestilente flagellato, stultus sapientior erit.
paras.en: Further, subjects ought to correct their prelates in faults that are manifest or deserve correction, keeping however the due circumstances: a fitting place, not in the assembly; a due time; and a due manner, not boldly and harshly but reverently and gently. Hence the Apostle urges the Colossians to admonish their bishop, namely Archippus, son of Philemon, to whom Paul wrote a short and special epistle, saying: [[Col 4:17|say to Archippus: Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfil it|Archippo dicite: Vide ministerium tuum quod accepisti in Domino, ut illud impleas]]. Hence too Moses, who daily enjoyed converse, teaching and instruction from the angels, did not disdain to receive the rebuke and instruction of a Gentile, Jethro[[Ex 18:14||]]. Indeed, the more a prelate is busied with many things and distracted, the more he needs frequent and careful admonition, unless he were exceedingly perfect, which he ought not to think of himself. But he ought to receive the humble correction and charitable exhortation of his sons graciously and with affection. For Solomon says in Proverbs: [[Prov 9:8|Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee|Argue (inquiens) sapientem, et diliget te]]; [[Prov 9:9|Give an occasion to a wise man, and wisdom shall be added to him. Teach a just man, and he shall make haste to receive it|da sapienti occasionem, et addetur ei sapientia; doce justum, et festinabit accipere]]. Moreover, fraternal correction, as an act of justice belonging to prelates, is not to be omitted lest the one corrected become worse, since such correction has the power of coercion; so the sinner must be compelled by punishment to cease from evil, if he will not stop otherwise. And from such correction benefit arises for the community, since the order of justice is kept and others are frightened by the example of the one punished from doing the like. Hence it is written: [[Prov 19:25|The wicked man being scourged, the fool shall be wiser|Pestilente flagellato, stultus sapientior erit]].

paras.t: Oportet insuper scire, quod quædam peccata sunt publica: et in talibus providere oportet, non solum peccanti, sed etiam aliis, ne scandalizentur. Talia itaque mox publice redarguenda sunt, prout Timotheo jubet Apostolus: Peccantem, inquiens, coram omnibus argue, ut ceteri timorem habeant. Quædam vero peccata contrariantur fidei, vel bono communi: et in talibus, quamvis occulta sint, statim procedendum est ad publicationem, ut si quis machinetur civitatem incendere, vel fidem aliorum corrumpere. Si tamen verisimiliter æstimet quis, quod taliter peccantem possit per secretam increpationem corrigere, potest primo occulte corripere. Quædam autem sunt peccata occulta soli peccanti nociva, et ei in quem peccat, qui ex ipsa peccati notitia læditur, quantum est ex parte peccantis: et in istis servandus est ordo correptionis quem hoc loco docet Salvator. Unde de necessitate præcepti est, ut publicam denuntiationem præcedat secreta correptio, et inter extrema hæc mediare debet testium inductio, sic ut ostensum est. Peccatum namque occultandum non est, ne putrescat in corde. Hinc Augustinus: Si neglexeris (inquit) corrigere, pejor eo qui peccavit efficieris: et iterum: Nescientes quis ad numerum prædestinatorum, et quis ad sortem reproborum pertineat, sic affici debemus caritatis affectu, ut omnes velimus salvari; et ideo omnibus fraternæ correptionis debemus affectum impendere sub spe divini auxilii. Testium quoque inductio intelligi potest tripliciter: primo, ut per eos ostendatur peccanti id esse peccatum quod fecit, si forte hoc ignoret aut neget; secundo, ad convincendum peccantem, si denuo peccet; tertio, ad probandum quod correptor fecit id quod ad se pertinebat.
paras.en: It must also be known that some sins are public, and in such cases provision must be made not only for the sinner but also for others, lest they be scandalized. Such sins, then, are to be rebuked publicly at once, as the Apostle commands Timothy: [[1 Tim 5:20|Them that sin reprove before all that the rest also may have fear|Peccantem, inquiens, coram omnibus argue, ut ceteri timorem habeant]]. Some sins are against the faith or the common good, and in these, though they be hidden, one must proceed at once to making them public: as if someone were plotting to set fire to the city, or to corrupt the faith of others. Yet if someone reasonably judges that he can correct such a sinner by a secret rebuke, he may first rebuke him secretly. Some sins, again, are hidden, harmful only to the sinner and to the one against whom he sins, who is hurt by the very knowledge of the sin, as far as the sinner's part goes: and in these the order of correction that the Saviour teaches here is to be kept. So it is of the necessity of the precept that secret correction come before public denunciation, and between these extremes the bringing in of witnesses must come, as has been shown. For sin is not to be hidden, lest it rot in the heart. Hence Augustine says: "If you neglect to correct him, you become worse than he who sinned"; and again: "Not knowing who belongs to the number of the predestined and who to the lot of the reprobate, we ought to be so moved with the feeling of charity as to will all to be saved; and therefore we owe to all the disposition of fraternal correction, in the hope of divine help." The bringing in of witnesses can be understood in three ways: first, so that through them it may be shown to the sinner that what he did is a sin, if perhaps he does not know it or denies it; second, to convict the sinner if he sins again; third, to prove that the one correcting did what belonged to him.

paras.t: Sed his obviare videtur, quod in capitulis religiosorum fiunt proclamationes sine admonitione prævia. Augustinus etiam ait in regula, peccatum prius denuntiandum prælato quam testes inducantur. Unde nonnulli prælati subditis suis præcipere solent, ut si emendatione dignum quid noverint, sibi revelent: et tamen ad prælatum publica denuntiatio pertinet. Et respondendum, quod proclamationes prædictæ non sunt nisi de levibus culpis, quæ non derogant famæ, et sunt potius oblitarum commemorationes culparum, quam accusationes vel denuntiationes. Si vero aliquis gravia mala et famæ contraria, alteri in proclamando objiceret, ageret contra præceptum Salvatoris, cujus præceptorum transgressio mortale peccatum censetur. Præterea verbum Augustini intelligendum est de prælato, in quantum est singularis persona, non in quantum est judex et loco Ecclesiæ. Et simili modo de præcepto prælatorum jubentium sibi insinuari occulta peccata subditorum, dicendum est. Vehementer timeo, quod multi præscriptum ordinem correptionis fraternæ male observent, qui de peccato mortali indigent pertimescere. Postremo, quam virtuosum sit correptionem patienter, gratanter et amorose recipere, quam item vitiosum sit eam abjicere, constat ex his quæ in Proverbiis sapientissimus Salomon loquitur: Viro qui corripientem dura cervice contemnit, repentinus superveniet interitus; et rursus: Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis. Ideo ait Psalmista: Corripiet me justus in misericordia, et increpabit me. Et in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Quam bonum est correptum ostendere pœnitentiam! sic enim effugies peccatum. Hinc Seneca notabiliter fatur: Moneberis libenter, et reprehenderis patienter. Si merito objurgavit te aliquis, scito quia profuit; si immerito, scito quia prodesse voluit. Non acerba, sed blanda timeas verba.
paras.en: But against this seems to be the fact that in the chapters of religious, proclamations are made without previous admonition [the "chapter of faults", where faults are publicly mentioned]. Augustine too says in his Rule that a sin is to be reported to the superior before witnesses are brought in. Hence some prelates are accustomed to command their subjects to reveal to them anything they know that deserves amendment; and yet public denunciation belongs to the prelate. The answer is that these proclamations concern only light faults which do not harm a person's good name, and are rather reminders of forgotten faults than accusations or denunciations. But if anyone in a proclamation were to charge another with grave evils damaging to his good name, he would act against the precept of the Saviour, the transgression of whose precepts is reckoned mortal sin. Further, Augustine's word is to be understood of the prelate as a private person, not as judge and in the place of the Church; and the same must be said of the command of prelates who order the hidden sins of their subjects to be made known to them. I greatly fear that many keep the order of fraternal correction described here badly, who have need to fear mortal sin. Lastly, how virtuous it is to receive correction patiently, gratefully and lovingly, and how sinful to reject it, is plain from what the most wise Solomon says in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:1|The man that with a stiff neck despiseth him that reproveth him, shall suddenly be destroyed|Viro qui corripientem dura cervice contemnit, repentinus superveniet interitus]]; and again: [[Prov 13:18|Poverty and shame to him that refuseth instruction|Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam]]; [[Prov 15:32|but he that yieldeth to reproof, possesseth understanding|qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis]]. So the Psalmist says: [[Ps 140:5|The just man shall correct me in mercy, and shall reprove me|Corripiet me justus in misericordia, et increpabit me]]. And it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 20:4|How good is it, when thou art reproved, to shew repentance! for so thou shalt escape wilful sin|Quam bonum est correptum ostendere pœnitentiam! sic enim effugies peccatum]]. Hence Seneca says strikingly: "You will be admonished willingly and rebuked patiently. If someone has scolded you deservedly, know that he has done you good; if undeservedly, know that he wished to do you good. Fear not harsh words, but flattering ones."

paras.t: Quoniam vero in superioribus plura induxit et docuit Christus, ut nos ad caritatem et mutuam pacem provocaret, idcirco subdit quam utile sit concordiam possidere cum aliis, quatenus incitemur ad pacem sanctissimam. Iterum dico vobis: Si duo, et multo fortius si plures, ex vobis, hoc est de numero servorum meorum in caritate viventium, consenserint, id est, concorde animo idem senserint vel optaverint, super terram, id est in præsenti peregrinatione atque exsilio, ubi est locus merendi ac demerendi, opportunitasque orandi, de omni re quamcumque petierint, id est de quocumque bono eis salubri, fiet illis, id est exaudientur, a Patre meo qui in cœlis est. Oportet enim ut petant quod decet et expedit, orentque perseveranter. Quum autem orat quis pro se, pie ac perseveranter, indubitanter exauditur a Deo. Ex quibus patet, quod spiritualis amicitia societasque fraterna ad interiorem profectum relata, fructuosa et ad gratiæ magnæ adeptionem proficua est. Frater enim qui juvatur a fratre, quasi urbs munita. Et quanto major est multitudo orantium, tanto deprecatio exaudibilior redditur, ceteris paribus.
paras.en: Since in what went before Christ brought forward and taught many things to stir us to charity and mutual peace, He adds how useful it is to live in concord with others, so that we may be spurred on to most holy peace. [[18:19|Again I say to you, that if two of you shall consent upon earth|Iterum dico vobis: Si duo … ex vobis … consenserint, … super terram]]: two, and much more if more, of you, that is, of the number of My servants living in charity, shall consent, that is, think or desire the same thing with one mind, upon earth, that is, in this present pilgrimage and exile, where there is a place for meriting and demeriting and an opportunity for praying, [[18:19|concerning anything whatsoever they shall ask|de omni re quamcumque petierint]], that is, any good that is wholesome for them, [[18:19|it shall be done to them by my Father who is in heaven|fiet illis, id est exaudientur, a Patre meo qui in cœlis est]], that is, they will be heard. For they must ask for what is fitting and expedient, and pray perseveringly. And when someone prays for himself devoutly and perseveringly, he is without doubt heard by God. From this it is plain that spiritual friendship and brotherly fellowship directed to inward progress is fruitful and profitable for gaining great grace. For [[Prov 18:19|A brother that is helped by his brother, is like a strong city|Frater enim qui juvatur a fratre, quasi urbs munita]]. And the greater the number of those praying, the more readily the prayer is heard, other things being equal.

paras.t: Ubi enim sunt duo vel tres congregati in nomine meo, id est in me, videlicet in caritate et gratia, vel secundum voluntatem meam, seu ad honorem et gloriam nominis mei, ut sint corporaliter spiritualiterque uniti, ibi sum in medio eorum, id est, inter eos atque in cordibus singulorum, per Spiritus Sancti directionem, piam gubernationem, et precum illorum gratiosam exauditionem. Tales ergo Christus custodit, protegit et illustrat: qui in Proverbiis testatus est, delicias suas esse cum filiis hominum. Unde per Moysen sæpe prædixit: Ego sum qui habito in medio filiorum Israel. Hinc ergo credendum generales synodos atque concilia, a Spiritu Sancto regi, et in medio totius conventus Deum laudantis, Christum clementer adsistere.
paras.en: [[18:20|For where there are two or three gathered together in my name|Ubi enim sunt duo vel tres congregati in nomine meo]], that is, in Me, namely in charity and grace, or according to My will, or for the honour and glory of My name, so as to be united bodily and spiritually, [[18:20|there am I in the midst of them|ibi sum in medio eorum]], that is, among them and in the hearts of each, by the guidance of the Holy Ghost, by loving governance, and by graciously hearing their prayers. Such, then, Christ guards, protects and enlightens, He who testified in Proverbs that [[Prov 8:31|my delights were to be with the children of men|delicias suas esse cum filiis hominum]]. Hence He often foretold through Moses: [[Num 35:34|I am the Lord that dwell among the children of Israel|Ego sum qui habito in medio filiorum Israel]][[Ex 25:8||]][[Ex 29:45||]]. So it is to be believed from this that general synods and councils are ruled by the Holy Ghost, and that Christ graciously stands in the midst of the whole assembly praising God.

paras.t: Tunc accedens Petrus ad eum, dixit. Quoniam Petrus audivit Christum docentem, quod peccans in aliquem caritative monendus sit, quod fieri nequit, nisi peccatum ei ex corde dimittatur, saltem quantum ad culpam; ideo quærit: Domine, quoties peccabit in me frater meus, et dimittam ei? id est, quot vicibus proximo meo in me peccanti indulgebo? An usque septies, id est septem vicibus? Quoniam Petrus novit Judæos ad talionem proclives, idcirco putavit se multum dicere, quum paratum se offerret ad ignoscendum septies. Dicit illi Jesus: Non dico tibi, et sub persona tua omni fideli, Usque septies tantum esse dimittendum; sed, Usque septuagies septies, id est toties quoties te offendit. Ponitur enim numerus determinatus pro numero indeterminato. Nam toties oportet proximo in nos peccanti remittere, quoties volumus nobis peccantibus a Deo ignosci (a quo utique volumus nobis indesinenter ignosci, quotiescumque peccamus): aliter non possemus jugiter dicere, Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris. Non ergo vincamur a malo, nec fatigemur bene agendo, sed incessanter parcamus peccantibus, culpam dimittendo. Pœna tamen dimittenda non est, si ex remissione pœnæ peccator ad peccandum fiat proclivior, vel alii scandalizentur, vel disciplina et ordo justitiæ periclitetur: imo tunc pertinet ad magnam caritatem infligere pœnam secundum juris processum. Propter quod dicit Augustinus: Peccat semel, ignovi; peccat secundo, ignovi; peccat tertio, vapulet.
paras.en: [[18:21|Then came Peter unto him and said|Tunc accedens Petrus ad eum, dixit]]. Since Peter had heard Christ teaching that one who sins against someone is to be admonished charitably, which cannot be done unless the sin is forgiven him from the heart, at least as to the guilt, he asks: [[18:21|Lord, how often shall my brother offend against me, and I forgive him|Domine, quoties peccabit in me frater meus, et dimittam ei]]? That is, how many times shall I pardon my neighbour who sins against me? [[18:21|till seven times|usque septies]], that is, seven times? Since Peter knew that the Jews were inclined to retaliation, he thought he was saying a great deal in offering himself ready to forgive seven times. [[18:22|Jesus saith to him: I say not to thee, till seven times|Dicit illi Jesus: Non dico tibi usque septies]], and in your person to every believer, that one must forgive only up to seven times, [[18:22|but till seventy times seven times|sed, Usque septuagies septies]], that is, as often as he offends you. For a definite number is put for an indefinite one. For we must forgive our neighbour who sins against us as often as we want God to pardon us when we sin (and we certainly want Him to pardon us unceasingly, however often we sin); otherwise we could not say continually: [[Matt 6:12|forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors|Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris]]. So [[Rom 12:21|Be not overcome by evil|Non ergo vincamur a malo]], [[Gal 6:9|in doing good, let us not fail|nec fatigemur bene agendo]], but let us spare sinners unceasingly, forgiving the guilt. The punishment, however, is not to be remitted if by remitting it the sinner becomes more inclined to sin, or others are scandalized, or discipline and the order of justice are endangered; indeed, then it belongs to great charity to inflict punishment according to the process of law. Hence Augustine says: "He sins once: I have pardoned; he sins a second time: I have pardoned; he sins a third time: let him be beaten."

paras.t: Denique Christus proponit similitudinem valde terribilem, qua monstratur quam necesse sit proximo in se peccanti semper ignoscere, si quis velit divinam clementiam impetrare. Ideo, id est ex quo toties dimittendum est delinquenti, assimilatum est regnum cœlorum, id est status et regimen Ecclesiæ militantis, cujus conversatio est in cœlis, homini regi qui voluit rationem ponere, id est computationem et justam exactionem seu inquisitionem facere, cum servis suis. Et quum cœpisset rationem ponere, oblatus est ei unus qui debebat ei decem millia talenta. Juxta litteram non est aliqua difficultas in ista parabola. Porro juxta mysticum intellectum, dominus iste, est Christus Rex regum et Dominus universorum: qui licet in die extremi judicii, vel in hora mortis ac particularis judicii nullum peccatum relinquat inultum, nec tempus pœnitentiæ tribuat, tamen quotidie ponit rationem cum fidelibus per vicarios suos prælatos, per Scripturarum admonitiones, et per inspirationes internas. Per illum autem qui debuit decem millia talenta, intelligitur quicumque magnis multisque peccatis obnoxius.
paras.en: Next Christ sets out a very terrible comparison, by which it is shown how necessary it is always to pardon a neighbour who sins against us, if one wishes to obtain the divine mercy. [[18:23|Therefore|Ideo]], that is, since the offender is to be forgiven so often, [[18:23|is the kingdom of heaven likened|assimilatum est regnum cœlorum]], that is, the state and government of the Church militant, whose [[Phil 3:20|conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]], [[18:23|to a king, who would take an account of his servants|homini regi, qui voluit rationem ponere cum servis suis]], that is, make a reckoning and a just demand or inquiry. [[18:24|And when he had begun to take the account, one as brought to him, that owed him ten thousand talents|Et quum cœpisset rationem ponere, oblatus est ei unus qui debebat ei decem millia talenta]]. In the letter there is no difficulty in this parable. In the mystical sense, this lord is Christ, [[Apoc 19:16|KING OF KINGS|Rex regum]][[Apoc 17:14||]] and Lord of all, who, although at the day of the last judgment, or at the hour of death and the particular judgment, He leaves no sin unpunished and grants no time for repentance, nevertheless daily takes account with the faithful through His vicars the prelates, through the admonitions of the Scriptures, and through inward inspirations. By the one who owed ten thousand talents is understood anyone liable for many great sins.

paras.t: Quum autem talis transgressor non haberet unde redderet, id est opera virtuosa ac satisfactoria quibus Deum placaret, et suæ justitiæ condignam recompensationem honoris pro illata injuria exhiberet, jussit eum dominus venundari, id est pœnis immergi, seu dæmonibus tradi, ut pro nummo culpæ, et pro peccatore eis tradito, solverent Deo nummum vindictæ, subserviendo divinæ justitiæ in punitione damnati. Ista facit Christus quotidie per excommunicationem et pronuntiationem Scripturæ prælatorum Ecclesiæ. Et uxorem ejus, et filios, id est sensualitatem seu insipientiam et opera mala, et omnia quæ habebat, quia omnia ista obligata sunt ad pœnam propter peccata, et reddi, id est divinæ justitiæ satisfieri pro peccatis illius. Procidens autem, id est se prosternens, servus ille, id est peccator Deo per pœnitentiam se humilians, rogabat eum, dicens: Patientiam habe in me, id est, emendationem et satisfactionem meam clementer exspecta, nec statim me damnes, sed æterna supplicia in temporalem pœnam commuta, et omnia reddam tibi, id est, pro universis peccatis pœnitentiam et emendationem efficiam, et sicut te inhonoravi male agendo, sic te honorabo bene vivendo. Misertus autem dominus Jesus servi illius, dimisit eum, et debitum dimisit ei: quia quacumque hora peccator ingemiscit pro peccatis suis, omnia ei donantur, et larga Dei pietas veniam non dimidiat, sed omnia mortalia simul dimittit.
paras.en: [[18:25|And as he had not wherewith to pay it|Quum autem talis transgressor non haberet unde redderet]], such a transgressor, that is, virtuous and satisfying works by which to appease God and offer to His justice a fitting compensation of honour for the injury done, [[18:25|his lord commanded that he should be sold|jussit eum dominus venundari]], that is, plunged into punishment, or handed over to the demons, so that for the coin of guilt, and for the sinner handed over to them, they might pay God the coin of vengeance, serving the divine justice in punishing the damned. Christ does this daily through the excommunication and the Scriptural sentence of the prelates of the Church. [[18:25|and his wife and children|Et uxorem ejus, et filios]], that is, sensuality, or folly, and evil works, [[18:25|and all that he had|et omnia quæ habebat]], since all these are liable to punishment because of sins, [[18:25|and payment to be made|et reddi]], that is, that the divine justice be satisfied for his sins. [[18:26|But that servant falling down|Procidens autem servus ille]], that is, prostrating himself, that is, the sinner humbling himself before God by penance, [[18:26|besought him, saying: Have patience with me|rogabat eum, dicens: Patientiam habe in me]], that is, wait mercifully for my amendment and satisfaction, and do not condemn me at once, but change the eternal torments into a temporal punishment, [[18:26|and I will pay thee all|et omnia reddam tibi]], that is, I will do penance and make amends for all my sins, and as I dishonoured You by doing evil, so I will honour You by living well. [[18:27|And the lord of that servant being moved with pity, let him go and forgave him the debt|Misertus autem dominus Jesus servi illius, dimisit eum, et debitum dimisit ei]], the Lord Jesus: for in whatever hour the sinner groans for his sins, all is forgiven him[[Ezech 18:21||]], and God's generous mercy does not grant pardon by halves, but forgives all mortal sins together.

paras.t: Egressus autem, id est mente aversus, servus ille, liber a debito, sed servus peccati: egressus ergo, id est, Deum relinquens per recidivum peccati, invenit unum de conservis suis, qui debebat ei centum denarios, id est modicum comparatione debiti sui ad Deum. Secundum Augustinum, omnis homo debitor est Dei, a quo multa bona sortitus est, et quem multum multisque modis offendit; et debitorem habet proximum suum qui in se peccavit, vel aliquid ei alio modo tenetur. Sed debitum quo proximus nobis obligatur, minimum est comparatione debiti quo Deo adstricti sumus, in quem tanto gravius est peccare, quanto major est dignitas ejus præ cunctis. Quod insinuatur in libro Regum, quo legitur: Si peccaverit vir in virum, placari ei potest Deus; si autem in Dominum peccaverit, quis orabit pro eo? Et tenens suffocabat, id est strangulabat eum, vitalem spiritum includendo, ne respiraret, dicens: Redde mihi quod debes. Hoc agunt crudeles, qui persolutionem et satisfactionem vindictæ a proximis suis violenter vel ultra vires eorum requirunt. Et procidens conservus ejus, rogabat eum, dicens: Patientiam habe in me, et omnia reddam tibi, id est, solvam totum quod debeo, et satisfaciam tibi. Ille autem noluit acquiescere deprecanti, sed abiit, id est, cum conservo suo a se tento et comprehenso recessit, et misit eum in carcerem, donec redderet debitum: in quo patet ejus sæva nimis crudelitas.
paras.en: [[18:28|But when that servant was gone out|Egressus autem servus ille]], that is, turned away in mind, free of his debt but [[John 8:34|the servant of sin|servus peccati]]: gone out, then, that is, leaving God by falling back into sin, [[18:28|he found one of his fellow-servants that owed him an hundred pence|invenit unum de conservis suis, qui debebat ei centum denarios]], that is, a little in comparison with his own debt to God. According to Augustine, every man is God's debtor, from whom he has received many good things and whom he has offended much and in many ways; and he has as his debtor his neighbour who has sinned against him, or is bound to him in some other way. But the debt by which our neighbour is bound to us is very small compared with the debt by which we are bound to God, against whom it is the more grievous to sin as His dignity is greater than all. This is suggested in the book of Kings, where we read: [[1 Kings 2:25|If one man shall sin against another, God may be appeased in his behalf: but if a man shall sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him|Si peccaverit vir in virum, placari ei potest Deus; si autem in Dominum peccaverit, quis orabit pro eo]]? [[18:28|and laying hold of him, he throttled him|Et tenens suffocabat eum]], that is, strangled him, shutting in his breath so that he could not breathe, [[18:28|saying: Pay what thou owest|dicens: Redde mihi quod debes]]. The cruel do this, who demand payment and the satisfaction of revenge from their neighbours violently or beyond their strength. [[18:29|And his fellow-servant falling down, besought him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all|Et procidens conservus ejus, rogabat eum, dicens: Patientiam habe in me, et omnia reddam tibi]], that is, I will pay all I owe and satisfy you. [[18:30|And he would not|Ille autem noluit]] give in to his entreaty, [[18:30|but went|sed abiit]], that is, went off with the fellow-servant he had seized and held, [[18:30|and cast him into prison, till he paid the debt|et misit eum in carcerem, donec redderet debitum]]: in which his exceedingly savage cruelty is plain.

paras.t: Videntes autem conservi ejus quæ fiebant inter hos duos, contristati sunt valde: quia sicut ad caritatem pertinet de bono proximi exsultare, ita spectat ad eam de malo ejus tristari; et venerunt, et narraverunt domino suo omnia quæ facta fuerant inter servos præfatos. Servi isti intelligi possunt angeli, qui sunt administratorii spiritus: quorum unus ait Joanni in Apocalypsi, Conservus tuus sum, et fratrum tuorum. Hi tanquam diligentes custodes considerant facta nostra; et sicut de nostro profectu vere lætantur, ita de nostris peccatis et afflictionibus metaphorice contristari dicuntur, quia per modum dolentis se habent, dum displicet eis quod impie agimus. Hi narrant Christo, non quasi ignoranti, sed ut judicanti opera nostra, verba, etc., sicut Tobiæ angelus loquitur: Ego obtuli orationem tuam Domino. Secundo, per conservos intelligi possunt homines justi, prælati ac judices zelo æquitatis succensi: qui videntes quomodo unus opprimat alium, coram Deo cor suum effundunt, et divinam ultricem justitiam invocant, non zelo vindictæ, sed amore justitiæ, et ut in præsenti corrigatur crudelis, ne postea gravius judicetur.
paras.en: [[18:31|Now his fellow servants seeing what was done, were very much grieved|Videntes autem conservi ejus quæ fiebant inter hos duos, contristati sunt valde]], what was done between these two: for as it belongs to charity to rejoice at a neighbour's good, so it belongs to it to grieve at his evil; [[18:31|and they came, and told their lord all that was done|et venerunt, et narraverunt domino suo omnia quæ facta fuerant]] between these servants. These servants can be understood as the angels, who are [[Heb 1:14|ministering spirits|administratorii spiritus]], one of whom says to John in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:9|I am thy fellow servant, and of thy brethren|Conservus tuus sum, et fratrum tuorum]]. As careful guardians they consider our deeds; and as they truly rejoice at our progress, so they are said metaphorically to be grieved at our sins and afflictions, because they behave like one grieving when what we do wickedly displeases them. They tell Christ our works, words and so on, not as if He did not know, but as to the one who judges them; as the angel says to Tobias: [[Tob 12:12|I offered thy prayer to the Lord|Ego obtuli orationem tuam Domino]]. Second, the fellow servants can be understood as just men, prelates and judges fired with zeal for equity, who, seeing how one man oppresses another, pour out their hearts before God and call upon the avenging justice of God, not out of zeal for revenge but out of love of justice, and so that the cruel man may be corrected in the present, lest he be judged more severely afterwards.

paras.t: Tunc, istis perceptis, vel circiter et cito post hæc, vocavit illum suffocatorem crudelemque servum dominus suus, videlicet Christus, qui quotidie quosdam per mortem ad se vocat; et ait illi: Serve nequam, id est nocive in proximum, et domino infidelis, omne debitum, id est omnia peccata tua, dimisi tibi, quoniam rogasti me pro dilatione, et feci plusquam rogasti, omnia relaxando; nonne ergo oportuit et te, qui dominum tuum imitari debueras, et ad misericordiam naturali præcepto teneris, ut facias alteri quod tibi vis fieri (oportuit ergo debito condecentiæ ac præcepti, necessitateque finis, id est ad obtinendam salutem, necessarium fuit), misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego tui misertus sum dimittens te liberum?
paras.en: [[18:32|Then his lord called him|Tunc … vocavit illum … dominus suus]]: then, when these things had been heard, or about then and soon after, his lord, namely Christ, who daily calls some to Himself by death, called that cruel servant who throttled the other; [[18:32|and said to him: Thou wicked servant|et ait illi: Serve nequam]], that is, harmful to your neighbour and unfaithful to your lord, [[18:32|I forgave thee all the debt, because thou besoughtest me|omne debitum dimisi tibi quoniam rogasti me]], all your sins, that is, because you asked Me for delay, and I did more than you asked, releasing everything: [[18:33|Shouldst not thou then have had compassion also on thy fellow servant, even as I had compassion on thee|nonne ergo oportuit et te misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego tui misertus sum?]], you who ought to have imitated your lord, and are bound by the natural precept to mercy, to do to another what you would have done to yourself[[Matt 7:12||]] (shouldst thou, that is, by the debt of fittingness and of precept, and by the necessity of the end, that is, it was necessary for obtaining salvation), releasing you free?
