Porro beatitudo seu vita æterna appellatur denarius, quia est præmium bene agentis. Dicitur quoque diurnus, quoniam propter eum quotidie laboratur, et quotidie ingredientibus regnum cæleste confertur, eumque meremur in die gratiæ, et accipiemus in die gloriæ. Misit eos in vineam suam, id est ad Ecclesiam instruendam, vel ad bene vivendum in ea.
paras.en: [[20:2|And having agreed with the labourers|Conventione autem facta cum operariis]], having, that is, made the promise or entered into the compact with the labourers already mentioned, [[20:2|for a penny a day|ex denario diurno]], that is, for eternal happiness to be paid them for their labour. This agreement, then, is the promise of eternal life, of which the Lord says through Jeremias: [[Jer 31:16|Let thy voice cease from weeping, and thy eyes tears: for there is a reward for thy work|Quiescat vox tua a ploratu, et oculi tui a lacrimis, quia est merces operi tuo]]. Beatitude or eternal life is called a penny [denarius, a day's wage] because it is the reward of one who does well; and it is called a day's penny because it is laboured for daily, and is daily bestowed on those who enter the heavenly kingdom; and we merit it in the day of grace and shall receive it in the day of glory. [[20:2|he sent them into his vineyard|Misit eos in vineam suam]], that is, to instruct the Church, or to live well in it.

paras.t: Et egressus (secundum modum prædictum) Deus circa horam tertiam, id est statim post diluvium, vel a tempore Noe usque ad Abraham, invenit alios stantes in foro, id est in sæculo isto negotiationibus temporalium rerum repleto, otiosos, id est a bonis operibus vacantes. Et dixit illis, per inspirationem internam, angelicam revelationem, vel alio modo: Ite et vos in vineam meam, hoc est ad fidelium sortem seu congregationem, dimittendo opera tenebrarum et faciendo fructus justitiæ; et quod justum fuerit dabo vobis, videlicet justam mercedem pro opere virtuoso, qui do unicuique quod meretur.
paras.en: [[20:3|And going out about the third hour|Et egressus circa horam tertiam]]: God going out (in the way just said) about the third hour, that is, straight after the flood, or from the time of Noe to Abraham, [[20:3|he saw others standing in the marketplace|invenit alios stantes in foro]] [the margin notes the reading vidit, "saw", as in the Vulgate; Denis's text has invenit, "found"], that is, in this world, full of the trading of temporal things, [[20:3|idle|otiosos]], that is, empty of good works. [[20:4|And he said to them|Et dixit illis]], by inward inspiration, by the revelation of angels, or in some other way: [[20:4|Go you also into my vineyard|Ite et vos in vineam meam]], that is, into the lot or company of the faithful, putting away [[Rom 13:12|the works of darkness|opera tenebrarum]] and bearing the fruits of justice; [[20:4|and I will give you what shall be just|et quod justum fuerit dabo vobis]], namely a just wage for virtuous work, for I give to each what he deserves[[Jer 17:10||]].

paras.t: Illi autem abierunt in vineam Domini, obedientes locutioni divinæ. Tales fuerunt Noe, Sem, Japhet, Heber. Iterum autem exiit circa sextam, hoc est a tempore Abrahæ usque ad Moysen, et nonam horam, id est a tempore Moysis usque ad Christum; et fecit similiter, otiosos faciendo operarios, seu quosdam mittendo in vineam suam, utpote Moysen, Aaron, Josue, judices et Prophetas, aliosque innumerabiles perducendo ad statum salutis in illis duabus ætatibus.
paras.en: [[20:5|And they went their way|Illi autem abierunt]] into the Lord's vineyard, obeying God's word. Such were Noe, Sem, Japheth, Heber. [[20:5|And again he went out about the sixth|Iterum autem exiit circa sextam]], that is, from the time of Abraham to Moses, [[20:5|and the ninth hour|et nonam horam]], that is, from the time of Moses to Christ; [[20:5|and did in like manner|et fecit similiter]], making the idle into labourers, or sending some into His vineyard, such as Moses, Aaron, Josue, the judges and the Prophets, and bringing countless others to the state of salvation in those two ages.

paras.t: Circa undecimam vero horam, id est ab adventu Christi, exiit, mittendo Unigenitum suum in similitudinem carnis peccati, et Apostolos ad gentiles. Tunc quoque Verbum Dei verus Deus exiit, nostram naturam assumendo, et personaliter hominibus apparendo, loquendo et bene agendo, quemadmodum apud Joannem ipse testatur: Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum. Et invenit alios stantes, id est, rebus temporalibus inhærentes, spiritualiter non proficientes: per quos præcipue intelliguntur gentiles, quorum aliquibus, tamen paucis et parum, Christus in propria prædicavit persona, ceteris per Apostolos, eorumque discipulos et successores. Et dicit illis: Quid hic, id est in isto exsilio, in hac peregrinatione ubi non habemus civitatem manentem, statis tota die, id est toto tempore vitæ vestræ, otiosi, non festinantes ad patriam? Gentiles namque fide caruerunt, nil meritorium operabantur: idcirco toto tempore vitæ suæ vacabant a bonis, præsertim quum dicat Apostolus: Quidquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Dicunt ei: Quia nemo nos conduxit, id est, nullus ad bene agendum nos invitavit, promittendo nobis regnum cæleste pro præmio: nullus quippe Propheta aut doctor missus est nobis. Prioris enim ignorantiæ tempora despexit Deus, ut ait Paulus. Verumtamen quibusdam gentilibus dati sunt viri sancti, videlicet Job, Melchisedech; sed tempore Christi, et diu ante, in toto mundo regnavit idololatria, exceptis Judæis. Dicit illis: Ite et vos in vineam meam. Hoc Deus dixit gentilibus per prædicationem Apostolorum, ut converterentur ad Christum, fieretque ex eis et populo Judæorum electo una Ecclesia.
paras.en: [[20:6|But about the eleventh hour|Circa undecimam vero horam]], that is, from the coming of Christ, [[20:6|he went out|exiit]], sending His Only-begotten [[Rom 8:3|in the likeness of sinful flesh|in similitudinem carnis peccati]], and the Apostles to the Gentiles[[Matt 28:19||]]. Then too the Word of God, true God, went out, by taking our nature and appearing to men in person, speaking and doing good, as He Himself testifies in John: [[John 16:28|I came forth from the Father and am come into the world|Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum]]. [[20:6|and found others standing|Et invenit alios stantes]], that is, clinging to temporal things and making no spiritual progress: by whom are chiefly meant the Gentiles, to some of whom (though few, and little) Christ preached in His own person, and to the rest through the Apostles and their disciples and successors. [[20:6|and he saith to them: Why stand you here|et dicit illis: Quid hic statis]], here, that is, in this exile, in this pilgrimage where [[Heb 13:14|we have not here a lasting city|non habemus civitatem manentem]], [[20:6|all the day|tota die]], that is, the whole time of your life, [[20:6|idle|otiosi]], not hastening to the fatherland? For the Gentiles lacked faith and did nothing meritorious, so that the whole time of their life they were empty of good, especially since the Apostle says: [[Rom 14:23|all that is not of faith is sin|Quidquid non est ex fide, peccatum est]]. [[20:7|They say to him: Because no man hath hired us|Dicunt ei: Quia nemo nos conduxit]], that is, no one has invited us to do well by promising us the heavenly kingdom as a reward: for no Prophet or teacher was sent to us. For God [[Acts 17:30|having winked at the times of this ignorance|Prioris enim ignorantiæ tempora despexit Deus]], as Paul says. Yet to some Gentiles holy men were given, namely Job and Melchisedech; but in the time of Christ, and long before, idolatry reigned in the whole world, except among the Jews. [[20:7|He saith to them: Go ye also into my vineyard|Dicit illis: Ite et vos in vineam meam]]. God said this to the Gentiles through the preaching of the Apostles, that they might be converted to Christ, and one Church be made of them and the chosen people of the Jews.

paras.t: Denique S. Hieronymus exponit parabolam hanc de vocatis ad gratiam secundum diversas hominum ætates: ut illi dicantur primo mane conducti, et in vineam missi, qui in pueritia ad Dei obsequium perducuntur: quales potissimum fuerunt sanctificati in utero, ut Joannes et Jeremias, et alii qui mox usum rationis sortiti, cœperunt Domino famulari, ut Samuel. Tertia vero hora conducti vocantur, qui in juventute convertuntur seu adolescentia, quæ interdum pro eodem sumuntur, juxta illud Ecclesiastæ: Lætare, juvenis, in adolescentia tua. Sexta, qui in ætate virili; nona, qui in senectute; undecima, qui in ætate decrepita.
paras.en: Lastly, St. Jerome expounds this parable of those called to grace at the different ages of men: so that those are said to be hired early in the morning and sent into the vineyard who are brought to God's service in childhood, such as above all those sanctified in the womb, like John and Jeremias, and others who, as soon as they had the use of reason, began to serve the Lord, like Samuel. Those hired at the third hour are those who are converted in youth or adolescence (which are sometimes taken for the same thing, according to that saying of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 11:9|Rejoice therefore, O young man, in thy youth|Lætare, juvenis, in adolescentia tua]]); at the sixth, those in manhood; at the ninth, those in old age; at the eleventh, those in decrepit age.

paras.t: Quum sero autem factum esset. Secundum Augustinum, Gregorium, et alios expositores communiter, per sero intelligitur finis mundi, seu dies judicii. Sed hoc quidam nititur improbare, quia de recipientibus mercedem sero dicitur, quod quidam eorum murmuraverunt, quibus sub persona unius eorum dicitur: An oculus tuus nequam est? Qui autem in fine mundi remunerationem felicem, de qua jam agitur, sortientur, nec murmurabunt nec nequam erunt. Sed quam facile hoc solvatur, patebit dum ad horum verborum explanationem pervenero. Rursus, quam extorta sit expositio ejus qui per sero intelligit tempus gratiæ seu præsentem statum Ecclesiæ, patet litteram intuenti. Jam enim dictum est, quod per horam undecimam intelligatur tempus gratiæ, quod a Christi adventu incepit: oportet ergo per sero intelligi terminum temporis seu horæ istius. Iterum præsens tempus non est tempus præmiorum, sed meritorum. Præterea clarum est, quod Christus per sero intelligat horam in qua finiuntur labores pro quibus redditur merces: quæ non est nisi in die judicii.
paras.en: [[20:8|And when evening was come|Quum sero autem factum esset]]. According to Augustine, Gregory and the commentators generally, by evening is understood the end of the world, or the day of judgment. But someone tries to disprove this, because it is said of those who receive the wage in the evening that some of them murmured, to whom it is said in the person of one of them: [[20:15|Is thy eye evil|An oculus tuus nequam est]]? But those who at the end of the world receive the happy reward that is spoken of here will neither murmur nor be evil. How easily this is answered will be seen when I come to explain those words. Again, how forced is the exposition of the one who takes evening to be the time of grace, or the present state of the Church, is plain to anyone who looks at the letter. For it has already been said that by the eleventh hour is meant the time of grace, which began with Christ's coming; so evening must be understood as the end of that time or hour. Again, the present time is not a time of rewards but of merits. Moreover, it is clear that by evening Christ means the hour at which the labours for which the wage is paid come to an end, and that is only on the day of judgment.

paras.t: Est igitur sensus: Quum sero autem factum esset, id est, quum finis mundi advenerit, dicit dominus vineæ, id est, tunc Deus Pater seu Trinitas, summus princeps Ecclesiæ, dicet procuratori suo, id est Christo secundum quod homo est, quem Pater constituit dominum domus suæ et principem omnis possessionis suæ: Voca operarios, id est eos qui in Ecclesia laboraverunt, a morte eos resuscitando, et ad judicium convocando. Hæc vocatio est, de qua inquit Apostolus: Quoniam ipse Dominus in jussu et in voce Archangeli, et in tuba Dei, descendet de cælo. Et Christus: Veniet (inquit) hora, in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus. Et redde illis mercedem, videlicet vitam æternam, de qua Salvator in Apocalypsi profitetur: Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est. Hæc merces est clara visio divinitatis Christi, prout apud Joannem ipse ait: Qui diligit me, manifestabo ei me ipsum. Unde Pater ait in Psalmo, Ostendam illi salutare meum, videlicet Christum. Incipiens dare mercedem a novissimis, qui hora undecima vocati sunt, progrediendo ab illis usque ad primos, qui primo mane vocati sunt, per intermedios. Hi vocati sunt vel hora nona, vel sexta, vel tertia. In fine mundi omnes electi simul remunerabuntur a Christo, videlicet in momento, in ictu oculi: quomodo ergo novissimi dicuntur primo remunerari? Dicendum, quod ista prioritas non est referenda ad intervalla divinæ remunerationis, quæ instantanea erit, sed ad ordinem vocatorum, ita quod licet omnes simul præmium consequantur quoad tempus, tamen primo præmiari perhibentur, qui minus diu præstolati sunt præmium, et qui ultimo finierunt laborem. Sic enim communiter dicimus, illos prius aliquid adipisci, qui minorem dilationem passi sunt, quam eos qui diu exspectaverunt, quamvis insimul præmientur.
paras.en: This, then, is the sense: [[20:8|And when evening was come|Quum sero autem factum esset]], that is, when the end of the world has come, [[20:8|the lord of the vineyard saith|dicit dominus vineæ]], that is, God the Father, or the Trinity, the supreme prince of the Church, will then say [[20:8|to his steward|procuratori suo]], that is, to Christ as man, whom the Father [[Ps 104:21|made him master of his house, and ruler of all his possession|constituit dominum domus suæ et principem omnis possessionis suæ]]: [[20:8|Call the labourers|Voca operarios]], that is, those who have laboured in the Church, raising them from death and calling them together to judgment. This is the calling of which the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 4:15|For the Lord himself shall come down from heaven with commandment and with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God|Quoniam ipse Dominus in jussu et in voce Archangeli, et in tuba Dei]] [[1 Thess 4:15|shall come down from heaven|descendet de cælo]]. And Christ says: [[John 5:28|the hour cometh wherein all that are in the graves shall hear the voice|Veniet (inquit) hora, in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem]] of Him. [[20:8|and pay them their hire|Et redde illis mercedem]], namely eternal life, of which the Saviour declares in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:12|Behold, I come quickly: and my reward is with me|Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est]]. This reward is the clear vision of Christ's Godhead, as He Himself says in John: He that loveth me, I [[John 14:21|will manifest myself to him|manifestabo ei me ipsum]]. Hence the Father says in the Psalm: [[Ps 90:16|I will shew him my salvation|Ostendam illi salutare meum]], namely Christ. [[20:8|beginning from the last|Incipiens dare mercedem a novissimis]], who were called at the eleventh hour, going on from them through those between [[20:8|even to the first|usque ad primos]], who were called early in the morning; those between were called at the ninth, sixth or third hour. At the end of the world all the elect will be rewarded by Christ together, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye: how then are the last said to be rewarded first? It must be said that this priority is not to be referred to intervals in the divine rewarding, which will be instantaneous, but to the order of those called: so that though all receive the reward at the same time, those are said to be rewarded first who waited for the reward a shorter time and finished their labour last. For so we commonly say that those who suffered less delay obtain something sooner than those who waited long, though they are rewarded together.

paras.t: Quum venissent ergo ad judicium qui circa undecimam horam, id est in ultima mundi ætate, venerant ad vineam Christi, seu vitam bonam, acceperunt a Christo pro mercede, singulos denarios, id est quilibet proportionatum præmium, seu vitam æternam in cælis. Venientes autem et primi ad tribunal Christi, arbitrati sunt, id est, æstimabant in die judicii, quod plus, id est majus præmium, essent accepturi a Christo, quam novissimi, quia diutius et gravius laboraverunt in ætatibus. Nempe his qui Christi adventum præcesserunt minor fuit gratia et longior vita, ideo diutius et durius laboraverunt quam fideles tempore gratiæ, quibus merito Salvatoris et gratiæ ejus affluentia, suave est jugum Dei et onus ejus leve. Acceperunt autem et ipsi singulos denarios, id est tantum ut primi, videlicet unusquisque suum denarium seu proprium præmium. Non enim respicit Deus principaliter ad laborem exteriorem, seu temporis diuturnitatem, sed ad interiorem fervorem, et rectam intentionem, cordisque munditiam, per quam fit homo capax visionis divinæ essentiæ.
paras.en: [[20:9|When therefore they were come|Quum venissent ergo]] to judgment [[20:9|that came about the eleventh hour|qui circa undecimam horam venerant]], that is, who in the last age of the world had come to Christ's vineyard, or to the good life, [[20:9|they received every man a penny|acceperunt singulos denarios]] from Christ as their wage, that is, each a proportionate reward, or eternal life in heaven. [[20:10|But when the first also came|Venientes autem et primi]] to the judgment seat of Christ, [[20:10|they thought|arbitrati sunt]], that is, they reckoned on the day of judgment, [[20:10|that they should receive more|quod plus essent accepturi]], that is, a greater reward, from Christ than the last, because they had laboured longer and harder in their ages. For those who went before the coming of Christ had less grace and longer life, and so laboured longer and harder than the faithful in the time of grace, to whom, through the merit of the Saviour and the abundance of His grace, [[Matt 11:30|my yoke is sweet and my burden light|suave est jugum Dei et onus ejus leve]] [Denis has "the yoke of God and his burden"]. [[20:10|And they also received every man a penny|Acceperunt autem et ipsi singulos denarios]], that is, as much as the first, namely each his own penny or his own reward. For God looks chiefly not at outward labour or length of time but at inward fervour, right intention, and purity of heart, by which a man is made capable of the vision of the divine essence[[Matt 5:8||]].

paras.t: Et accipientes primi singulos (ut dictum est) denarios, murmurabant adversus patremfamilias, scilicet Deum, dicentes: Hi novissimi una hora fecerunt, id est, modico tempore in Ecclesia laboraverunt; et pares in præmio illos nobis fecisti, qui per procuratorem tuum illis et nobis idem præmium contulisti, qui portavimus pondus diei, id est, graves temporis labores et laboriosos actus justitiæ sustinuimus, et æstus tentationum, id est vehementes tentationes et anxietates. Murmuratio ista Sanctorum, non est murmuratio turbationis, rancoris vel impatientiæ, sed vehemens replicatio propriæ causæ, seu admirationis eruptio procedens ex zelo justitiæ, quemadmodum et inter angelos sanctos, secundum Gregorium, Thomam, et alios multos, dicitur esse resistentia, dicente Gabriele ad Danielem, Princeps Persarum restitit mihi: quod prædicti exponunt de bono angelo Persarum custode ac principe. Dicuntur itaque murmurasse, vel quia dilationem dolenter sustinuerunt, secundum Gregorium, vel quia de magnitudine liberalitatis pietatisque divinæ, tantum de præmio dantis novissimis ut eis, vehementer mirabantur. Nihilominus unusquisque Beatorum de sua felicitate plenissime contentatur. Sed quæritur, quomodo priores Sancti in die judicii æstimabunt se plus recepturos, quum tamen errare non possint. Et respondendum, quod illa æstimatio non est assertionis, sed opinationis. Sancti autem in patria non præcognoscunt determinate, quantum beatitudinis quilibet hominum electorum finaliter obtinebit, nisi ex speciali causa eis divinitus reveletur.
paras.en: [[20:11|And receiving it|Et accipientes]], the first, each his penny (as was said), [[20:11|they murmured against the master of the house|murmurabant adversus patremfamilias]], that is, God, [[20:12|Saying: These last have worked but one hour|dicentes: Hi novissimi una hora fecerunt]], that is, have laboured in the Church a short time; [[20:12|and thou hast made them equal to us|et pares in præmio illos nobis fecisti]] in reward, who through Your steward have given them and us the same reward, [[20:12|that have borne the burden of the day|qui portavimus pondus diei]], that is, we have endured the heavy labours of the time and the toilsome acts of justice, [[20:12|and the heats|et æstus]] of temptations, that is, vehement temptations and anxieties. This murmuring of the Saints is not the murmuring of disturbance, rancour or impatience, but an earnest pleading of their own case, or an outburst of wonder proceeding from zeal for justice; just as, according to Gregory, Thomas and many others, there is said to be resistance even among the holy angels, when Gabriel says to Daniel: [[Dan 10:13|the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me|Princeps Persarum restitit mihi]], which they expound of the good angel who was guardian and prince of the Persians. So they are said to have murmured either because they bore the delay with grief, according to Gregory, or because they wondered greatly at the greatness of the divine liberality and kindness, which gave the last as much reward as themselves. Nonetheless each of the Blessed is most fully content with his own happiness. But it is asked how the earlier Saints on the day of judgment will reckon that they are to receive more, since they cannot err. The answer is that this reckoning is not one of assertion but of opinion. For the Saints in the fatherland do not know beforehand with certainty how much beatitude each of the elect will finally obtain, unless for some special reason it is revealed to them by God.

paras.t: At ille paterfamilias respondens uni eorum murmurantium, dixit. Et quod uni, hoc omnibus dixit; potestque per hunc unum intelligi Protoplastus. Amice, non facio tibi, nec aliis primis, injuriam, aliquid tibi injuste subtrahendo, ob hoc quod alium ultra condignum glorifico, et tibi in mercede parem facio. Nonne ex denario, hoc est pro certo præmio tibi præstando, convenisti mecum? id est, acquievisti et concors factus es mihi, eundo in vineam meam, ut denarium diurnum reciperes. Advertendum, quod sicut denarius diurnus unus est secundum suam formam et rationem specificam, multiplicatur autem ex parte materiæ et recipientium, et est æqualis quantum ad omnes; sic vita seu beatitudo æterna, per denarium figurata, una est ex parte objecti, videlicet Dei, multiplicatur vero ex parte recipientium atque fruentium, est quoque æqualis omnibus quantum ad durationem, nam omnes æternaliter eam possidebunt, tamen in perfectione magna distantia est secundum exigentiam meritorum. Unde in domo Patris mansiones multæ sunt, hoc est diversi gradus præmiorum.
paras.en: [[20:13|But he answering said to one of them|At ille paterfamilias respondens uni eorum murmurantium, dixit]], the householder answering one of those who murmured. And what He said to one He said to all; and by this one may be understood the first-formed man [Adam]. [[20:13|friend, I do thee no wrong|Amice, non facio tibi injuriam]], nor the others who were first, by unjustly taking anything from you because I glorify another beyond his desert and make him equal to you in wage. [[20:13|didst thou not agree with me for a penny|nonne ex denario convenisti mecum?]], that is, for a fixed reward to be paid you? That is, you consented and came to accord with me by going into my vineyard to receive a day's penny. It should be noted that, just as a day's penny is one in its form and specific nature, but is multiplied on the side of the matter and of those who receive it, and is equal for all; so eternal life or beatitude, figured by the penny, is one on the side of its object, namely God, but is multiplied on the side of those who receive and enjoy it; it is also equal for all as to its duration, for all will possess it eternally; yet in its perfection there is a great difference according to what their merits require. Hence [[John 14:2|In my Father's house there are many mansions|in domo Patris mansiones multæ sunt]], that is, different degrees of reward.

paras.t: Tolle quod tuum est, id est denarium seu præmium tibi debitum ac promissum, et vade in gaudium Domini tui. Volo autem et huic novissimo dare sicut et tibi, id est tantum de præmio, quantum tibi largitus sum, propter fervorem caritatis suæ, et meritum Christi, aliasque rationes jam tactas. Quemadmodum de primis locutus est singulariter, uni pro omnibus respondendo; sic nunc de novissimis singulariter loquitur, dicens, Volo huic novissimo dare, per unum omnes intelligens. Aut non licet mihi quod volo facere? quasi dicat, Utique: quia voluntas Dei quum sit essentialiter idem quod sapientia et justitia ejus, nec injusta, nec irrationalis esse valet; sed eo ipso quod Deus aliquid vult, justum ac licitum est. Unde in libro Sapientiæ legitur: Virtus tua, Domine, justitiæ initium est. An oculus tuus, id est æstimatio seu consideratio tua, nequam est, id est erronea, quia ego bonus sum essentialiter (quemadmodum dictum est, Nemo bonus nisi Deus), hoc est, an bonitas mea, liberalitas, seu misericordia, est tibi occasio murmurationis, eo quod tantum tribuo novissimis sicut primis? Loquitur ergo de nequitia inconsiderationis, et non culpæ: quod probatur per hoc quia jam loquitur de operariis vineæ Dei, qui omnes salvantur.
paras.en: [[20:14|Take what is thine|Tolle quod tuum est]], that is, the penny or reward owed and promised to you, [[20:14|and go thy way|et vade]] [[Matt 25:21|into the joy of thy lord|in gaudium Domini tui]][[Matt 25:23||]]. [[20:14|I will also give to this last even as to thee|Volo autem et huic novissimo dare sicut et tibi]], that is, as much reward as I have bestowed on you, because of the fervour of his charity and the merit of Christ, and the other reasons already touched on. As He spoke of the first in the singular, answering one for all, so now He speaks of the last in the singular, saying, I will give to this last, meaning all by one. [[20:15|Or, is it not lawful for me to do what I will|Aut non licet mihi quod volo facere?]]? As if to say: Certainly it is; for the will of God, since it is essentially the same as His wisdom and justice, can be neither unjust nor unreasonable; but by the very fact that God wills something, it is just and lawful. Hence it is read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 12:16|thy power is the beginning of justice|Virtus tua, Domine, justitiæ initium est]]. [[20:15|Is thy eye|An oculus tuus]], that is, your reckoning or consideration, [[20:15|evil|nequam est]], that is, mistaken, [[20:15|because I am good|quia ego bonus sum]] essentially (as it was said: [[Mark 10:18|None is good but one, that is God|Nemo bonus nisi Deus]]), that is, is My goodness, liberality or mercy an occasion of murmuring to you, because I give as much to the last as to the first? He speaks, then, of the evil of thoughtlessness, not of guilt: which is proved by the fact that He is speaking here of the labourers in God's vineyard, all of whom are saved.

paras.t: Ex quibus concludit Salvator: Sic erunt novissimi primi, et primi novissimi. Hoc idem in fine præcedentis capituli dictum atque expositum est. Multi enim sunt vocati, hoc est ad fidem et gratiam per prædicationem invitati atque perducti, quemadmodum Christus ait in Psalmo: Annuntiavi et locutus sum, multiplicati sunt super numerum. Pauci vero electi, hoc est prædestinati seu gloriam adepturi. Sed videtur contrarium quod de electis cantatur: Dinumerabo eos, et super arenam multiplicabuntur; et in Apocalypsi, Vidi turbam magnam, quam dinumerare nemo poterat. Et respondendum, quod pauci sunt comparative seu relative ad reprobos, multi autem simpliciter. Imo secundum Gregorium, tantus est numerus hominum electorum, quantus angelorum sanctorum. Probabile quoque est, quod numerus hominum reproborum excedat numerum angelorum ac dæmonum et hominum electorum. Quum ergo ignoremus an electi simus, et an digni simus amore, non debemus inaniter gloriari, securi esse aut elevari, nec alios, quamvis impii videantur, aspernari seu desperare. Nam quales futuri sint, nescimus; et forte in brevi præcedent nos in omni virtute.
paras.en: From this the Saviour concludes: [[20:16|So shall the last be first and the first last|Sic erunt novissimi primi, et primi novissimi]]. The same was said and expounded at the end of the preceding chapter[[Matt 19:30||]]. [[20:16|For many are called|Multi enim sunt vocati]], that is, invited and brought to faith and grace by preaching, as Christ says in the Psalm: [[Ps 39:6|I have declared and I have spoken they are multiplied above number|Annuntiavi et locutus sum, multiplicati sunt super numerum]]. [[20:16|but few chosen|Pauci vero electi]], that is, predestined, or to attain glory. But against this seems to be what is sung of the elect: [[Ps 138:18|I will number them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand|Dinumerabo eos, et super arenam multiplicabuntur]]; and in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 7:9|I saw a great multitude, which no man could number|Vidi turbam magnam, quam dinumerare nemo poterat]]. The answer is that they are few comparatively, or relatively to the reprobate, but many simply. Indeed, according to Gregory, the number of elect men is as great as that of the holy angels. It is also probable that the number of reprobate men exceeds the number of the angels and demons and elect men together. Since, then, we do not know whether we are elect, and whether we are worthy of love[[Eccles 9:1||]], we ought not to glory vainly, be secure or be lifted up, nor despise others or despair of them, however wicked they seem. For we do not know what they will be; and perhaps in a short time they will go before us in every virtue.

paras.t: Et ascendens Jesus Jerosolymam, assumpsit duodecim discipulos, puta Apostolos, secreto, ut eis tanquam familiaribus suam passionem prænuntiaret, ne eam videntes, scandalizarentur, nec putarent magistrum suum præventum, vel improvise captum, aut invite occisum. Secreta ergo non omnibus, sed familiaribus, sunt pandenda, et mystica majoribus revelanda sunt.
paras.en: [[20:17|And Jesus going up to Jerusalem, took the twelve disciples apart|Et ascendens Jesus Jerosolymam, assumpsit duodecim discipulos, puta Apostolos, secreto]], that is, the Apostles, to foretell His Passion to them as to His intimates, lest seeing it they should be scandalized, and think their Master had been taken unawares, or seized unexpectedly, or killed against His will. Secrets, then, are to be opened not to all but to intimates, and mysteries revealed to the greater.

paras.t: Et ait illis: Ecce ascendimus Jerosolymam, et Filius hominis tradetur a Deo Patre, a se ipso, a Juda proditore, a diabolo, sed diversimode, principibus sacerdotum et Scribis in lege peritis, et condemnabunt eum morte, hoc est, reum mortis eum esse judicabunt. Sic enim dixerunt coram Pilato: Nos legem habemus, et secundum legem debet mori, quia Filium Dei se fecit. Et tradent eum principes sacerdotum et Scribæ, gentibus, scilicet Pilato et ejus militibus, ad illudendum. Induerunt enim eum veste purpurea, et arundinem posuerunt in dextera ejus, spineamque coronam in capite, et genu flexo adorabant eum dicentes: Ave, rex Judæorum. Et flagellandum, et crucifigendum. Ista prædixit Christus discipulis suis frequenter, ut firmiter recordarentur eorum. Et tertia die resurget. Hoc adjecit ad consolationem mœrentium.
paras.en: [[20:17|and said to them|et ait illis]]: [[20:18|Behold we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of man shall be betrayed|Ecce ascendimus Jerosolymam, et Filius hominis tradetur]], by God the Father, by Himself, by Judas the traitor, and by the devil, but in different ways, [[20:18|to the chief priests and the scribes|principibus sacerdotum et Scribis]] learned in the law, [[20:18|and they shall condemn him to death|et condemnabunt eum morte]], that is, they will judge Him guilty of death[[Matt 26:66||]][[Mark 14:64||]]. For so they said before Pilate: [[John 19:7|We have a law; and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God|Nos legem habemus, et secundum legem debet mori, quia Filium Dei se fecit]]. [[20:19|And shall deliver him to the Gentiles|et tradent eum gentibus]], the chief priests and scribes, that is, to Pilate and his soldiers, [[20:19|to be mocked|ad illudendum]]. For they clothed Him in a purple garment[[Mark 15:17||]], and put a reed in His right hand and a crown of thorns on His head, and bowing the knee they worshipped Him, saying: [[Matt 27:29|Hail, King of the Jews|Ave, rex Judæorum]]. [[20:19|and scourged and crucified|Et flagellandum, et crucifigendum]]. Christ foretold these things to His disciples often, so that they might remember them firmly. [[20:19|and the third day he shall rise again|Et tertia die resurget]]. This He added to comfort them in their sorrow.

paras.t: Tunc accessit ad eum mater filiorum Zebedæi cum filiis suis Jacobo et Joanne, adorans eum, vel adoratione latriæ, si credidit eum esse Deum verum, vel adoratione duliæ seu magnæ reverentiæ, prosternens se coram eo; et petens aliquid ab eo: quod non statim expressit, sed adorando insinuavit se aliquid desiderare. In Marco scribitur, quod ipsi filii accesserunt ad Jesum dicentes: Magister, volumus ut quodcumque petierimus facias nobis. Verumtamen mater formavit atque proposuit petitionem; sed hoc filii fecisse scribuntur, quoniam matrem suam ad hoc induxerunt, quam putabant a Christo honorandam et exaudiendam quasi materteram ejus, et quoniam viro suo (ut videtur) relicto, Christum erat secuta.
paras.en: [[20:20|Then came to him the mother of the sons of Zebedee with her sons|Tunc accessit ad eum mater filiorum Zebedæi cum filiis suis]] James and John, [[20:20|adoring|adorans]] Him, either with the adoration of latria, if she believed Him to be true God, or with the adoration of dulia, or great reverence [latria is the worship due to God alone; dulia the honour paid to creatures], prostrating herself before Him; [[20:20|and asking something of him|et petens aliquid ab eo]], which she did not express at once, but by her adoring hinted that she desired something. It is written in Mark that the sons themselves came to Jesus, saying: [[Mark 10:35|Master, we desire that whatsoever we shall ask, thou wouldst do it for us|Magister, volumus ut quodcumque petierimus facias nobis]]. Yet the mother framed and put forward the petition; but the sons are written to have done it, because they led their mother to it, thinking that Christ would honour and hear her as His mother's sister, and because she had followed Christ, having (it seems) left her husband.

paras.t: Dicit ei Jesus: Quid vis? Non ex ignorantia quærit, sed ut ad ejus verba congruenter respondeat, errantesque instruat. Ait illi: Dic, id est, dicendo concede et fac: tuum enim dixisse, fecisse est. Quamvis mulier ista nondum intellexit profunditatem verbi hujus, Dic; tamen quoad hoc subtiliter dixit, Dic: ipse enim cui hoc dixit, est de quo scriptum est, Ipse dixit, et facta sunt. Ut sedeant hi duo filii mei, unus ad dexteram tuam, et alius ad sinistram, id est, tibi collaterales et singulariter assidentes, ceterisque majores consistant, in regno tuo.
paras.en: [[20:21|Who said to her: What wilt thou|Dicit ei Jesus: Quid vis]]? He does not ask out of ignorance, but so as to answer her words fittingly and to instruct those in error. [[20:21|She saith to him: say|Ait illi: Dic]], that is, by saying it grant it and do it; for with You to have said is to have done. Though this woman did not yet understand the depth of this word "Say", yet in this respect she said it shrewdly, for He to whom she said it is the one of whom it is written: [[Ps 32:9|he spoke and they were made|Ipse dixit, et facta sunt]][[Ps 148:5||]]. [[20:21|that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left|Ut sedeant hi duo filii mei, unus ad dexteram tuam, et alius ad sinistram]], that is, may be at Your side and sit beside You alone, and be greater than the rest, [[20:21|in thy kingdom|in regno tuo]].

paras.t: Quidam dicunt, quod mulier ista et filii ejus petierunt cum Christo regnare in sæculo isto, putantes Christum post resurrectionem statim in hoc mundo et in Jerusalem regnaturum, quemadmodum David et Salomon illic regnasse leguntur. Hæc namque, ut dicunt, fuit Judæorum opinio, quod Christus temporaliter regnaret in Jerusalem, omnia regna subjiciendo Judæis. Sed huic assertioni obviare videtur, quod Christus respondendo subjungit: Sedere ad dexteram meam et sinistram, non est meum dare vobis, sed quibus paratum est a Patre meo. Ex quo patet, quod electis a Deo Patre paratum sit sedere ad dexteram Christi et sinistram, non utique in regno terreno, sed cælesti. Per regnum ergo Christi, intellexerunt mater et filii regnum cælorum: de quo et latro dixit in cruce: Domine, memento mei, dum veneris in regnum tuum. Nam ex quotidiana Christi prædicatione, sciverunt quod non terrenum, sed cæleste regnum promisit fidelibus. Sic quippe exorsus est prædicare: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum. In quo isti duo inordinate exaltari quærebant. Quia enim filii audierunt futuram Christi resurrectionem, credebant quod statim post resurrectionem regnaret: et hoc matri suæ intimaverunt, quod tamen a Christo in secreto audierunt.
paras.en: Some say that this woman and her sons asked to reign with Christ in this world, thinking that after the resurrection Christ would at once reign in this world and in Jerusalem, as David and Solomon are read to have reigned there[[2 Kings 5:5||]][[3 Kings 11:42||]]. For this, they say, was the opinion of the Jews: that Christ would reign temporally in Jerusalem, subjecting all kingdoms to the Jews. But against this assertion seems to be what Christ adds in answer: [[20:23|to sit on my right or left hand is not mine to give to you, but to them for whom it is prepared by my Father|Sedere ad dexteram meam et sinistram, non est meum dare vobis, sed quibus paratum est a Patre meo]]. From this it is clear that it is prepared for the elect by God the Father to sit at Christ's right and left, not indeed in an earthly kingdom but in the heavenly one. By the kingdom of Christ, then, the mother and sons understood the kingdom of heaven, of which the thief also said on the cross: [[Luke 23:42|Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom|Domine, memento mei, dum veneris in regnum tuum]]. For from Christ's daily preaching they knew that He promised the faithful not an earthly but a heavenly kingdom. For thus He began to preach: [[Matt 4:17|Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum]]. In this kingdom these two sought to be exalted inordinately. For because the sons had heard of Christ's coming resurrection, they believed He would reign at once after it; and they told this to their mother, though they had heard it from Christ in secret.

paras.t: Respondens autem Jesus, dixit, non matri, sed filiis: per quod ostenditur, quod mater petivit, inducta a filiis. Nescitis quid petatis, id est, quid vel quomodo petere debeatis. Petitio siquidem ista fuit multipliciter inordinata: Primo, quoniam petierunt coronam ante victoriam. Secundo, quia de carnali propinquitate confidebant. Tertio, quia ex quadam præsumptione et elatione petiisse videntur, optantes coapostolis anteferri, et volentes summi esse in gloria, qui nondum prioribus Sanctis similes erant in merito. Quantum ad hoc tenebant typum eorum qui a magnis prælatis ad ecclesiasticas dignitates postulant propter consanguinitatis lineam promoveri. Potestis bibere calicem, id est sustinere cruciatum, quem ego bibiturus sum? De quo in passione habetur: Si non potest hic calix transire nisi bibam illum, fiat voluntas tua. Dicunt ei: Possumus calicem istum potare, hoc est, pro fide, pro justitia, pro te mori parati sumus. Hoc dixerunt potius ex aviditate obtinendi quod postulaverunt, quam ex vera circumspectione: imo incaute responderunt, quia in Christi passione, instante periculo, fugerunt. Itaque dicendo tam absolute, Possumus, propriam fragilitatem non pensaverunt: sicut nec Petrus dicendo, Paratus sum tecum in mortem et in carcerem ire. Non enim sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis. Si autem dixissent, Possumus per gratiam tuam, tute dixissent: quomodo dixerat Paulus, Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat.
paras.en: [[20:22|And Jesus answering, said|Respondens autem Jesus, dixit]], not to the mother but to the sons: by which it is shown that the mother asked at the sons' prompting. [[20:22|You know not what you ask|Nescitis quid petatis]], that is, what or how you ought to ask. For this petition was disordered in many ways. First, because they asked for the crown before the victory. Secondly, because they trusted in kinship according to the flesh. Thirdly, because they seem to have asked out of a certain presumption and pride, wishing to be put before their fellow Apostles and to be highest in glory, though they were not yet like the earlier Saints in merit. In this they bore the type of those who ask great prelates to be promoted to ecclesiastical dignities on account of their line of kinship. [[20:22|Can you drink the chalice that I shall drink|Potestis bibere calicem, quem ego bibiturus sum?]], that is, endure the torment? Of which it is said in the Passion: [[Matt 26:42|if this chalice may not pass away, but I must drink it, thy will be done|Si non potest hic calix transire nisi bibam illum, fiat voluntas tua]]. [[20:22|They say to him: We can|Dicunt ei: Possumus]] drink this chalice, that is, we are ready to die for the faith, for justice, for You. They said this rather from eagerness to obtain what they asked than from true circumspection; indeed they answered rashly, for in Christ's Passion, when the danger was upon them, they fled[[Matt 26:56||]]. So in saying so absolutely, We can, they did not weigh their own frailty; nor did Peter in saying: [[Luke 22:33|I am ready to go with thee, both into prison and to death|Paratus sum tecum in mortem et in carcerem ire]]. For, as the Apostle says, [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves|Non enim sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis]]. But if they had said, We can by Your grace, they would have spoken safely, as Paul had said: [[Phil 4:13|I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me|Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat]].

paras.t: Ait illis: Calicem quidem meum bibetis, id est, passionem meæ passioni aliqualiter similem, et propter me infligendam, gustabitis. Joannes enim affectu sustinuit mortem pro Christo, ferventis olei dolium ingrediendo, pessimumque venenum potando: a quorum utroque mansit illæsus. Quotidianum quoque martyrium passus est, præsertim in exsilio insulæ Patmos. Jacobus vero ab Herode Agrippa decollatus est, ut in Actibus Apostolorum legitur.
paras.en: [[20:23|He saith to them: My chalice indeed you shall drink|Ait illis: Calicem quidem meum bibetis]], that is, you will taste a passion in some way like My Passion, and inflicted for My sake. For John suffered death for Christ in will, by entering a vat of boiling oil and drinking a most deadly poison, from both of which he remained unharmed. He also suffered a daily martyrdom, especially in his exile on the island of Patmos[[Apoc 1:9||]]. And James was beheaded by Herod Agrippa, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 12:2||]].

paras.t: Sedere autem ad dexteram meam et sinistram, id est mihi collateralem et proximum esse in cælo, non est meum, hoc est, non spectat ad me justum judicem, qui personam non accipio, sed secundum merita reddo, dare vobis, sed illis quibus paratum est a Patre meo. Et utique a Patre paratum fuit Jacobo et Joanni præmium istud, præsertim quum regnum cælorum ab origine mundi paratum est prædestinatis, juxta illud: Venite, benedicti Patris mei, etc. Quomodo ergo non fuit Christi dare Jacobo et Joanni sessionem prædictam? Et respondendum, quod non fuit Christi dare eam illis, eo modo quo ipsam petebant, videlicet ratione consanguinitatis, et secundum statum in quo tunc fuerunt, quando adhuc carnales et ambitiosi fuerunt. Puto tamen, quod erant in statu salutis, quia non quilibet motus elationis est peccatum mortale; sed non erant tantæ perfectionis, ut digni essent sedere tam proxime Christo. Ideo subditur: Sed quibus paratum est a Patre meo, hoc est perfectis vere humilibus, quibus Pater decrevit gloriam esse præstandam: illis, inquam, est meum dare, ut sedeant ad dexteram meam et sinistram in regno, id est in circuitu meo, in præmio essentiali et accidentali.
paras.en: [[20:23|but to sit on my right or left hand|Sedere autem ad dexteram meam et sinistram]], that is, to be at My side and nearest to Me in heaven, [[20:23|is not mine|non est meum]], that is, it does not belong to Me, the just Judge, who am no respecter of persons but render according to merits, [[20:23|to give to you, but to them for whom it is prepared by my Father|dare vobis, sed illis quibus paratum est a Patre meo]]. And surely this reward was prepared by the Father for James and John, especially since the kingdom of heaven has been prepared from the beginning of the world for the predestined, according to that saying: [[Matt 25:34|Come, ye blessed of my Father|Venite, benedicti Patris mei]], etc. How then was it not Christ's to give James and John the seat in question? The answer is that it was not His to give it to them in the way they asked for it, namely by reason of kinship, and according to the state they were then in, when they were still carnal and ambitious. Yet I think they were in the state of salvation, for not every movement of pride is a mortal sin; but they were not of such perfection as to be worthy to sit so near to Christ. So it is added: [[20:23|but to them for whom it is prepared by my Father|Sed quibus paratum est a Patre meo]], that is, to the perfect who are truly humble, to whom the Father has decreed that glory be given: to them, I say, it is Mine to give that they sit at My right and left in the kingdom, that is, around Me, in essential and accidental reward [the essential reward is the vision of God itself; the accidental, the further joys added to it].

paras.t: Et audientes decem Apostoli quid isti duo petissent, indignati sunt de duobus fratribus, hoc est, econtra eos commoti sunt, quod sibi præferri rogassent, et tam immoderate petissent. Unde patet, quod decem quoque discipuli adhuc similes erant istis duobus in imperfectionibus multis: non enim zelo justitiæ, sed cujusdam livoris, indignati fuerunt, more ambitiosorum qui irascuntur dum cernunt socios suos sibi velle præponi, quum tamen in regno cælorum promotio unius non noceat alteri, nec ejus exaltationem impediat.
paras.en: [[20:24|And the ten, hearing it|Et audientes decem]], the ten Apostles, hearing what these two had asked, [[20:24|were moved with indignation against the two brethren|indignati sunt de duobus fratribus]], that is, were stirred against them, because they had asked to be put before them and had asked so immoderately. From this it is clear that the ten disciples too were still like these two in many imperfections: for they were indignant not from zeal for justice but from a kind of envy, in the manner of ambitious men who are angry when they see their companions wishing to be set over them; whereas in the kingdom of heaven the promotion of one does no harm to another, nor hinders his exaltation.

paras.t: Jesus autem, tanquam pius sapiensque magister et sobrius reprehensor, vocavit eos, videlicet omnes Apostolos pariter, ad se, ut vitium elationis ab eorum cordibus propulsaret, et errorem corrigeret; et ait: Scitis quia principes gentium dominantur eorum, id est, majores seu domini hominum mundanorum, cum imperio et tumore præsident subditis suis, et qui majores sunt, videlicet dominatores subditorum, potestatem exercent in eos, id est, per violentiam quandoque opprimunt ipsos, et sua potestate inordinate utuntur. Non ita erit inter vos tumor elationis, violentia, sive ambitio. Sed quicumque voluerit inter vos major fieri, id est ampliorem gratiam et gloriam adipisci, sit vester minister, id est, præ ceteris se humiliet, atque in actibus humilitatis se ipsum indesinenter exerceat. Quanto enim aliquis se sub alio dejicit, tanto Deus eum exaltat. Et qui voluerit inter vos primus esse, id est aliis præfici, et a me sublimius promoveri, erit vester servus. Hoc, ut arbitror, intelligi potest dupliciter: primo, quod ambitiosus ceteris supponetur et subjicietur; secundo, quod is qui licet prælationem non cupiat, tamen cupit esse talis ut dignus sit aliis præsidere, oportet ut primo discat subesse, studeatque sociis suis servire.
paras.en: [[20:25|But Jesus called them to him|Jesus autem vocavit eos ad se]], as a kind and wise master and a sober corrector, calling them, namely all the Apostles alike, to drive the vice of pride from their hearts and to correct their error; [[20:25|and said: You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them|et ait: Scitis quia principes gentium dominantur eorum]], that is, the great men or lords of worldly men rule their subjects with command and swelling pride; [[20:25|and that they that are the greater|et qui majores sunt]], namely the lords of subjects, [[20:25|exercise power upon them|potestatem exercent in eos]], that is, at times oppress them by violence and use their power inordinately. [[20:26|It shall not be so among you|Non ita erit inter vos]]: no swelling of pride, violence or ambition. [[20:26|but whosoever is the greater among you|Sed quicumque voluerit inter vos major fieri]] [Denis's text reads "whosoever will be greater"], that is, to gain more grace and glory, [[20:26|let him be your minister|sit vester minister]], that is, let him humble himself before the rest and exercise himself unceasingly in acts of humility. For the more a man casts himself down beneath another, the more God exalts him. [[20:27|And he that will be first among you|Et qui voluerit inter vos primus esse]], that is, to be set over others and promoted higher by Me, [[20:27|shall be your servant|erit vester servus]]. This, as I think, can be understood in two ways: first, that the ambitious man will be put beneath and subjected to the rest; secondly, that one who, though he does not desire prelacy, yet desires to be such as to be worthy to preside over others, must first learn to be subject, and be eager to serve his companions.

paras.t: Et quia exempla plus movent quam verba, Salvator qui cœpit facere et docere, proponit se in exemplum. Sicut Filius hominis non venit ministrari, hoc est ad hoc, quod servos haberet qui ei famularentur in corporalibus et humanis obsequiis, ad instar sæcularium dominorum, sed ministrare. Nam et discipulis suis frequenter ministravit, juxta illud: Ego in medio vestrum sum sicut qui ministrat. Patri quoque indesinenter servivit cum incomparabili humilitate, quemadmodum ait in Evangelio: Sicut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio. Et quum duodecim esset annorum, descendens cum Virgine Matre et Joseph, fuit subditus illis. Nec dubium quin quotidie ministraverit ipsis, tanquam vere humillimus, licet esset Altissimus, cui angelorum exercitus cum ingenti reverentia et tremore adsistit. Et dare animam suam, id est vitam corporalem ac animalem, seu ipsam animam suam, redemptionem, id est pretium liberativum, pro multis hominibus, non pro dæmonibus. Tradidit enim in mortem animam suam, et ipse peccata multorum tulit, ut Isaias ait. Imo se ipsum dedit pro nobis, sponte se offerens. Propter quod ait ore proprio: Nemo tollit animam meam a me; et Apostolus, Qui dilexit me, et tradidit semetipsum pro me.
paras.en: And because examples move more than words, the Saviour, who [[Acts 1:1|began to do and to teach|cœpit facere et docere]], sets Himself forth as an example. [[20:28|Even as the Son of man is not come to be ministered unto|Sicut Filius hominis non venit ministrari]], that is, to have servants who would wait on Him with bodily and human services, after the manner of worldly lords, [[20:28|but to minister|sed ministrare]]. For He often ministered to His disciples, according to that saying: [[Luke 22:27|I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth|Ego in medio vestrum sum sicut qui ministrat]]. He also served the Father unceasingly with incomparable humility, as He says in the Gospel: [[John 14:31|as the Father hath given me commandments, so do I|Sicut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio]]. And when He was twelve years old[[Luke 2:42||]], going down with the Virgin Mother and Joseph, He [[Luke 2:51|was subject to them|fuit subditus illis]]. Nor is there any doubt that He ministered to them daily, as one truly most humble, though He was the Most High, before whom the hosts of angels stand with great reverence and trembling. [[20:28|and to give his life|Et dare animam suam]], that is, His bodily and animal life, or His very soul [anima means both "life" and "soul"], [[20:28|a redemption|redemptionem]], that is, a price that sets free, [[20:28|for many|pro multis]] men, not for demons. For [[Is 53:12|he hath delivered his soul unto death|Tradidit enim in mortem animam suam]], [[Is 53:12|and he hath borne the sins of many|et ipse peccata multorum tulit]], as Isaias says. Indeed He gave Himself for us, offering Himself willingly[[Heb 9:14||]]. Hence He says with His own mouth: [[John 10:18|No man taketh it away from me|Nemo tollit animam meam a me]]; and the Apostle: [[Gal 2:20|who loved me and delivered himself for me|Qui dilexit me, et tradidit semetipsum pro me]].

paras.t: Sed quare non ait, Dare animam suam redemptionem pro omnibus, quum alibi dicat, Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum? Ipse equidem est universorum salvator, dicente Apostolo: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. Et respondendum, quod Christus dedit animam suam redemptionem pro omnibus sufficienter, pro solis autem electis efficienter seu efficaciter. Quoniam ergo non omnes, sed multi, fructum dominicæ passionis consequuntur, ideo ait, Pro multis. Denique, licet Christus dicatur pro nobis dedisse animam suam, et etiam vitam corporalem, hoc tamen est differenter. Nam animam dedit per hoc quod eam tormentis exposuit, non quod ipsa exstincta sit. Vitam vero suam corporalem sic dedit, quod eam pro nostra spirituali vivificatione exstingui permisit: quæ tamen vita, seu vitalis actio, erat incomparabilis dignitatis ac pretii, propter unionem cum Verbo.
paras.en: But why does He not say, to give His life a redemption for all, since elsewhere He says: [[John 12:32|if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself|Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum?]]? For He is indeed the Saviour of all, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:22|And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive.|Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur]]. The answer is that Christ gave His life as a redemption for all sufficiently, but for the elect alone efficiently or effectually. Since, then, not all but many obtain the fruit of the Lord's Passion, He says, for many. Further, though Christ is said to have given for us both His soul and His bodily life, this is in different ways. For He gave His soul by exposing it to torments, not in that it was extinguished; but He gave His bodily life in such a way that He allowed it to be extinguished for our spiritual quickening: a life, or vital activity, that was nonetheless of incomparable dignity and price because of its union with the Word.

paras.t: Et egredientibus illis, videlicet Jesu ejusque discipulis, ab Jericho, civitate famosa, secutæ sunt eum turbæ multæ, propter causas diversas, ut dictum est sæpius; etiam quia desertum quod erat inter Jericho et Jerusalem, per quod Jesus pergebat, erat latronibus plenum: propter quod homines illuc tendere non audebant, nisi cœtu collecto.
paras.en: [[20:29|And when they went out from Jericho|Et egredientibus illis ab Jericho]], namely Jesus and His disciples, from Jericho, a famous city, [[20:29|a great multitude followed him|secutæ sunt eum turbæ multæ]], for various reasons, as has often been said; and also because the desert between Jericho and Jerusalem, through which Jesus was going, was full of robbers, so that men did not dare to go there except in a company.

paras.t: Et ecce duo cæci sedentes secus viam, ut pergentibus eleemosynas peterent tanquam mendici, audierunt quia Jesus transiret. Audientes enim tumultum, interrogaverunt quid hoc esset: quibus responsum est, quod Jesus illic cum suis perambularet. Et clamaverunt, ex magnitudine desiderii in altam vocem prorumpentes. Clamabant ergo, corde ferventer optando, et ore alte sonando. Domine, miserere nostri, o fili David. Credebant cæci isti verum esse, quod a populo interdum audierunt, videlicet, quod Jesus esset rex Messias in lege promissus, et de semine David nasciturus prænuntiatus: ideo nominabant eum Dominum, tanquam regem Israel. Et aliqui dicunt, quod ejus divinitatem agnoverant: quod non est multum probabile. Turba autem increpabat eos ut tacerent, vel quia multum importune clamabant, vel quia Jesum offendi timebant et inquietari ex clamore eorum, vel quia clamando impedierunt multos ab auditu sermocinationum Christi, qui etiam ambulando docebat frequenter. At illi magis clamabant, formidantes ne propter strepitum increpantium, non audiretur clamor eorum a Christo; dicentes: Domine, miserere nostri, fili David. Per laudem ejus qui oratur, capitur benevolentia ejus. Ideo isti orando Jesum, laudant eum a majestate, quum dicunt, Domine; et ab origine, quum dicunt, Fili David: sicque facilius exaudiri merentur. Unde Psalmista: Laudans, inquit, invocabo Dominum, et ab inimicis meis salvus ero.
paras.en: [[20:30|And behold two blind men sitting by the way side|Et ecce duo cæci sedentes secus viam]], to beg alms of the passers-by as beggars, [[20:30|heard that Jesus passed by|audierunt quia Jesus transiret]]. For hearing the noise, they asked what it was, and were answered that Jesus was passing that way with His followers. [[20:30|And they cried out|Et clamaverunt]], breaking out in a loud voice from the greatness of their desire: they cried, then, longing fervently in heart and sounding loudly with the mouth: [[20:30|O Lord, thou son of David, have mercy on us|Domine, miserere nostri, o fili David]]. These blind men believed to be true what they had heard at times from the people, namely that Jesus was the King Messias promised in the Law, and foretold to be born of the seed of David; so they called Him Lord, as King of Israel. Some say they had recognized His Godhead, but this is not very probable. [[20:31|And the multitude rebuked them that they should hold their peace|Turba autem increpabat eos ut tacerent]], either because they cried out very importunately, or because they feared Jesus would be annoyed and disturbed by their crying, or because by crying they kept many from hearing Christ's discourses, for He often taught even as He walked. [[20:31|But they cried out the more, saying|At illi magis clamabant, dicentes]], afraid that because of the noise of those rebuking them their cry would not be heard by Christ: [[20:31|O Lord, thou son of David, have mercy on us|Domine, miserere nostri, fili David]]. By praise of the one prayed to, his goodwill is won. So these men, in praying to Jesus, praise Him for His majesty when they say, Lord, and for His origin when they say, Son of David; and so they deserve to be heard more readily. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 17:4|Praising, I will call upon the Lord: and I shall be saved from my enemies.|Laudans, inquit, invocabo Dominum, et ab inimicis meis salvus ero]].

paras.t: Et stetit Jesus, et vocavit eos. In quo manifestatur pietas atque dignatio Christi, qui personas tam modicas non despexit. Et ait: Quid vultis ut faciam vobis? Non ignorans inquirit, sed ut quærendo, illorum desiderium augeretur, oratio repeteretur, meritum cresceret, omnesque scirent quod non eleemosynam, sed naturæ reparationem implorassent. Dicunt ei: Domine, hoc volumus, ut aperiantur oculi nostri carnales, et visum recipiant. Misertus autem eorum Jesus, tetigit oculos eorum, ut ostenderet quod virtus divina in ipso consistens ac latens, operabatur per corpus suum sicut per instrumentum animatum, conjunctum ac proprium, sicut et anima nostra operatur per corpus cui unita est. Et confestim viderunt, et secuti sunt eum, non solum gressibus corporis, sed imitatione virtutis, tanquam spiritualiter illuminati a Christo, et grati beneficio ejus. Christus namque mente sanavit atque illustravit, quos corporaliter reparavit. Ipsius nempe perfecta sunt opera; et totum hominem salvum fecit in sabbato. Quæritur, cur Matthæus referat de duobus cæcis, quum Marcus non scribat nisi de uno. Respondet Augustinus quod ideo, quoniam unus eorum famosior fuit, et forte importunius exclamavit: quem Marcus Bartimæum, id est filium Timæi, appellat.
paras.en: [[20:32|And Jesus stood and called them|Et stetit Jesus, et vocavit eos]]. In this is shown the kindness and condescension of Christ, who did not despise persons so lowly. [[20:32|and said: What will ye that I do to you|Et ait: Quid vultis ut faciam vobis?]]? He does not ask in ignorance, but so that by His asking their desire might be increased, their prayer repeated, their merit grow, and all might know that they had begged not for alms but for the restoring of nature. [[20:33|They say to him: Lord|Dicunt ei: Domine]], this we will, [[20:33|that our eyes be opened|ut aperiantur oculi nostri]], our bodily eyes, and receive their sight. [[20:34|And Jesus having compassion on them, touched their eyes|Misertus autem eorum Jesus, tetigit oculos eorum]], to show that the divine power that dwelt hidden in Him worked through His body as through a living instrument, joined to Him and His own, as our soul too works through the body to which it is united. [[20:34|And immediately they saw and followed him|Et confestim viderunt, et secuti sunt eum]], not only with the steps of the body but by imitation of virtue, as men spiritually enlightened by Christ and grateful for His benefit. For those whom Christ restored in body He healed and enlightened in mind. For [[Deut 32:4|The works of God are perfect|Ipsius nempe perfecta sunt opera]]; and [[John 7:23|I have healed the whole man on the sabbath day|totum hominem salvum fecit in sabbato]] [Denis: "he healed the whole man"]. It is asked why Matthew tells of two blind men, whereas Mark writes only of one[[Mark 10:46||]]. Augustine answers that it is because one of them was better known, and perhaps cried out more importunately: the one whom Mark calls Bartimeus, that is, the son of Timeus.

paras.t: Iterum quæritur, an cæcus de quo Lucas scribit, sit idem de quo recitat Marcus, unusque istorum duorum. Ad hoc aliqui dicunt quod non. Nam apud Lucam legitur solum: Quum appropinquaret Jericho, cæcus quidam sedebat secus viam. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod ille cæcus fuerit illuminatus ante introitum Jericho. Porro Marcus refert: Proficiscente eo de Jericho; similiter hic, Egredientibus illis ab Jericho. Per quod ostenditur, quod cæcus iste sit sanatus post egressum ex Jericho. Alii asserunt quod fuit idem cæcus, quia historia de utroque omnino concordat, ut patet litteram intuenti, excepto verbo prædicto, quod isti ita exponunt: Quum appropinquaret Jericho, id est, adhuc prope esset huic civitati. Potest etiam dici, quod Lucas non servat in omnibus ordinem rei gestæ: et ita, quamvis Christo accedente ad Jericho, cæcus sedebat prope viam, non tamen a Christo vocatus sanatusque fuit, nisi post egressionem a Jericho. Juxta spiritualem intelligentiam, per clamorem horum cæcorum, figuratur clamor utriusque populi Judæorum et gentilium ad Salvatorem, quum audissent quod in terris visus, et cum hominibus conversatus fuisset. Turba vero, videlicet obstinati et infideles, increpabant eos, sed illi occidi malebant, quam ab invocatione Christi cessare. Imo beatissimi martyres tanto validius atque frequentius clamaverunt ad Christum, quo amplius a tyrannis et eorum satellitibus prohibebantur. Quorum vestigia sequi debemus, orantes jugiter cum Propheta: Illumina oculos meos, ne unquam obdormiam in morte.
paras.en: It is asked again whether the blind man of whom Luke writes is the same as the one Mark tells of, and one of these two. Some say not. For in Luke it reads only: [[Luke 18:35|when he drew nigh to Jericho, that a certain blind man sat by the way side|Quum appropinquaret Jericho, cæcus quidam sedebat secus viam]]. From which it seems to follow that that blind man was given sight before the entry into Jericho. But Mark relates: [[Mark 10:46|as he went out of Jericho|Proficiscente eo de Jericho]]; and likewise here: [[20:29|when they went out from Jericho|Egredientibus illis ab Jericho]]; by which it is shown that this blind man was healed after the going out from Jericho. Others assert that it was the same blind man, because the story agrees entirely in both, as is plain to one who looks at the letter, apart from the word just mentioned, which they expound thus: when he drew nigh to Jericho, that is, while He was still near this city. It can also be said that Luke does not keep the order of events in everything: and so, though the blind man was sitting near the way as Christ was approaching Jericho, he was not called and healed by Christ until after the going out from Jericho. In the spiritual sense, the cry of these blind men figures the cry of both peoples, Jews and Gentiles, to the Saviour, when they had heard that He [[Bar 3:38|was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|in terris visus, et cum hominibus conversatus fuisset]]. The crowd, namely the obstinate and unbelieving, rebuked them; but they would rather be killed than cease calling upon Christ. Indeed the most blessed martyrs cried to Christ the more strongly and often, the more they were forbidden by tyrants and their henchmen. We ought to follow in their footsteps, praying continually with the Prophet: [[Ps 12:4|Enlighten my eyes, that I never sleep in death|Illumina oculos meos, ne unquam obdormiam in morte]].

21.title: Elucidatio capituli vicesimi primi: Et quum appropinquasset Jerosolymis, et venisset Bethphage
21.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-first chapter: And when they drew nigh to Jerusalem and were come to Bethphage

paras.t: Et quum appropinquasset Jesus Jerosolymis, et venisset Bethphage, id est ad villam quamdam sacerdotum, ad montem Oliveti, in quo olivarum copia crevit: juxta cujus pedem seu latus sita fuit hæc villa, uno (ut dicitur) milliario a Jerusalem distans. Tunc Jesus misit duos discipulos. Dicunt aliqui, quod secundum Chrysostomum, isti discipuli fuerunt Petrus et Philippus. Sed hoc Chrysostomus non affirmat; sed in commento cujusdam se legisse commemorat. Misit autem duos, propter socialis vitæ commendationem, et ad ostendendum quod per duplicem vitam, videlicet activam et contemplativam, vel per scientiam et operationem, ad ipsum pertingitur. Ista historia facta est in die Palmarum, altero die postquam Jesus cœnavit in domo Simonis leprosi in Bethania, quando Lazarus fuit unus discumbentium, et Maria Magdalene accepit libram unguenti, effundens super pedes ipsius.
paras.en: [[21:1|And when they drew nigh to Jerusalem|Et quum appropinquasset Jesus Jerosolymis]] (when Jesus drew nigh) [[21:1|and were come to Bethphage|et venisset Bethphage]], that is, to a certain village of the priests, [[21:1|unto mount Olivet|ad montem Oliveti]], on which olives grew in plenty; this village lay at its foot or side, one mile (as is said) from Jerusalem. [[21:1|then Jesus sent two disciples|Tunc Jesus misit duos discipulos]]. Some say that according to Chrysostom these disciples were Peter and Philip. But Chrysostom does not affirm this; he says he read it in someone's commentary. He sent two to commend the life of fellowship, and to show that He is reached by a twofold life, the active and the contemplative, or by knowledge and work. This story took place on Palm Sunday, the day after Jesus supped in the house of Simon the leper in Bethania, when Lazarus was one of those at table, and Mary Magdalene took a pound of ointment and poured it on His feet[[Matt 26:6||]][[Matt 26:7||]][[John 12:1||]][[John 12:2||]][[John 12:3||]].

paras.t: Dicens eis: Ite in castellum quod contra vos est. Communiter per castellum intelligitur urbs ipsa Jerusalem, vel propter fortitudinem murorum, quibus circumdata fuit per modum castelli, vel despective, propter discordiam atque invidiam habitantium in ea, et quia alienigenis seu Romanis erat subjecta. Videtur autem per castellum posse intelligi aliqua domus lapidea eminens, forte muro propinqua: in qua vel juxta quam, asina fuit. Itaque, Ite in castellum quod contra vos, id est, ex opposito vestro est. Sic ait Psalmista: In die tribulationis meæ Deum exquisivi, manibus meis nocte contra eum. Et apud Marcum ait Salvator: Transeamus contra. Vel, Contra vos est, hoc est, contrariatur, quorum magistrum ac Dominum necare molitur. Et statim invenietis asinam alligatam præsepio vel alteri rei, ne vaganda discurrat, et pullum ejus cum ea. Hæc asina deputata fuit ad pauperum usum, et ad hunc usum pullus ejus nutriebatur. Solvite asinam, et adducite mihi eam cum pullo suo. In evangelio Lucæ legitur dixisse: Invenietis pullum asinæ alligatum. Cui Marcus concordat. Asina ergo et pullus ligati erant, et utrumque jussit Christus solvi, et sibi adduci. Invenerunt autem discipuli animalia ista foris in bivio juxta Jerusalem, ut dicit Marcus.
paras.en: [[21:2|Saying to them: Go ye into the village that is over against you|Dicens eis: Ite in castellum quod contra vos est]] [castellum: literally "stronghold" or "walled town"; the Douay-Rheims has "village"]. By the castellum is commonly understood the city of Jerusalem itself, either because of the strength of the walls with which it was surrounded like a fortress, or contemptuously, because of the discord and envy of those who lived in it, and because it was subject to foreigners, the Romans. But it seems that the castellum can be understood as some prominent stone house, perhaps near the wall, in or beside which the ass was. So: Go into the castellum that is over against you, that is, opposite you. So the Psalmist says: [[Ps 76:3|In the days of my trouble I sought God, with my hands lifted up to him in the night|In die tribulationis meæ Deum exquisivi, manibus meis nocte contra eum]] [the Latin is literally "with my hands by night over against him"]. And in Mark the Saviour says: [[Mark 4:35|Let us pass over to the other side|Transeamus contra]]. Or: is over against you, that is, is hostile to you, since it is plotting to kill your Master and Lord. [[21:2|and immediately you shall find an ass tied|Et statim invenietis asinam alligatam]] to a manger or something else, so that it should not stray off, [[21:2|and a colt with her|et pullum ejus cum ea]]. This ass was set apart for the use of the poor, and her colt was reared for the same use. [[21:2|Loose them and bring them to me|Solvite asinam, et adducite mihi]] [Denis reads "Loose the ass and bring her to me with her colt"]. In the Gospel of Luke He is read to have said: [[Luke 19:30|you shall find the colt of an ass tied|Invenietis pullum asinæ alligatum]]; and Mark agrees with him[[Mark 11:2||]]. Both the ass and the colt, then, were tied, and Christ ordered both to be loosed and brought to Him. The disciples found these animals outside, at a meeting of two ways near Jerusalem, as Mark says[[Mark 11:4||]].

paras.t: Et si quis vobis aliquid dixerit, interrogando cur animalia ista solvatis, dicite ei quia Dominus rex Messias, his, scilicet asino et pullo, opus habet, non necessitate absoluta sive coacta, sed conditionata atque spontanea, videlicet ad verificandum vaticinium Zachariæ, et ad nostram informationem; et confestim dimittet eos solvi et mihi adduci.
paras.en: [[21:3|And if any man shall say anything to you|Et si quis vobis aliquid dixerit]], asking why you are loosing these animals, [[21:3|say ye that the Lord hath need of them|dicite … quia Dominus … opus habet]], the Lord, the King Messias, has need of them, the ass and the colt: not by an absolute or compelled necessity but by a conditional and voluntary one, namely to make the prophecy of Zachary come true[[Zach 9:9||]], and for our instruction; [[21:3|And forthwith he will let them go|et confestim dimittet eos]] to be loosed and brought to Me.

paras.t: Quæritur, quid isti custodes seu domini asinæ et pulli (qui secundum Lucam et Marcum dixerunt discipulis, cur solverent pullum) intellexerunt per Dominum, quando discipuli responderunt: Dominus operam ejus desiderat. Ad quod dicendum opinor, quod Apostoli Christi, ex habitu, vel aliis signis, facile agnoscebantur esse discipuli Jesu. De Jesu quoque tunc rumor fuit, quod ipse esset Christus: idcirco custodes cognoscentes quod isti essent discipuli Jesu, per Dominum intellexerunt Jesum. Chrysostomus vero respondet, quod virtus Christi movit corda custodum, ita quod nomine Domini audito, contradicere non audebant. Sed cur humilis Jesus se ipsum tam sublimi nomine exprimit, quod Deo est proprium (sicut per Isaiam testatur: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum; de quo scriptum est in Amos: Faciens Arcturum et Orionem, Dominus nomen ejus)? Dicendum, quod Christus hoc die voluit majestatem suam verbis et factis suis ac aliorum, multipliciter declarare, sicut patebit. Unde et alibi ait: Dominus est Filius hominis etiam sabbati.
paras.en: It is asked what these keepers or owners of the ass and colt (who, according to Luke and Mark, asked the disciples why they were loosing the colt[[Luke 19:33||]][[Mark 11:5||]]) understood by "the Lord" when the disciples answered: The Lord needs its service. To this I think it must be said that Christ's Apostles were easily recognized as Jesus' disciples by their dress or other signs; and there was a rumour then about Jesus that He was the Christ: so the keepers, knowing that these were Jesus' disciples, understood Jesus by "the Lord". But Chrysostom answers that the power of Christ moved the keepers' hearts, so that on hearing the name of the Lord they did not dare to refuse. But why does the humble Jesus speak of Himself by so lofty a name, which belongs to God (as He testifies through Isaias: [[Is 42:8|I the Lord, this is my name|Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum]]; and of whom it is written in Amos: [[Amos 5:8|that maketh Arcturus, and Orion|Faciens Arcturum et Orionem]] … [[Amos 5:8|The Lord is his name|Dominus nomen ejus]])? It must be said that on this day Christ willed to declare His majesty in many ways, by His own words and deeds and those of others, as will appear. Hence elsewhere too He says: [[Matt 12:8|the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath|Dominus est Filius hominis etiam sabbati]].

paras.t: Hoc autem totum, videlicet, quod discipulos misit, et asinam ejusque pullum solvi et sibi adduci præcepit, factum est, ut adimpleretur quod dictum est per Prophetam Zachariam, dicentem: Dicite filiæ Sion, hoc est plebi Jerusalem: quæ plebs dicitur filia, propter paternum affectum Dei ad eam. Unde in Prophetis sæpissime nomine filiæ, congregatio populi designatur. Sion vero fuit mons in quo erat templum Dei atque palatium regis: propter quod nomine Sion, civitas tota significatur, tanquam a parte principali. Ecce rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus, id est mitis et humilis, non cum terribili apparatu aut animo bellicoso, ut moris est regum mundanorum, sedens successive super asinam, deinde et super pullum filium subjugalis, id est asinæ, quæ fuit assueta portare jugum atque sessores; super pullum vero usque ad illam horam nemo ascendit, secundum Lucam et Marcum, sed Christus primo sedit super eum. Ratio horum infra tangetur. Ex hac prophetia debuissent Scribæ et sacerdotes merito Christum cognovisse. Ex qua etiam apertissime declaratur, quod primum Christi adventum descripserunt Prophetæ in paupertate et humilitate, non in regno temporali, secundum quod Christus dixit coram Pilato: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Denique prædicta Zachariæ prophetia in nostra translatione plenius continetur, hoc modo: Exsulta satis, filia Sion; jubila, filia Jerusalem: ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus et salvator; ipse pauper, et ascendens super asinam, et super pullum filium asinæ.
paras.en: [[21:4|Now all this was done|Hoc autem totum factum est]], namely His sending the disciples and ordering the ass and her colt to be loosed and brought to Him, [[21:4|that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying|ut adimpleretur quod dictum est per Prophetam Zachariam, dicentem]], by the prophet Zachary: [[21:5|Tell ye the daughter of Sion|Dicite filiæ Sion]], that is, the people of Jerusalem, a people called a daughter because of God's fatherly love for it; hence in the Prophets the gathering of the people is very often signified by the name of daughter. Sion was the mount on which stood the temple of God and the king's palace, so that by the name of Sion the whole city is signified, as by its chief part. [[21:5|Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek|Ecce rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus]], that is, gentle and humble, not with fearful array or warlike spirit, as is the way of worldly kings, [[21:5|and sitting upon an ass|sedens successive super asinam]], sitting on them in turn, first on the ass and then [[21:5|and a colt, the foal of her that is used to the yoke|et super pullum filium subjugalis]], that is, of the ass, who was accustomed to bear the yoke and riders; but on the colt, according to Luke and Mark, no one had ever sat until that hour[[Luke 19:30||]][[Mark 11:2||]], but Christ first sat on it. The reason for these things will be touched on below. From this prophecy the scribes and priests ought rightly to have recognized Christ. From it too it is declared most plainly that the Prophets described Christ's first coming in poverty and humility, not in a temporal kingdom, according to what Christ said before Pilate: [[John 18:36|My kingdom is not of this world|Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo]]. Lastly, this prophecy of Zachary is contained more fully in our translation [the Vulgate], thus: [[Zach 9:9|Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Sion, shout for joy, O daughter of Jerusalem: BEHOLD THY KING will come to thee, the just and saviour: he is poor, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass|Exsulta satis, filia Sion; jubila, filia Jerusalem: ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus et salvator; ipse pauper, et ascendens super asinam, et super pullum filium asinæ]].

paras.t: Euntes autem discipuli, fecerunt sicut præcepit illis Jesus. Et adduxerunt asinam et pullum, et imposuerunt super eos vestimenta sua, ut Jesus mollius honestiusque sederet, et eum desuper sedere fecerunt successive, ut dictum est. Quidam videntur asserere, quod Christus non sedit super utrumque animal. Itaque secundum eos, historia vel impossibilitatem, vel turpitudinem continet: impossibilitatem, quia in tam brevi itineris spatio, super utrumque animal sedere non potuit: turpitudinem, quoniam indecens fuisset ut asinæ sederet. Verumtamen, propter manifestam auctoritatem Scripturæ canonicæ utriusque Testamenti, dicendum videtur sicut nunc dictum est.
